No closed formulas exist for this structured backward error, so the framework is fully numerical and optimization-based. Worked examples show how the numbers behave.
arxiv-2512-05012:
Francielle Vargas and Daniel Pedronette present a method meant to make retrieval-augmented generation more honest about its evidence. These systems fetch passages to ground a language model's answers, but weak ranking can surface opinion or misleading text and invite made-up claims. Their method, called CER, rebuilds the retrieval step around factual support from the start.

CER fine-tunes the text-matching model with contrastive training, pulling passages with solid factual reasoning closer and pushing aside subjective or misleading ones, with the hard cases picked out by a subjectivity test. It also writes word-level notes showing which parts of a passage support the match. Tested on clinical trial reports, the method improved retrieval accuracy, cut the risk of invented answers, and made each result easier to audit. That trait matters most where safety is on the line.
arxiv-2512-05112:
Dongzhi Jiang and eleven co-authors introduce DraCo, a way for multimodal models to plan pictures with pictures. Models that generate images from text often reason first in words, but word plans are coarse, and rare combinations of attributes trip the generators up. DraCo instead lets the model sketch a small draft image as the first step of its reasoning — a concrete preview it can then inspect with its own visual understanding.

The model checks the draft against the request, spots mismatches, and fixes them selectively while enlarging the image. To train this behavior, the team built a large dataset targeting three skills: correcting errors, manipulating individual objects, and reorganizing layouts, together with a guidance strategy tuned for interleaved reasoning. DraCo posts large gains on standard generation benchmarks over direct generation and over text-only reasoning approaches, showing that a draft can serve as a chain of thought for images.
arxiv-2512-05312:
Charles Curry and Dominique Manchon prove a sewing lemma for families of metric spaces, generalizing a tool that has become central to the modern theory of rough paths. Sewing lemmas say when local, approximately consistent pieces can be stitched into a single global object — the licence that lets analysts build paths and flows from infinitesimal data. Bailleul proved a flow version in 2015; this work places it in a far broader frame.

The families here are indexed not by time alone but, in the generalization, by other parameter spaces as well. The stitches produce a representation of the groupoid formed by thin-equivalent Lipschitz paths over that parameter space. Under a stronger hypothesis the authors prove a two-dimensional analogue, the knitting lemma, which yields a representation of the Lipschitz homotopy groupoid with no thinness condition at all. The pair of results extends the sewing philosophy from lines to surfaces.
arxiv-2512-05412:
Yida Lin and four co-authors combine a real-time object detector with classical stereo vision to let drones find and measure pine branches for autonomous pruning. Manual pruning of radiata pine is dangerous work at heights on difficult terrain, and automating it needs machines that can spot a branch and judge its distance using cheap sensors. Their framework pairs YOLO detection with semi-global block matching stereo, dispensing with expensive lidar.

In evaluation, YOLO out-segmented the Mask R-CNN alternative on branch masks. The integrated system localized branches accurately within its two-metre working range and processed each frame in under a second. The authors conclude that a camera-only setup is already feasible for cost-effective autonomous pruning. It brings direct benefits for worker safety and efficiency in commercial forestry. The paper is a companion piece to the group's work on tuning the same stereo pipeline.
arxiv-2512-05912:
Snorre Christiansen and Francesca Rapetti reinterpret a numerical method for partial differential equations, and in doing so strengthen what is known about it. The Discrete de Rham method builds discrete versions of the calculus of differential forms, the language of electromagnetism and fluid flow. The authors show it secretly defines a computable, consistent inner product on a conforming finite element system.

From it, conformity and consistency properties follow that are stronger than those previously proved, even in low dimensions. Other known results about the method can then be recovered from theorems already established for finite element systems in general, in principle importing a whole literature for free. The virtual element method enters the same discussion. Finding the right frame for a method can be a result in itself.
arxiv-2512-06512:
James Binney, Thomas Wright, and Eugene Vasiliev release code that computes orbital tori for galaxies, a tool for reading how stars move. A torus here is a surface in phase space that one orbit traces out, and action based models of galaxies are built from such surfaces. Their code extends the AGAMA galaxy modeling package as the AGAMAb library, mostly usable from Python despite a C++ core.

The new generator handles orbits from near circular to wildly stretched, beyond the reach of the older torus code, and fills gaps between tori by cheap interpolation. Added functions help users face models against real data, with sky positions, distances, and dust dimming handled. An action finder in the package also serves as an orbit integrator, more accurate if slower than the usual shortcut. The team shows it building cheap models of tidal streams, and uses it on the GD1 stream.
arxiv-2512-06612:
Kazuya Nishimura and four co authors rethink how to read gene activity from images of tissue. In spatial transcriptomics, a slide of tissue is paired with measures of which genes are active at each spot. Reading those levels from the pathology image alone would cut the cost of sequencing. But the measured levels carry noise and batch effects from the lab process. Matching their exact values is a losing game.

The authors aim lower and smarter: learn the relative pattern of expression between genes, which they argue stays steady across experiments even when absolute levels wobble. Their loss function, STRank, grades a model on getting those relative trends right. On synthetic and real data sets, models trained with it beat the usual point by point losses. The work offers a sturdier target for image based estimates of gene activity, one that respects how messy the ground truth really is.
arxiv-2512-06712:
Miriam Locke and three co authors decide where an MRI scanner should sample when the goal is to fit a personal model of a patient's blood flow. Such models of the aorta are tuned from four dimensional flow scans, but full scans are long and taxing. Sparse sampling in the frequency domain, k-space, cuts the scan, yet the choice of which samples to keep, the mask, strongly shapes how well the model's parameters can be recovered.

The authors bring in optimal experimental design, a framework normally used to place sensors in space, and aim it at k-space masks, a first in this setting. Masks chosen by their method consistently beat conventional sampling patterns at recovering the target flow parameters from sparse data. The payoff is shorter, cheaper scans that still carry the information a clinician's model needs, a step toward routine patient specific flow modeling.
arxiv-2512-06812:
Tiago Rodrigues and Carla Teixeira Lopes test whether large language models can draft the summaries doctors write when a patient leaves care. These discharge summaries pull together the key facts of a hospital stay. They matter for safe follow-up care, but writing them eats clinician time and invites error. The authors try five models, from open systems such as Mistral and Llama 2 to closed ones such as GPT-4 and Gemini.

Working from a well-known set of hospital records and notes, the team scores the drafts in several ways, including a check by a clinical expert. The closed models did best, with Gemini strongest when shown a single example first. Open models showed promise after extra training, yet they repeated facts and invented details more often. The authors see real help for busy staff, provided patient privacy stays protected.
arxiv-2512-07012:
Daniele Fargion and co-authors offer an explanation for a strange sight in high-energy astronomy: tails of gamma rays found far from the binary system SS433. That system pairs a black hole with a heavy companion star, which it steadily strips. The pair drives a thin, slowly swirling jet that telescopes know well. Yet gamma-ray tails at huge energies have turned up hundreds of light-years away, disconnected from the jet, puzzling observers.

The authors propose that rare, violent tidal eruptions in the system fire off jets of neutrons at energies far beyond those of the gamma rays themselves. Neutrons, being neutral, fly straight; as some decay in flight or scatter light, they can seed the distant gamma beams. The energies line up if the eruptions smash protons into ultraviolet light inside the system. Rival explanations, the team argues, fit the observations less well.
arxiv-2512-07112:
Ziqing Wen and co-authors slim the hidden memory bill of training large language models. The bill comes less from the model than from the optimizer: Adam, the standard trainer, keeps two extra numbers per parameter, and at modern scales that overhead is enormous. Earlier savings schemes project, decompose, or freeze weights, paying in extra computation, extra memory of their own, or lost quality. FOAM instead compresses the optimizer's state by folding it into blocks.

Within each block, gradient means replace individual values, and a residual correction recovers what the averaging threw away. In theory the method converges at the same rate as ordinary Adam under standard conditions. In practice it wipes out most of the optimizer-state memory and reaches good models faster. It also stacks with other memory-saving optimizers rather than replacing them.
arxiv-2512-07512:
Zawar Hussain, Arslan Majal, Aamir Hussain Chughtai, and Talha Nadeem wrote this 2025 engineering paper. Satellite navigation signals guide transport, industry, and everyday travel. Their received power is tiny, so interference and deliberate jamming can easily drown them out.

Spotting jamming fast, on a small receiver with little power, is the hard part. Heavy learning models are too costly for such embedded hardware. The authors build a leaner detector around dictionary-based contrastive learning. It blends transfer learning with losses that pull matching signal features together. Training still works when labeled data are scarce. Pruning and knowledge distillation then shrink the model without gutting its accuracy. Across varied data regimes, the detector beats several well-known image networks. It also uses far less memory and answers with much lower delay. Real-time jamming defense on cheap receivers is the clear target.
arxiv-2512-07612:
Kairong Luo and eleven co-authors wrote this 2025 technical report on an open language model. Industry models train on closed data and secret recipes, leaving open researchers behind. Their answer is a fully open model, PCMind-2.1-Kaiyuan-2B, with two billion parameters.

Three ideas drive the work, all aimed at doing more with limited resources. A quantile benchmarking method compares open datasets of mixed quality and guides how to blend them. A selective repetition scheme reuses rare, high-quality data inside a multi-phase plan. A curriculum policy orders training samples by quality across many domains. A fast data pipeline and tweaks that keep half-precision training stable support the plan. The model matches strong fully open rivals in the team's tests. All assets, from weights to code, are released under an open license. The report offers a practical recipe for pretraining on a budget.
arxiv-2512-07712:
Sayak Dutta, Harish Katti, Shashikant Verma, and Shanmuganathan Raman wrote this 2025 computer vision paper. Tracking animals and reading their poses is routine in open spaces. Cage bars ruin the picture, blocking bodies in a regular, stubborn pattern.

Existing trackers lose much of their accuracy behind those bars. The authors build UnCageNet, a three-stage cleanup pipeline for caged footage. First, a segmentation network finds the cage structure in each frame. Its design uses Gabor filters tuned to many orientations, catching bars at any angle. Second, an inpainting method rebuilds the hidden regions with plausible content. Third, standard pose and tracking tools run on the cleaned frames. The uncaged video behaves almost like footage shot without bars at all. Keypoint accuracy rises, and movement trails grow far more consistent.  Removing the cage in software beats removing it in fact.
arxiv-2512-07812:
David Bick wrote this 2025 relativity paper on dust collapsing under its own gravity. In the Einstein-dust system, matter flows without pressure along its own paths. Where those paths cross, shell-crossing singularities mar the solution.

Caustics are envelopes traced by the fluid particles' trajectories. They arise in proposed extensions that step past those singularities. Bick proves a local existence result around such a caustic. His spacetimes are spherically symmetric and contain the caustic as a boundary. On one side sits a region of layered dust; on the other, vacuum. The construction solves a partial differential problem with spacelike evolution. Curvature and energy density both blow up near the caustic itself. The metric there keeps only modest smoothness, satisfying Einstein's equations weakly. Away from the caustic, everything is smooth and classical again.  Static examples close the work.
arxiv-2512-08012:
Aryaman Bansal and Divya Sharma, computer science researchers, posted a benchmarking study on arXiv in December 2025. Their setting is the intensive care unit, where doctors must balance keeping patients alive against using fewer resources and shorter stays. They test whether multi objective reinforcement learning, trained only on past records, can support such choices better than single goal methods.

The team compares three offline multi objective algorithms against three scalarized baselines on the MIMIC IV hospital dataset. One method, a modified decision transformer called PEDA DT, offers more flexibility than the fixed baselines. Because it learns a set of trade off policies, clinicians could adjust priorities at test time without retraining. The findings suggest offline multi objective learning is a promising path for personal care decisions.
arxiv-2512-08112:
Yifan Mai, Scott M Croom, Emily Wisnioski, and a large team of astronomers posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 from the MAGPI survey. They measure how the metal content of gas changes across seventy star forming galaxies, seen as they were a few billion years ago. A Bayesian tool called Blobby3D corrects for atmospheric blurring, so the gradients reflect the galaxies themselves.

Most galaxies in the sample have flat metal gradients, with about a third clearly falling outward and a tenth rising. The pattern with galaxy mass matches theory, where feedback, gas flows, and infalling gas all play a part. Galaxies with more turbulent gas tend to have flatter or flipped gradients, likely because mixing evens the metals out. Smaller galaxies also lean flat or positive. In them, dilution by new gas or wind losses seem to beat enrichment from new stars.
arxiv-2512-08512:
Jiang Liu, Yan Qin, Wei Dai, and Chau Yuen, engineers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about watching battery health in autonomous air vehicles. A drone battery state of health guides flight safety, but conditions vary from mission to mission, and a monitor trained for one setting may fail in another. Transfer learning can adapt it, yet the adaptation itself usually burns computing power that a small aircraft cannot spare.

Their method grows a network constructively, adding nodes one by one during transfer, guided by unlabeled data from the new setting. Three safeguards keep the transfer honest: a risk bound, a mismatch penalty, and a consistency demand on the data manifold, and the scheme provably converges while staying compact. On a real dataset from dozens of drone missions, it beat five rival transfer methods by wide margins: health monitoring light enough to fly with the aircraft it watches.
arxiv-2512-08612:
Cham Oumie, Wu Ming Liu, and Kashif Ammar Yasir, physicists, posted a theory study on arXiv in December 2025. They examine a hybrid device coupling a microwave cavity to magnetic waves, called magnons, in a crystal sphere tied to a mechanical vibration. Such systems can show induced transparency, a window where an opaque cavity lets a probe through.

With ordinary coupling, the device shows one transparency window. It splits into two once the mechanical mode joins in. The team then adds a traveling field that makes the system non Hermitian and parity time symmetric in a broken regime. There the window stops being passive: transmission becomes lopsided, amplified on one side of the resonance and absorbed on the other. Tuning the detuning reshapes the response into asymmetric Fano profiles, and slow and fast light can both be dialed widely. Such control suits quantum signal processing and sensitive detectors.
arxiv-2512-08712:
Aprem Joy, Roman Lange, and Achim Rosch study how excitations move and fade in layered quantum spin liquids. In those materials, order is topological, and single excitations can move freely inside a layer. Only pairs or larger groups can hop between layers, a direct result of that topological order.

Using exact solutions of diffusion equations and particle based simulations, the authors work out signatures for pump probe experiments. The time scale of such tests is set by the starting excitation density, which the pump controls. A surface excitation spreads into the bulk more slowly than normal diffusion, and pair loss makes that spread even slower, growing only with the log of time. Pair hopping between layers also gives a new slow decay law for total density. The results offer clear targets for experiments on finite samples.
arxiv-2512-08812:
Anna Jordanous studies whether the emotional content of jazz improvisation can be measured, and whether it links to creativity. Improvisation is a live creative act, often played over a set chord sequence from a lead sheet. Judging its creativity is hard, and automated measures are needed if generative music systems are to be evaluated at scale.

The study proposes that improvisations with more emotion laden content are more likely to be judged creative. A method based on embeddings captures emotional content in audio, using a psychology grounded classification of musical traits linked to emotions. The resulting vectors, called emovectors, are then compared across many improvisations to test the hypothesis. Capturing emotion in a countable form could support new creativity metrics for music. Such metrics could apply both to human performance and to output from current generative systems.
arxiv-2512-09312:
Ziheng Yang and colleagues address beam hopping, a technique high-throughput satellites use to aim their signal beams where ground demand is highest. Demand shifts over time, so the satellite must keep computing illumination patterns, the schedules of which cells to light and when. Older algorithms are far too slow for modern satellites covering hundreds of cells.

Their framework, Tyche, pairs two algorithms. A Monte Carlo tree search method computes strong patterns much faster than genetic algorithms, cutting one pattern's computation from minutes to seconds. A greedy method supplies a provisional pattern instantly while the search finishes in the background, using sliding windows and pruning to keep the search lean. In evaluations, the search method raised throughput by up to nearly double over existing solutions. The authors present Tyche as a step toward real-time beam hopping on real satellite networks.
arxiv-2512-09512:
Marceau Limousin leads the SLICE team in a study of AC 114, a galaxy cluster famous as one of the first strong gravitational lensing clusters found from the ground. That was in the early 1990s, before the Hubble telescope flew. Despite that fame, no lensing analysis had been done for over fifteen years. New JWST images change that.

The JWST data reveal ten multiply imaged systems, and the team builds a parametric mass model that fits X-ray data from Chandra in one combined analysis. The dark matter distribution comes out as a single lump centered on the brightest cluster galaxy, with a large core. The fit also demands an external shear pointing toward a second mass concentration about a megaparsec away, which they name AC114b. X-ray coverage of the structure supports a merger caught late, after collision, with the smaller system stripped of its hot gas.
arxiv-2512-09612:
J. L. Chau, A. Berera, and D. Huyghebaert report rogue vertical drafts, up-and-down air motions in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere, the atmosphere fifty to one hundred kilometers up. Observations have recorded vertical velocities far beyond the usual spread, sometimes exceeding fifty meters per second, appearing as updraft and downdraft structures in a varicose pattern.

Four-dimensional observations show these events are intermittent, recurrent, and unpredictable. Over northern Norway in summer, they occur about every twelve days on average. Different instruments may catch only part of an event, such as only the rising or the sinking branch, if their altitude coverage is limited. Despite their rarity, the authors argue the drafts' size and frequency could matter for dust-sized matter escaping planets, for human-made material in the upper atmosphere, and for that region's climate. They propose rogue vertical drafts are an under-recognized feature needing global observation.
arxiv-2512-09812:
Jan Moser revisits a formula he and coauthors published in 1985 involving the Riemann zeta function. The old work built two integrals of the squared Riemann Z function over two separate sets. The sets have nearly equal size as they grow, yet the two integrals differ by a surprisingly large excess. That excess becomes the raw material for the present paper. Moser works within his long running study of objects he calls Jacob's ladders.

Using the 1985 excess formula, he constructs a new statement about the zeta function that he shows is equivalent to the Fermat-Wiles theorem, the result better known as Fermat's Last Theorem. The equivalence is set on a two parameter family of Bernoulli lemniscates, a classic figure eight shaped curve. The paper is a specialized contribution to analytic number theory, tying a decades old construction about the zeta function to a famous theorem.
arxiv-2512-09912:
Erin Craig and Robert Tibshirani borrow the attention idea from large neural networks and put it to work in ordinary supervised learning. Their setting is tabular data, fitted with tools like lasso regression and gradient boosting. The goals are twofold. Each prediction should get a model tailored to its own test point. At the same time, the models should stay simple and interpretable, unlike a black box network.

Their method fits a local model for every test observation. Training points are weighted by attention, a supervised similarity score that stresses whichever features and interactions predict the outcome. Because the weights are learned from data, the method adapts to mixed populations without predefined clusters. It also explains itself: for each prediction, it names the most predictive features and the most relevant training cases. Extensions cover time series, spatial data, and correcting pretrained tree models under shift.
arxiv-2512-10012:
Mattes Mollenhauer and Christian Fiedler derive a sharp probability inequality for heavy tailed random processes in Banach spaces. Martingales are processes whose future expectation equals the present value, a model of fair accumulation. A Fuk-Nagaev inequality bounds how large the running maximum of such a process can get. The authors work in smooth Banach spaces and allow only finitely many higher conditional moments, the realistic setting for heavy tails. Their proof merges an optimized Chernoff bound approach with a classical estimate for moment generating functions of smooth norms.

The result improves existing infinite dimensional bounds in two ways: it removes unnecessary centering terms and it supplies precise constants. As an application, the authors propose a McDiarmid type bound for vector valued functions whose conditional higher moments are uniformly controlled. Such bounds underlie concentration results in modern statistics.
arxiv-2512-10312:
Julian Rodriguez and four coauthors document the work of a university Big Data course, from first data processing to a running distributed cluster. The report follows the course's sequence of practices. It begins with the Epsilon dataset, a standard large classification benchmark, processed first by group strategies and then individually. Text analysis and classification come next, using the RestMex shared task materials. A further practice analyzes movie features from the IMDb dataset, a different flavor of large scale data.

The final section describes the technical capstone: standing up a distributed computing cluster with Apache Spark on Linux, programmed in Scala. As a document, this is a course report rather than a research paper. Its value is pedagogical and practical. It is a worked record of how the standard big data toolchain fits together, in the order a learner meets it. That includes the unglamorous cluster setup that tutorials often skip.
arxiv-2512-10412:
Kyudong Choi, In-Jee Jeong, and Young-Jin Sim give a rigorous treatment of a fluid curiosity noticed in the nineteenth century. A travelling vortex drags a bubble of outside fluid along with it, its atmosphere. Reynolds and Lodge described the effect, and Hicks later noted shapes. But most later work rested on thin-core approximations or asymptotics rather than proof.

The authors define the vortex atmosphere precisely for flows that are incompressible and free of viscosity, and prove it exists and is unique. They compare two cases side by side. The flat case is a two-dimensional vortex dipole, whose atmosphere always forms an oval region. The round case is a three-dimensional vortex ring, where both spheroidal and toroidal atmospheres can occur. This confirms Hicks's old observation. The proof rests on identifying each atmosphere as an exact superlevel set of its stream function.
arxiv-2512-10612:
Thomas Goetz and co-authors couple two processes that feed on each other: opinions and epidemics. People who think a disease is dangerous behave differently, and catching the disease can change minds. Their model joins a two-state voter-style opinion process to SIS infection dynamics. In that dynamics, the sick recover and can be infected again. Transmission rates are set by opinion. A switch fires when someone falls ill.

Analytically, the authors find when disease-free and endemic states are stable. Simulations then show richer behaviour: past a certain infectivity, the system can settle into a steady endemic balance or swing in stable cycles, depending on where it starts. Stranger still, the winning opinion and the epidemic outcome do not move monotonically with infectivity. The lesson is that shifting norms and trust can permanently redirect an epidemic, rivalling medical controls in importance.
arxiv-2512-11512:
Patrick Manya and colleagues speed up a classic network measurement when it is computed across many machines with no central coordinator. Closeness centrality scores how near a node sits to all others, marking the best connected members of a network. In huge decentralised networks, approximation methods prune the search but still drown in exchanged messages.

Their enhancement lets nodes bundle results into multi packet messages, sending fewer, larger, consolidated blocks instead of many small ones. Message counts and computation time fell substantially compared with the original pruning technique, while the accuracy of the centrality estimates survived intact. Each node uses somewhat more memory and local effort, a trade the authors show is well worth it at scale. The method offers a practical route to centrality analysis for very large, complex networks.
arxiv-2512-11912:
Liu Peng and Yaochu Jin compare how badly dirty data hurts different kinds of probabilistic models. They corrupt training data in a controlled way and watch performance slide. The spread across model families is stark.

Autoregressive language models barely flinch: for GPT-2, test loss rose only from 2.87 to 3.59 under 50 percent token corruption. Class conditional diffusion models fell apart instead, with image label match dropping 56.81 percent. Classifiers sat in between, and bigger data softened their fall. The authors explain the split with information theory, PAC learning, and gradient views. Rich conditioning and sheer information volume, they argue, are what shield a model.
arxiv-2512-12012:
Antonio Guillen-Perez presents Semantic-Drive, a local system for mining rare driving scenes from fleet video. Self driving cars need training on long tail events like wild jaywalking or odd road works. Fleets record petabytes, but finding those moments by hand is slow, and cloud vision models raise privacy and cost issues.

Semantic-Drive splits the job in two. A fast open vocabulary detector anchors attention on candidate objects. A reasoning vision model then does forensic scene analysis. A judge and scout consensus scheme curbs hallucination. On nuScenes, scored against the Waymo taxonomy, recall hit 0.966 versus 0.475 for CLIP, and risk scoring error fell 40 percent. It all runs on one consumer graphics card.
arxiv-2512-12112:
Padmeswari Nandiya and co-authors present BRIDG-ICS, a knowledge graph system for defending smart factories. Industry 5.0 links IT and plant floor systems, widening the attack surface. Siloed defenses miss attack chains that hop between the two worlds.

The graph fuses assets, flaws, and attacker behavior with risk numbers like exploit chance and attack cost. Large language models mine threat text to add missing links as graph triples. Multi stage attack paths can then be simulated and ranked. In test scenarios the system scaled well and cut potential attack exposure. It offers security teams a shared map of how a plant floor breach could unfold, step by step.
arxiv-2512-12312:
David Kordahl and Emma Foster turn a beer bottle into a physics lab tool in a 2025 paper. Blowing across a bottle mouth makes a clear tone, set by the air inside. The bottle acts like a one dimensional driven, damped oscillator, a system that vibrates when pushed and slowly loses energy.

Older lab work measured the bottle's response tone by tone, which takes time. With Fourier methods, a few seconds of data can pin down the model values. The paper gives enough detail for undergraduate lab classes to run the experiment. It is set to appear in the American Journal of Physics.
arxiv-2512-13012:
Menglu Li and co-authors introduce HQ-MPSD, a data set for spotting partial deepfake speech, where only a short stretch of audio is fake. Older data sets rely on dated synthesis tools and leave telltale artifacts. Detectors may learn those artifacts instead of true signs of manipulation.

Their set holds 350.8 hours of speech in eight languages from 550 speakers. Splice points were chosen with fine alignment to keep the speech smooth and natural, and background effects were added. Listening tests and sound analysis confirmed high quality. When top detectors were tried on it, their scores dropped by more than 80 percent, showing the task is far harder.
arxiv-2512-13212:
Hikaru Awazu studies residually exact groups, a class in pure group theory tied to operator algebras. A group is exact when its reduced C-star algebra, a kind of algebra built from the group, is exact. A group is residually exact when each nontrivial element can be mapped onto an exact group without being sent to the identity.

Awazu proves this class is closed under several constructions used to build new groups from old ones. They are Green's graph products, double amalgamated products, and special HNN extensions. Such permanence results matter because they let researchers certify new examples from known ones, widening a class that links group theory with functional analysis.
arxiv-2512-13312:
Yu Mao and Mohamed Saidi prove a version of a theorem by Hoshi in anabelian geometry, a field that tries to rebuild number fields from their symmetry groups. Hoshi showed that open maps between certain Galois groups that respect cyclotomic data must come from actual field embeddings.

Mao and Saidi prove the analogous result for m-step solvable Galois groups, a truncated version of the full group. Given a map at level m plus three that respects the cyclotomic characters, they show the induced map at level m comes from a field embedding exactly when the compatibility holds. The result sharpens how much group data pins down a number field.
arxiv-2512-13512:
Daniel Erkensten, Alexey Chernikov, and Ermin Malic study how an electron Wigner crystal affects moving excitons in a flat material. An exciton is a bound pair of an electron and a hole. A Wigner crystal forms when electrons repel each other so strongly that they settle into a regular pattern.

The authors find that the weak, repeating pull from the crystal has a large effect on how excitons spread. Yet it has only a small effect on exciton energy. The effect can be tuned by charge density, which sets the crystal grip, and by heat. Their work gives clear signs to look for in exciton transport tests.
arxiv-2512-13612:
Rodrigo Alonso, Susobhan Chattopadhyay, and James Ingoldby use geometry to study Higgs Effective Field Theory and the scale of new physics. HEFT extends the Standard Model with a Higgs-like scalar and Nambu-Goldstone bosons. The question is how HEFT relates to the more restricted SMEFT frame.

They compute closed-form results for tree-level scattering with any number of Goldstone and Higgs-like states. From those, they derive cross sections, decay rates, and unitarity bounds. They then study three classes of models in the Standard Model scalar sector. Two match known behavior. The third, based on a dilaton theory, gives a smooth path from HEFT straight to the Standard Model, without passing through a SMEFT regime.
arxiv-2512-14012:
Ruanqianqian Huang and co-authors study how professional software developers actually use AI coding agents in 2025. Agents promise faster coding, parallel delegation, and software written from natural language alone. What role they play in real professional work was still an open question.

Through field observations of 13 developers and qualitative surveys of 99, they find experienced developers value agents as a productivity boost. Yet those developers keep control of design and implementation, insisting on core software quality traits. They use expert strategies to steer agent behavior and judge which tasks suit agents. They enjoy agents as collaborators rather than as full delegates. The results highlight best practices and point to better agentic interfaces and guidelines.
arxiv-2512-14812:
Ali Fatemiabhari and three coauthors study how fast quantum systems grow complex, using gravity models of quiver gauge theories. Quiver theories describe forces with chains of linked groups, and their gravity duals live in curved AdS space. The team's measure, Krylov complexity, tracks how a quantum state spreads over time.

In these models, a probe must move both outward in AdS space and along the quiver direction, which holds the color and flavor data. That extra motion fades early on, so growth depends on the quiver's shape at first. Later the motion freezes and growth turns universal, matching plain AdS results. The work shows how complexity can reveal both fine detail and broad patterns in these theories.
arxiv-2512-15012:
Shuichi Hayashida proves a bridge between two kinds of modular forms, special functions at the heart of number theory. On one side sit Jacobi forms whose index is a lattice called D with odd index, written D_{2n+1}. On the other side sit elliptic modular forms of level 2, a much more classical family.

The paper has three goals. It establishes an isomorphism, an exact matching, between the two families. It gives an explicit formula for the Fourier coefficients of Jacobi-Eisenstein series of that index. And it builds a holomorphic modular form of weight 3/2 and level 8 from a Zagier-Eisenstein series. A striking byproduct: four named functions share the same Hecke eigenvalue, 1+p, for every odd prime p. That coincidence falls straight out of the new isomorphism.
arxiv-2512-15512:
Opeyemi Bamigbade, Mark Scanlon, and John Sheppard present VAAS, a system for spotting manipulated images for forensic work, in a 2025 paper. New image generators can forge pictures that look consistent and fool detectors tuned to pixel or compression traces. Most detectors also give no sense of how severe a manipulation is.

VAAS pairs a global attention based score from a Vision Transformer with a patch level consistency score from SegFormer embeddings. Together they give a continuous, readable anomaly score showing both where and how much an image was altered. Tests on the DF2023 and CASIA v2.0 data sets show competitive detection scores, plus attention maps that help explain each verdict.
arxiv-2512-15712:
Vincent Huang and co authors train Predictive Concept Decoders, end to end interpretability assistants for neural networks, in a 2025 paper. Reading a network's internal activations faithfully is hard, and most scalable tools use hand designed agents that form and test hypotheses about them. The team turns that craft into a training objective instead.

An encoder compresses activations into a sparse list of concepts, and a decoder reads that list to answer plain language questions about the model's behavior. After pretraining on large unstructured data and fine tuning, the assistants improve with scale. They can detect jailbreaks, secret hints, and implanted latent concepts, and surface latent user attributes accurately.
arxiv-2512-15912:
Marek Balcerzak and co authors study Borel 1 type mappings and their equi-families in a 2025 math paper. Borel class 1 functions are the first level of measurable functions built from open sets, and families of them with uniform control, called equi-families, behave almost like single functions. The paper extends that theory to related function classes.

Following Lecomte's equi-Baire 1 idea, the authors define equi-families for the classes they consider and show the study reduces to one orbit map into a product space. They examine closures under pointwise convergence. A final part treats functions of two variables whose sections are equi-continuous, equi-Baire 1, or have a generalized Lebesgue property, generalizing a result of Grande.
arxiv-2512-16212:
Chunzhang Liu, Ning Zhang, and Wenjian Liu formulate a new chemistry method in a paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025. Strongly correlated electrons, as in many catalysts and magnets, defeat single-reference quantum chemistry methods. Multi-reference perturbation theory adds corrections on top of a flexible starting state, but careless formulations break basic rules about how energy scales with system size.

Their method, PASPT2, works in a partial active space with several states at once. It descends from a coupled-cluster theory, but a clever choice of starting Hamiltonian removes all disconnected terms, a flaw the parent theory suffers from. As a result, PASPT2 is strictly size-extensive, and size-consistent when fragments separate cleanly. Test cases on prototypical strongly correlated systems show the method working as designed. The 57-page paper lays out the full derivation for other chemists to implement.
arxiv-2512-16412:
Rahim Kargar studies an integral operator in a mathematics paper posted to arXiv in 2025. Volterra-type operators transform one analytic function into another by repeated integration against a fixed partner function. The higher-order version nests that integration n times over the unit disk, a basic domain in complex analysis.

Kargar asks when this operator behaves well on two classic function spaces: Hardy spaces and weighted Bergman spaces. He derives sharp estimates for its norm and essential norm, the measures of its size and of how far it sits from compact operators. Boundedness and compactness are characterized completely through Carleson measure conditions on the derivative of the partner function, with vanishing versions marking the compact cases. Such characterizations are the working tools analysts use to place new operators into known theory.
arxiv-2512-16512:
Hugo Pompougnac and five co-authors present a research platform in this 2025 arXiv paper. Making AI operators run fast takes tight control of math and data movement. Scheduling languages state those choices in code. But each language is locked inside one compiler world. That blocks fair tests. It also blocks reuse of good ideas across tools.

Their platform, XTC, puts scheduling and speed testing behind one shared interface. A common API states the schedule. One test harness then builds the code and times it. It works the same way for every backend. That split lets researchers run tests they can carry from tool to tool. They can weigh ideas on equal ground. The authors argue this kind of shared base speeds up work on faster AI operators. That work is a bottleneck for efficient AI as a whole.
arxiv-2512-16712:
J. Berteaud and coauthors hunt for millisecond pulsar candidates in the bulge of the Milky Way using data across many wavelengths. A crowd of such pulsars could explain the Fermi GeV excess, a gamma-ray glow near the center seen almost 15 years ago, yet radio pulse searches have found none there so far.

The team checked Chandra X-ray sources whose traits fit bulge pulsars. Sources with bright ultraviolet, optical, or strong infrared matches were ruled out, while radio or faint infrared matches marked strong candidates. More than a thousand X-ray sources passed the cuts, and five showed up for the first time in unpublished Very Large Array radio images.
arxiv-2512-16812:
Christoph Schönle and coauthors improve Monte Carlo sampling for molecular systems that get stuck in metastable states, long-lived traps that block fair sampling. Recent fixes propose nonlocal jumps in a collective-variable space, a small set of summary coordinates.

The team generalizes those methods and spells out an algorithm for nonlinear collective variables under underdamped Langevin dynamics, which keeps momentum effects. They prove the scheme is reversible, a key correctness trait. On test systems it runs much faster than overdamped versions. With machine-learned proposal samplers now able to handle tens to hundreds of variables, the result pushes the method toward real molecular systems.
arxiv-2512-16912:
Peter Chen and coauthors rethink reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, a method that boosts language model reasoning by rewarding checkable answers. Two odd findings frame the puzzle: fake rewards that ignore truth can help, and shrinking exploration can help too.

The team shows clipping bias is the link. Under fake rewards, clipping cuts policy entropy, making outputs more sure and fixed, while entropy cuts alone do not improve scores. A reward-misalignment model explains why fake rewards can help past the cases where test data leaked into training. The results clarify how exploration and exploitation balance in this training style.
arxiv-2512-17012:
Chiao-An Yang and coauthors present 4D-RGPT. It is a multimodal language model built to reason about 3D scenes that change over time. It also handles region-level questions. Past models grasp 4D structure weakly. Past benchmarks stress static scenes, with no region prompts.

Three parts make the system. The first part is the model itself. The second is a training frame called Perceptual 4D Distillation. It moves 4D skill from a frozen expert into the model. The third is R4D-Bench. It is a benchmark of dynamic scenes with depth and region prompts. Machines built it, and humans checked it. 4D-RGPT improves scores on older 4D question benchmarks. It also improves scores on the new bench. That is a step toward video models that track where things are as scenes evolve.
arxiv-2512-17512:
Vipin Kumar and three co-authors upgrade a tool that maps how DNA folds inside the cell nucleus. Hi-C experiments catch which DNA stretches touch each other, revealing nests of loops within loops at many scales. Most software reads those contact maps at one zoom level only, missing how the levels stack.

BHiCect 2.0 reads several zoom levels together and describes each chromosome as nested clusters that mostly interact within themselves. Spectral clustering, a graph method, draws the cluster tree across resolutions. The team ships the method as an R package so genomics pipelines can call it directly. A full multi-scale map of folding helps link genome shape to gene control and disease.
arxiv-2512-17612:
Alireza Samadifardheris and four co-authors sharpen MRI maps that measure tissue properties, without any sharp examples to learn from. Quantitative MRI gives true numbers for tissue, useful for tracking disease, but fine maps take long scans that clinics rarely spare. Their method starts from a one-minute fuzzy scan plus the routine pretty pictures every exam already takes.

A network guesses the sharp map, then checks itself by simulating what the scanner should have seen, a physics-based self-check needing no ground truth. In test data, fine-detail errors fell 45.4 percent below baseline. In three volunteers, maps from one-minute scans beat even five-minute ones at rebuilding standard images. A one-minute add-on could make measured MRI routine.
arxiv-2512-18012:
Alison L. Coil and four coauthors study an Odd Radio Circle, a huge faint ring of radio glow around a distant galaxy, known as ORC4. Such rings span hundreds of thousands of light years and their cause is unknown. The team used a Keck telescope spectrograph to map the gas in the galaxy at the ring's center.

The gas glows most strongly in one oxygen line and stretches farther out than other lines reach. It also moves in a messy way, with sharp speed changes and a wide spread near 200 kilometers per second. The line pattern fits shock waves of 200 to 300 kilometers per second better than starlight or a feeding black hole, tying the gas to the blast that made the ring.
arxiv-2512-18212:
Yang Liu and Yixian Gao study how well a hidden flaw inside a material can be pinned down from rim readings alone. Their model is a fourth order Schrödinger equation inside a bounded region, with a bumpy term standing for the flaw. The test is an inverse one: shake the rim, read the response, and infer the bump.

They prove stability bounds, which say that close rim readings force close bumps. The strength of the promise depends on what is known ahead about the flaw's smoothness and where it may sit. Special wave solutions that probe the inside, paired with frequency tools, carry the proof. Such bounds tell engineers how far rim based scans can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-18412:
Mykyta Lapin, Kostiantyn Bokhan, and Yurii Parzhyn build a picture classifier that learns from a handful of examples and never uses backpropagation. Most neural nets need thousands of labeled images and opaque training. Their design turns each outline drawing into a graph of key points and lines, tagged with lengths, angles, and directions.

Examples of one class merge into a concept graph, a kind of attractor that sums up the class. A new image is sorted by how closely its graph matches each concept, measured with an edit distance score. On a subset of the MNIST digit set, with just 5 to 6 examples per class and one pass, the method reached about 82 percent accuracy. Every call can be traced to a clear shape match.
arxiv-2512-18512:
H. Hassanabadi and four co-authors study a black hole that spins, carries charge, and sits in anti-de Sitter space, all inside Bumblebee gravity, a theory that breaks Lorentz symmetry. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works out how the violation reshapes the hole's horizons, heat, and shadow. Standard theory is the baseline they depart from.

They derive formulas for Hawking temperature, entropy, and heat capacity, finding leftover remnants and wider stability phases caused by the Lorentz violation. The Hawking radiation comes out sparser and less thermal. Tracking light paths, they show that raising the violation parameter or the charge squeezes and distorts the shadow, while spin shrinks it. The ergosphere swells and frame-dragging strengthens, which boosts energy extraction through the Penrose process. Such deviations could one day be observed.
arxiv-2512-18612:
Soumyadip Das, Luke Antoncich, and Jingbo B. Wang at the University of Western Australia clean noisy images with quantum reservoir computing, a method that uses a quantum system's natural dynamics as the processor, no fault tolerant machine required. Their 2025 framework is hybrid. A Rydberg atom array acts as the reservoir, while a classical neural network reads out the answer.

Images are first compressed by principal component analysis to fit the array. Each feature vector becomes detuning settings in the Hamiltonian steering the atoms. As it evolves, measurements over time produce nonlinear embeddings rich in correlations. The classical network rebuilds a denoised image from them. Against a matched classical baseline, the quantum model gives sharper images with similar structural recovery. The team ran the reservoir on QuEra's Aquila neutral atom processor, proving it works on real hardware. It is early proof that analog quantum devices can serve real signal tasks.
arxiv-2512-18912:
Hao Geng and three co-authors probe a strange promise of holography: that events deep inside anti-de Sitter space can be read from its boundary instantly. Under the AdS/CFT correspondence, a local bulk excitation should be reconstructible from boundary operators at the same moment, an apparently nonlocal encoding. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, asks when that nonlocality is genuinely observable in semiclassical gravity.

They exhibit setups where exploiting the effect detects a bulk excitation faster than waiting for its signal to reach the boundary. They also give counterexamples where the protocol fails and information stays effectively local, which they read as the emergence of a perturbatively localized observer. In those cases, holography cannot be proven at leading order in Newton's constant through nonlocalizability alone. The results refine what holography's strangest claim can actually be made to show.
arxiv-2512-19012:
Shijian Ma, Yunqi Huang, and Yan Lin created DramaBench, a test suite for AI models that continue a drama script. A good continuation must keep characters in character, move the plot, and hold the dramatic shape. Older tests, the authors say, check none of this in a full way.

DramaBench scores six separate traits, from format and logic to emotion and conflict handling. It mixes rule checks, model labeling, and statistics. The team ran eight leading models through more than a thousand scripts, and checked scores against human judges. Each trait proved to measure something distinct, giving model builders clear, separate feedback.
arxiv-2512-19412:
Camilo Granados, Bálint Kiss, Eric Cormier, and Bikash Kumar Das sculpt ultrafast mid-infrared light into vortex beams that carry orbital angular momentum. Twisted light adds a powerful control knob for encoding, trapping, and symmetry rules. In the mid-infrared, though, the usual programmable modulators do not work, blocking nonlinear experiments in air.

A static shaping strategy gets around the gap, producing few-cycle Bessel-Gauss vortices and perfect optical vortices. The team drove second-harmonic and high-harmonic generation in solids with them. The harmonic beams kept the structure of the drivers, faithfully passing on their spatial character. Solid-state high-harmonic work gains a new shaping tool.
arxiv-2512-19512:
Ziyang Song, Zelin Zang, Zuyao Chen, and Xusheng Liang teach multimodal models to reason about surgical anatomy images. Anatomy questions demand precise, clinically coherent answers, but expert labels are scarce and fine-tuning data-hungry. Group-relative policy optimization can sharpen reasoning cheaply, yet in anatomy it stumbles twice, the authors find.

Knowledge fails to travel between different structures, and the model collapses early onto one reasoning path. Their cures are a curriculum ordered by anatomical similarity, so lessons transfer in steps, and a group diversity boost that keeps rival reasoning paths alive. Together, the fixes target steadier learning and richer exploration on hard clinical images.
arxiv-2512-19612:
Speech technology for low-resource languages motivates MauBERT, built by Angelo Ortiz Tandazo and four co-authors. MauBERT extends the self-supervised HuBERT model across languages by teaching it articulatory features, the physical gestures behind speech sounds. Training continues on multilingual data covering 55 languages, with targets drawn from a mapping between phones and those articulatory features.

Tests using ABX discriminability, which checks whether sounds stay distinguishable across contexts, show MauBERT's representations hold up better than rival multilingual self-supervised models. The models also transfer to languages never seen in training and to casual speech, needing only about ten hours of speech for light fine-tuning. The team presents it as a workable recipe for giving speech models a phonetic head start.
arxiv-2512-19912:
Thi-Hoa Nguyen and three co-authors improve a solver for mechanics with no formula for the material. In data-driven elasticity, the law is a data set, not an equation. The solver seeks stress and strain fields that obey balance laws. It must also stay close to the measured data points. Their plan mixes a greedy search with an alternating direction method. Load is applied in steps, and Newton-Raphson tools from past work join in.

Tests use bars and trusses in one and two dimensions. The strain measures are nonlinear. The mixed solver tends to land closer to the best global answer. The cost is more compute for each greedy search. The team also replays the first cycle of factory tests on a nylon mooring rope. Gains in accuracy and toughness show up when the data are skewed or noisy.
arxiv-2512-20512:
J Fransson, B C Sanders, and A P Sowa ask whether superpositions that differ macroscopically can exist across infinitely many sites. Their stage is an infinite array of boson sites, treated rigorously in Hilbert space theory. States split into local ones, touching finitely many degrees of freedom, and inherently nonlocal ones.

Earlier work showed such systems support nonlocal coherent states. Here the authors show those states evolve into nonlocal cat states under a nonlocal Hamiltonian, the square of the total number operator. The dynamics cannot be factored into local pieces. Studying generalized bosons reveals that coherent states and cat states are not naturally married; their fusion is special to ordinary bosons. Engineered quantum systems might one day realize these effects.
arxiv-2512-20612:
Yibin Lei, Shwai He, Ang Li, and Andrew Yates compress large language models into search engines. Fine-tuned language models make strong dense retrievers, encoding whole queries and documents into vectors, but their size makes them expensive. Generative tasks are known to tolerate heavy pruning; retrieval, which compresses a sequence into one representation, might differ.

A systematic redundancy analysis says it does, in a useful direction. Feed-forward MLP layers are far more prunable in retrievers, while attention layers stay critical for gathering meaning. Their approach, EffiR, removes MLP capacity coarse-to-fine, first depth, then width, and fine-tunes for retrieval. Across BEIR data sets and several backbones, the shrunken retrievers keep full-size accuracy at a fraction of the size and inference cost.
arxiv-2512-20812:
Nathaniël de Leeuw and four co-authors test whether language models truly reason with symbols or just lean on familiar meanings. They built what they call semantic deceptions: digits and math operators rewritten in new symbols whose shapes hint at wrong meanings. A model that grasps the rules should still add correctly, whatever the notation looks like.

Four models stumbled badly on very simple sums when the cues misled them. Even when models followed instructions on the surface, the misleading meanings still weakened basic skills. Step-by-step prompting seemed to deepen reliance on learned patterns rather than fix it. The authors warn against trusting such models where exact symbolic reasoning protects real decisions.
arxiv-2512-20912:
Sahinur Reja and Satoshi Nishimoto map the ground-state phase diagram of the spin-1 Kitaev-Heisenberg chain, a model of magnetic moments where bond-dependent interactions compete with ordinary exchange. They add a uniaxial single-ion anisotropy, a term that biases each spin along one axis, and compute with the density-matrix renormalization group on chains reaching 144 sites.

Four magnetically ordered phases appear, alongside disordered regimes that include two Kitaev spin-liquid regions and a topological Haldane phase near the Heisenberg limit. Both spin-liquid regimes gain finite width in the spin-1 model, while the Haldane phase proves fragile against the anisotropy. The map gives condensed-matter researchers a guide to where exotic, nonmagnetic states survive in realistic spin-1 materials.
arxiv-2512-21012:
Qian-Qian Hong, Dajun Ding, and four co-authors get molecules to point one way and stay pointing, with no field holding them. Field-free orientation matters for stereochemistry and precision spectroscopy, but standard tricks produce brief alignments that flip direction in cycles and demand superpositions across many rotational states. Their framework needs only two rotational states of a symmetric-top molecule, well chosen, with coherence between them doing the steering.

A single control pulse prepares the desired state, replacing multistate, multipulse routines. Tests on methyl iodide, including centrifugal distortion, confirm that both the strength and the direction of the orientation can be dialed in. Initial-state choice and coherence, rather than brute-force field shaping, carry the effect, which keeps the recipe simple.
arxiv-2512-21212:
Konstantin Popov, Alexander Aryshev, and eight co-authors from the KEK lab in Japan and IJClab in France test whether accelerator timing can ride on telecom fiber. Modern sites need laser pulses and electron beams to arrive together with sub-picosecond stability, a trillionth-of-a-second discipline that timing hardware struggles to hold across large sites. Their setup pairs low-level radio-frequency gear with White Rabbit, the precision timing scheme born at CERN, carried on an IDROGEN board with an embedded node.

A frequency standard and off-the-shelf synthesizers distribute phase-locked clocks through ordinary telecom fiber. Phase-noise spectra, measured at several radio-frequency sub-harmonics, confirm the synchronization holds. The test points toward one timing scheme serving whole accelerator complexes, laser diagnostics included, using network technology, not bespoke cabling for every device. Large sites gain a cheaper path to femtosecond-era timing.
arxiv-2512-21712:
Y. V. Kalyuzhnyi and P. T. Cummings solve an integral equation that describes the structure of a sticky hard-sphere fluid. The spheres attract at contact, but only at special patches: the adhesion has the tetrahedral, quadrupolar-like symmetry of a four-lobed pattern. Such patchy particles model colloids and proteins that bond in preferred directions.

The authors use the multidensity form of the Ornstein-Zernike equation with the Percus-Yevick closure, which tracks how particles are bonded. They obtain an analytic solution with the invariant expansion method and Baxter's factorization. At low stickiness, the multidensity theory and an earlier single-density molecular approach agree almost exactly. As stickiness grows, the two diverge, and the single-density approach stops converging at all. The comparison shows that strongly associating, directionally bonding fluids need the multidensity description.
arxiv-2512-21812:
James Saunderson studies when a large sum of objects from a convex cone can be replaced by a small, reweighted sub-sum without changing it much. The spectral sparsification theorem does this for sums of positive semidefinite matrices, keeping only linearly many terms. Saunderson generalizes the question to arbitrary convex cones.

He defines the sparsification function of a cone: in the worst case, how many terms an approximate sparsifier needs, as a function of the accuracy. For cones equipped with a self-concordant barrier, including all hyperbolicity cones, he bounds that size by a constant times the barrier parameter divided by the squared error. For general cones with an ordinary barrier, the bound is weaker but still explicit. He studies how sparsification interacts with operations such as conic lifts, and what it implies for conic optimization problems. The work turns a matrix trick into a piece of convex geometry.
arxiv-2512-22012:
Binomial edge ideals, attached to a graph through the two-minors of a two-row matrix, became a classic of combinatorial commutative algebra, known to be radical and Cartwright-Sturmfels. Aldo Conca, Emanuela De Negri, and Volkmar Welker prove that the generalized ideals, built from two-minors of matrices with more rows, are Cartwright-Sturmfels as well.

Rauh had earlier shown the generalized ideals are radical; the Cartwright-Sturmfels property, a strong form of well-behaved degeneration, was open. Along the way the authors develop results on which ideal constructions preserve the property, and give examples and counterexamples for ideals of higher minors. The theorem extends a fifteen-year line of work on edge ideals to the multi-row setting.
arxiv-2512-22312:
Debraj Das and Soumendra Lahiri settle when the high-dimensional central limit theorem truly holds. The theorem says averages of many variables look Gaussian, and recent work proved it under various sufficient assumptions linking how fast dimension grows to how heavy the values' tails are. Missing was necessity: are those moment conditions required? The authors answer under component independence across four exhaustive regimes.

The regimes run from variables with all polynomial moments down to variables with infinite variance that still sit in the normal distribution's domain of attraction. For each, they find the optimal growth rate of dimension against sample size and prove matching necessary and sufficient moment conditions for the theorem over hyper-rectangles. The limit theorem survives under much weaker conditions than earlier work assumed.
arxiv-2512-22412:
Yunhong Lyu, Bouchra R. Nasri, and Bruno N. Rémillard work on change-point detection for a class of models used for data that keeps pulling back toward a moving average. Their setting is generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes observed only at discrete times, with a drift that varies periodically. The task is sequential: spot the moment the process's behavior changes, as the observations stream in, rather than after the full record is in hand.

The authors propose two detection methods tailored to this process family. They then study how each method performs through numerical tests run under several choices of parameters. The paper contributes practical detection tools for a process class where periodicity in the drift complicates the usual change-point machinery.
arxiv-2512-22512:
Xingwu Zeng and Can Zhang prove that the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation can be steered roughly where one wants, quickly, using a single multiplicative control. The equation, posed on a torus of any dimension, carries a power-type nonlinearity of arbitrary integer degree. Bilinear control acts through the equation's coefficients rather than as an added force, which makes steering subtler than in additive settings.

Given a saturation premise on the control operator, the authors show small-time global approximate controllability. Any target state can be approached as closely as one wishes, in as short a time as one wishes. The proof develops a multiplicative version of the geometric control approach introduced by Agrachev and Sarychev. The result extends controllability theory for a classic equation of pattern formation and superconductivity.
arxiv-2512-22612:
Dafeng Zhang, Yongqi Song, and Shizhuo Liu make face clustering, grouping photos by identity without labels, more robust to noise. Clustering quality hinges on how relationships between face embeddings are measured. Jaccard similarity beats plain cosine distance, but it drags in too many irrelevant neighbor nodes, blunting its discrimination. The authors first propose a prediction-driven Top-K Jaccard coefficient that keeps neighborhoods purer.

Predicting the right number of neighbors is itself hard, so a transformer examines relationships around the cutoff to firm up the similarity estimates. Usual transformers add their own noise by over-weighting irrelevant feature relations, so the team built a Sparse Differential Transformer to suppress it. On benchmarks including MS-Celeb-1M, the approach reached state-of-the-art clustering performance.
arxiv-2512-22712:
Anaelia Ovalle and seven co-authors test whether language models' written reasoning supports their answers, and whether the answer depends on the language. They built a human-validated system for judging that support and applied it to 65,000 reasoning traces from GlobalMMLU questions, spanning six languages and six frontier models. Headline accuracy looked strong everywhere, which the study shows can be misleading.

Reasoning traces in non-Latin scripts showed at least twice as much reasoning-answer misalignment as traces in Latin scripts. A human-annotation error taxonomy traces most failures to evidential errors, unsupported claims and ambiguous facts, followed by illogical steps. The authors argue current multilingual evaluation gives an incomplete picture of reasoning quality and call for reasoning-aware evaluation systems.
arxiv-2512-23112:
Mohammad Rasoolinejad reframes viral evolution as a constrained optimization problem, arguing that the huge variety of viruses is what physics permits rather than a catalog of accidents. In this picture, a virion is a multi-component physical system that decays for good in the environment. The virus as a copier faces immune selection and a balance between mutation and selection pressure. Transmission ties the two levels together.

Major paths then fall out as necessary solutions. Viruses spread through the environment or air are predicted to be simple, stable, and dependent on sheer replication volume instead of immune suppression. Complex viruses can afford fast decay outside the host because they carry immune-modulating gear, latency, or replication, but they pay with reduced robustness to mutation. Even temperature-driven seasonality emerges from the heat-driven nature of viral decay, with no need to invoke changes in host behavior.
arxiv-2512-23512:
Vision-language models increasingly try to both understand images and generate them inside one system. Fengjiao Chen and five co-authors ask whether the generating side actually helps the understanding side when training data grows very large. Their test model, UniHetero, was pretrained on more than two hundred million samples, a scale where earlier small-scale conclusions may not hold.

Three findings stand out. Generation improved understanding only when it worked at the level of meaning, producing high-level visual representations, while pixel-level losses hurt. The unified model also used data more efficiently and scaled better than an understanding-only one. Finally, predicting the model's own input embeddings captured visual detail such as objects, positions, shapes, and colors with less accumulated error than a separate vision encoder.
arxiv-2512-23612:
Chandler Moore and seven co-authors report a recipe for 3D-printing plastic scintillators, materials that flash light when radiation passes through and so serve in radiation detectors. Vat polymerization printing can make shapes that machining cannot, but ordinary resin cures too deeply under ultraviolet light, blurring fine features.

Their formula adds coumarin 450 as a third dye, which limits how far the curing light penetrates. The dye barely changed the emission spectrum or light output, yet printed resolution improved dramatically: freestanding pillars were resolved below a millimeter. Fully supported structures reached features near a tenth of a millimeter on a desktop printer. All samples separated neutron from gamma events, and the best reached half the light output of a standard commercial scintillator. The work appeared in the Journal of Instrumentation.
arxiv-2512-24312:
Julia Tokarska and Andrzej Dragan test a proposed probe of quantum gravity. If gravity is quantum, it should entangle two masses that interact only through gravitation. Their system holds two particles in harmonic traps. The particles start in thermal states or in two-mode squeezed states. The authors compute how much entanglement gravity can build.

For thermal states, a ceiling appears. Above a maximum temperature, no entanglement forms at all. For fixed settings, one trap frequency works best. It maximizes the logarithmic negativity, their entanglement measure. Squeezing the start state does not add entanglement. It does widen the temperature range where entanglement survives. A general bound for all Gaussian states is also derived. Ground and squeezed states saturate that bound. The sober message is scale: the entanglement is extremely small. Observing it will challenge experimenters severely.
arxiv-2512-24512:
Srikumar Warrier, Anubhab Roy, and Pijush Patra study how charged particles collide in atmospheric flows. Tiny particles grow by colliding, building cloud droplets and volcanic ash aggregates. Those particles often carry electric charge. Textbook reasoning says like charges repel and hinder collisions. Finite particle size complicates that story.

The setup is a pair of like-charged dielectric spheres in a compressional flow. Finite size bends the electric interaction away from the point-charge picture. Far-field repulsion flips to near-field attraction. Trajectories and collision thresholds become nontrivial. Strong inward velocities appear for certain charge and size mixes. Uncharged pairs collide more as size ratio grows, monotonically. Charged pairs break that pattern at high charge ratios. Efficiency peaks at small size ratios, then falls. Like charges can thus enhance growth, counterintuitively, in the right regime.
arxiv-2512-24812:
Roberto Castorrini and Theophile Dolmaire study four one-dimensional inelastic hard spheres that may undergo inelastic collapse, an infinite burst of crashes in finite time. Collisions follow a fixed restitution coefficient below one, so energy is lost at each hit. A two-dimensional dynamic system, the b-to-b mapping, encodes all possible crash orders for the original particles.

That mapping is proved to be a piecewise projective change, which allows lean numeric exploration of collapse orders. Dynamical systems readers get a tractable reduction of a singular particle problem. Knowing which crash series can occur is the key step toward classifying collapse pattern.
arxiv-2512-24912:
Shiv Kumar Chaudhary and Om Prakash characterize linear maps on matrix algebras that preserve Lie products equal to fixed elements. A bijective linear map is required to send pairs whose commutator equals one fixed matrix to pairs whose commutator equals another fixed matrix. The general form of all such maps is determined for finite matrix algebras over the complex numbers.

A parallel result treats operators between infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, with a Jordan-type product in place of the commutator. Algebra readers get preserver theorems: rigid conclusions about maps that keep one algebraic relation fixed. Such results show how little freedom a map has once a single product value is preserved.
arxiv-2512-25012:
Nilima Nigam surveys computational spectral geometry, asking both how a domain's shape shapes an map's spectrum and how to compute that spectrum reliably. Eigenvalue approximation sits where numeric analysis meets spectral geometry. Many discretization methods, for the map and for the resulting discrete system, have been developed and analyzed over the years.

High-accuracy approaches and their pitfalls are revisited from a computational viewpoint. Readers get an expository bridge between two communities that study the same eigenvalues differently. Hearing the shape of a domain, the classic spectral question, depends in practice on trustworthy computation, which is the survey's central concern.
arxiv-2601-00212:
Han Liu leads seven coauthors in making fake MRI scans varied enough to train tumor segmenters well. The target task marks vestibular schwannoma and the cochlea in T2 scans. Labels exist for a different scan type, not for T2. Domain adaptation bridges that gap with synthetic images. But scanners and protocols vary inside one domain too.

Older methods ignore that inner spread. Their synthetic images come out too uniform. Downstream models then generalize poorly to real scans. IntraStyler discovers fine styles on its own. A 3D style encoder pulls style apart from anatomy. Each source image can then lend its own style. The output set grows far more diverse. The method builds on a past challenge winning solution. Segmentation after training becomes more reliable. Code is public for clinical imaging teams.
arxiv-2601-01212:
Jürgen Angst, Oanh Nguyen, and Guillaume Poly study random polynomials whose roots are scattered by chance. Take many roots drawn independently from some pattern, build the polynomial, then take derivatives again and again. A natural question is where the roots of those derivatives land. Earlier work could only handle a modest number of derivatives before the pattern was lost.

The authors show that for broad families of root patterns, the roots of the derivative settle back onto the original pattern, for derivative counts growing almost as fast as the degree itself. That breaks the old logarithmic barrier by a wide margin. They also prove a robustness result. Even if a small share of roots is drawn from a different, spread-out pattern, the outcome still converges to the original. The findings reveal a surprising stability in how repeated differentiation treats random roots.
arxiv-2601-01312:
Hambarde and 20 co-authors report a new test set and contest for finding the same person in video taken from far away. Matching people between drone and ground views is hard when images are tiny, angles are steep, and clothes change. Standard methods rest on clear appearance, which fades fast at long range.

The set holds 371 people, over eleven thousand short clips, and millions of frames, filmed from low heights up to 120 meters. Ten teams entered the 2025 challenge. Scores fell as height and distance grew, and top-down views hurt every method. Even the best system scored under forty-four percent on cross-view matching.
arxiv-2601-01612:
A P Isaev works on formulas that hold at once for all simple Lie algebras, a pattern known as Vogel universality. Lie algebras encode the symmetry rules behind much of modern physics and geometry, but results are usually proved case by case. Isaev builds special identities for operators named for Casimir, acting on combined representation spaces.

From those identities, he derives explicit projectors that pick out each smaller piece inside a combined space, for every simple Lie algebra except one exceptional case. The projectors and size formulas are written in one universal form using Vogel parameters. A new section works out color factors for endless families of Feynman diagrams in gauge theories.
arxiv-2601-01712:
Online recommender systems must rank items within tens of milliseconds, which caps how much of a user's history a generative ranking model can read. Jiarui Wang and forty co-authors present RelayGR, a production system. It works around the cap in a simple way. Most of the user's behavior sequence is computed ahead of time. The result is then reused at ranking.

RelayGR pre-computes long-term behavior prefixes for selected requests. It keeps their cached data in fast memory across pipeline stages. It also routes each request so the cache and the ranking meet on the same machine. A memory-aware expander also reuses short-term patterns through local storage. In tests with real queries on Huawei Ascend hardware, the system supported sequences up to one and a half times longer and raised throughput several-fold under the same latency limit.
arxiv-2601-01912:
Old observations from China's FAST telescope, the world's largest single-dish radio telescope, still hide undiscovered pulsars. Shi-Jie Gao, Yi-Xuan Shao, and Xiang-Dong Li mined archival data from a strip near the galactic plane. The data held about five hundred hours of observing over a small sky area. The search found nineteen new pulsars.

The newcomers spin with periods from a few hundredths of a second to over five seconds; two fast ones are likely young or mildly recycled. Four show very high dispersion measures. Those probe dense interstellar material. Two are rotating radio transients. They flash only sporadically. Several faint pulsars were caught only by the fast folding algorithm, not standard Fourier searches, underlining how search technique decides what a telescope archive can reveal.
arxiv-2601-02012:
Betelgeuse, the red supergiant in Orion, startled the public in late 2019 when it faded to a third of its normal brightness, sparking talk of an imminent supernova. Priya Hasan recounts the episode and its resolution: the dimming came from an episode of mass loss that released large dust grains, which veiled the star rather than heralding its death.

The story gained a new character in July 2025. The Gemini North telescope directly imaged a faint companion star. It is nicknamed Betelbuddy, or Siwarha. It orbits within Betelgeuse's outer layers. The detection is tentative, and the signal is modest. Still, it matched orbit models remarkably well. Position, brightness, and estimated mass all agreed. Better observations are hoped for in November 2027, when the companion's position should be most favorable.
arxiv-2601-02112:
Predicting a car's aerodynamic drag normally means expensive wind tunnels or fluid simulations. Both are too slow for early design exploration.
