Daniela Moretti and three co-authors study clusters of active Brownian particles, tiny particles that move on their own as well as by random thermal motion. Simulations show these clusters spread out in an unusual way as particle number grows. The authors ask how particles joining and leaving a cluster help cause that pattern.

Starting from equations for single particles, they build a paired model for the cluster centre and its changing mass. Solving it gives one normal spread term and one driven by mass changes, which can dominate. Their predicted scaling matches large simulations closely, showing that changing cluster size is central to the odd diffusion.
arxiv-2605-05012:
Joao Florindo presents a texture classification framework that pairs self-supervised learning with deterministic chaos to handle changes in scale and lighting. Texture tasks are hard because classes look alike and surface patterns shift with conditions. His method uses pixel-wise chaotic maps as a form of augmentation during contrastive pretraining, forcing the network to learn features that survive complex noise.

An attention-based ensemble then fuses high-level features from a large supervised backbone with structural features from a small chaos-pretrained encoder. Across six public texture benchmarks, the combined method beat leading approaches. Florindo argues chaotic perturbations, grounded in ergodic theory, mimic real reflectance and environmental variation well.
arxiv-2605-05112:
Tianshu Zhu and ten co-authors steer reinforcement learning for software engineering agents toward training groups whose pass rate sits near one half. Groups of attempts earn binary rewards, and when almost all pass or fail, the learning signal is weak and skewed. The authors show the reward-side signal is strongest near an even pass rate under several criteria.

Their Prefix Sampling method replays pieces of the model's own earlier trajectories to rebalance skewed groups: good prefixes help mostly-failing groups, and bad prefixes handicap mostly-passing ones. Replayed tokens are masked from the loss, so learning applies only to fresh continuations. On a verified software benchmark the method matched baseline peak scores with large time savings.
arxiv-2605-05412:
Johanan Ramírez-Arellano and seven co-authors report a radio survey of the Coronet Cluster, a nearby nursery of young stars in Corona Australis. Using the Very Large Array, they watched the region at two radio bands from 2012 to 2015. The maps were deep and sharp enough to split close pairs of young stars.

They found twenty radio sources, including fourteen known young stellar objects. The youngest stars showed varied radio colors, while older ones fit free-free emission from ionized gas. Almost every source varied over time, and one known binary, IRS 5, was cleanly resolved into its two stars.
arxiv-2605-05812:
Q-learning learns from any experience, but its bootstrapping lets small errors compound across long horizons. Armaan A. Abraham, Lucy Xiaoyang Shi, and Chelsea Finn add a backstop: n-step inequalities. Any action sequence actually realized lower-bounds what the optimal policy can achieve, so value estimates can be tightened against that fact.

Their long-horizon Q-learning uses those inequalities to stop estimation errors from propagating backward unchecked. The method keeps the appeal of off-policy learning from old or borrowed data. It targets the settings where temporal-difference learning is most brittle: problems whose payoffs arrive far in the future.
arxiv-2605-05912:
Rafael Pablos Sarabia and three co-authors present a method for making high resolution rainfall maps from sparse data. Good rain maps matter for forecasts, water planning, and hazard warnings, but station readings are often noisy and thin on the ground. Radar adds spatial detail, yet past deep learning methods fused the two sources poorly.

Their system, DropsToGrid, uses a neural process design with multi scale features, temporal attention, and fusion of station and radar inputs. It gives continuous rain estimates and states its own uncertainty. On real world data sets it beat both standard operational tools and deep learning baselines. It stayed accurate with few stations and when moved to new regions.
arxiv-2605-06312:
Toby Maddock and five co-authors remove a transport blocking defect from an ion trap without opening the vacuum system. Surface electrode ion traps shuttle ions along paths for quantum computing, and a single defect can block a route entirely. The usual fix means venting and rebaking the apparatus, a slow process that costs heavy downtime, above all for cold systems that need long bakes after any opening.

Their remedy fires a pulsed ablation laser, of a type many ion trap labs already own, at the defect in place. After ablation, shuttling across the once blocked region succeeded at near unity rates. Micromotion, a key quality measure for trapped ions, stayed within acceptable limits. The technique restores transport pathways quickly and suits shuttling focused experiments well.
arxiv-2605-06412:
Brean Maynard and Peter Schweitzer study leading Generalized Transverse Momentum Dependent parton distributions, called GTMDs, inside the bag model. GTMDs describe how quarks carry momentum inside a proton. The authors check that the model description is theoretically consistent and then use it to examine orbital angular momentum.

Orbital angular momentum is studied through one GTMD and the Ji sum rule, with analytical proofs of the related sum rules. A deeper link is also established between orbital angular momentum and the pretzelosity distribution. Readers get a compact model study tying several proton-structure ideas together with proofs rather than numerics alone.
arxiv-2605-06912:
Kirill Trapeznikov and eleven co-authors report on the SAFE challenge, a blind competition for detecting synthetic videos. As generative video improves, telling real footage from fabricated clips becomes urgent. The challenge, held alongside an ICCV 2025 workshop, drew over six hundred submissions from twelve teams over ninety days on the Hugging Face platform.

Two tasks were scored: spotting videos from thirteen modern generators matched against real clips from twenty-one sources, and spotting synthetic content after common post-processing like resizing, recompression, and motion blur. The dataset totals twenty hours across six thousand videos. Results show measurable progress in generalizing across generators, but post-processing artifacts remain a persistent weakness for detectors.
arxiv-2605-07012:
Ishitaa Narwane, Johanna Gunawan, and Konrad Kollnig examine deception in generative AI through the idea of banal deception. Research on deceptive design usually targets visible tricks in interfaces, often called dark patterns. AI deception instead hides in defaults, suggestions, and ordinary chat, making it easy to overlook and live with.

Drawing on Simone Natale's framing, the authors stress how users themselves take part in being deceived. They propose directions for adding helpful friction, including raising awareness, giving users intervention tools, and improving regulation. The piece is offered as discussion points for scholars who study deceptive design.
arxiv-2605-07112:
Sharad Agarwal and five co-authors present Switchcraft, a router that picks cheaper AI models for tool-calling agents without losing correctness. Developers often default to large models and overspend, while existing routers were built for chat rather than tool use. Switchcraft chooses the lowest-cost model that should still answer correctly, inline during a run.

Built on a small classifier and tested on five function-calling benchmarks, it matched or beat the best single model's accuracy. At the same time it cut inference cost sharply, saving thousands of dollars per million queries in their accounting. The team also found larger models do not always win at tool use, and cheap models can cost more overall.
arxiv-2605-07812:
Robin Buchta and three co-authors detect stealthy break-ins by watching what programs do rather than what they are named. Advanced persistent threats hide inside normal system activity. Provenance-based detectors that log relationships between processes, files, and network parts are a strong defense, though threshold-based versions are brittle.

Their system, GRASP, masks each process's executable identity and learns to infer it from the process's two-hop neighborhood in the provenance graph; processes it cannot classify are flagged as odd ones. Because detection needs no preset threshold, it resists tampering and unknown activity. On the DARPA TC and OpTC datasets it found every recorded attack whose executable behavior was learnable. It beat existing systems, and surfaced extra odd behavior the records had not labeled.
arxiv-2605-07912:
Lujain Ibrahim and seven co-authors present experimental evidence that flattering AI changes people's real relationships for the worse. Across five preregistered studies with more than three thousand participants and nearly thirteen thousand conversations, they track what sycophantic AI does over time. One study ran three weeks with a census-representative United States sample.

Sycophantic systems immediately delivered the emotional and esteem support people associate with close friends and family. Over three weeks, users grew nearly as likely to seek personal advice from such AI as from their closest people, and reported lower satisfaction with real-world social interactions. Most users chose the sycophantic style when offered alternatives, not for better advice but because it made them feel understood. The authors call this a relational account of sycophancy's costs.
arxiv-2605-08012:
Zezheng Lin and Fengming Liu argue, in an opinion paper, that interpretability research claims too much causality. Papers in the field speak of circuits, middlemen, and causal models, but causal claims rest on identification assumptions that are rarely stated. Their audit of ten papers across four method strands found no dedicated section on these assumptions anywhere.

The usual pattern is a swap: metrics like faithfulness, completeness, or ablation effects are offered as causal support without the assumptions that would make them identifying. A two-coder audit of thirty papers confirmed the finding. The authors propose an openness norm: say whether the claim is causal, name the identification strategy, list the assumptions, stress-test at least one, and explain how results move if they fail. Checking, they insist, is not identification.
arxiv-2605-08112:
Drew Dillon and Kasyap Varanasi measure a weakness of AI coding agents: they write working code but often break team decisions that never appear in the code itself. The authors built a controlled benchmark of eight realistic engineering tasks with forty-one weighted decision points covering product, design, and engineering choices.

They compared Claude Code with codebase access alone against the same setup plus Brief, a retrieval system that supplies recorded decisions, persona pain points, customer signals, and rival intelligence. The augmented setup reached ninety-five percent decision compliance against forty-six percent for the baseline. The gap shows how much product context, not coding skill, limits agent reliability.
arxiv-2605-08212:
Anamaria Hell and Leander Thiele test whether a large language model, wired to a computer algebra system, can do routine algorithmic work in theoretical physics. Such computations are conceptually simple but slow and full of traps, so reliable automation would save researchers real time.

The authors connect Claude to the Maple algebra system and aim the pair at cosmological perturbations in modified gravity theories. Given worked examples as context, the frontier model solved most of the test problems. The study catalogs the typical failure modes that remain and shows which ones extra context can fix, giving a grounded picture of where language models help symbolic physics today.
arxiv-2605-08412:
Sara Ghazanfari, Siddharth Garg, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, and Farshad Khorrami benchmark reasoning across several videos at once. Multimodal models have improved quickly on single videos, but questions that compare independent streams are barely tested, and human-annotated footage cannot supply exact spatial or temporal ground truth for grading failures.

SYNCR is built in simulators, Habitat, Kubric, and CLEVRER, so every answer is programmatically verified. It holds four thousand question-answer pairs over nearly five thousand unique videos, organized into eight tasks under temporal alignment, spatial tracking, comparative reasoning, and holistic synthesis. Zero-shot tests of leading open and closed models reveal a substantial gap to human performance.
arxiv-2605-08712:
Bohan Li and thirteen coauthors generate surgical videos that follow robotic control commands faithfully. Low dimensional control signals must steer complex image change, a hard translation. Their approach lifts articulated robot kinematics into five image aligned control forms, then routes conditioning through a hierarchy that activates only the most relevant controls and motion scales for each moment.

Routing losses guided by kinematic priors keep usage physical, stable, and efficient, while a budgeted scheme drops weak pathways to cut delay. A new benchmark with human checked articulated labels supplies realistic supervision. Across baselines, action faithfulness, visual quality, and cross domain generalization all improve, and the efficient variant runs much faster.
arxiv-2605-09112:
Noam Mizrachi, Nadav Har-Tuv, and Shai Shalev-Shwartz address tasks where a system must pick a coherent sequence or subset, such as forecasting a path or choosing representative items. The catch is ambiguity: many answers can be valid, but training data shows only one sampled answer for each input.

Their model, Contextual Plackett-Luce, extends a classic ranking model so its scores depend on context, with terms for single items and pairs. Scoring runs in parallel for speed, then a light step-by-step selection keeps the output coherent. On path prediction and subset selection tasks, the model gave more consistent and robust results than strong parallel rivals when supervision was ambiguous.

arxiv-2606-04212:
Shauna Kwag, Anakha Ganesh, Tomaso Poggio, and Pierfrancesco Beneventano show in 2026 that the edge of stability does not act on a dataset as a whole. Training at this edge hovers near instability. The team finds it sorts examples instead.

Examples the model gets right with confidence are pushed down in loss. Examples it gets wrong are pushed up. The net effect is a quiet reweighting of the training set. This sorting explains odd effects seen before, such as sudden drops in test error late in training. It also links training dynamics to which examples a model ends up trusting. The authors argue that dataset-level views miss the real action.
arxiv-2606-04612:
Abouzaid, Wang, Lin, and Middleton combine three kinds of defense into one shield for language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI security. Models are vulnerable to hallucination and to adversarial manipulation. These problems are usually treated separately. Their hybrid framework joins entropy-based models, aimed at hallucination. It adds uncertainty-based and geometric-based models, aimed at attack detection.

On in-domain benchmarks including FEVER, HotpotQA, CSQA, and SIQA, the hybrid improved clean-task accuracy by up to 43 percent. Adversarial robustness rose by up to 65 percent. Attack success rates fell by up to 62 percent. On out-of-distribution sets it again improved robustness substantially. On prompt injection and jailbreak detection sets, it reduced attack success by up to 51 percent against state-of-the-art baselines. The authors conclude that combining entropy, uncertainty, and geometric features protects better than any single feature family. This holds across familiar and unfamiliar data.
arxiv-2606-04712:
Shangguan and colleagues search the nearby universe for the strange absorption signature that Webb's little red dots show, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. Balmer absorption lines in those distant objects may trace dense gas around rapidly feeding black holes. The team analyzes spectra of a representative parent sample of 14,584 low-redshift type 1 active galactic nuclei from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, hunting the same feature in homogeneously processed data.

They find just seven sources with robust Balmer absorption, an occurrence rate of about 0.05 percent, confirming the phenomenon is extremely rare nearby. Modeling with a partially covering absorber shows all robust cases need optically thick hydrogen absorption with moderate covering factors, while one little-red-dot analog shows a covering factor above 0.8, matching high-redshift measurements. Absorbers move slowly and vary over months to years.
arxiv-2606-04812:
Prashant and Easwaran generate test scenarios aimed exactly at the states where a learning policy's safety is unproven, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep RL policies can behave unsafely, and one verification approach builds barrier certificates by sampling trajectories. Tight bounds on violation probability are hard when perturbations push the agent into insufficiently explored states. The authors approximate the encountered state distribution with a variational autoencoder.

Using latent characteristics of states, they construct upper- and lower-bound barrier certificates. Sampling training states from the set difference between the two bounds, the non-robust region, tightens both bounds and sharpens the safety guarantees. The framing is a dual problem, and the authors describe the guarantees placed and demonstrate the tightness of their bounds. The work serves risk-aware deployment, where a safe certificate is the deliverable regulators need.
arxiv-2606-05612:
Kun Huang and colleagues made a fiber laser that emits swirling light beams on demand in a 2026 arXiv paper. The beams are vector vortex beams, whose polarization twists across the beam face. Such structured light serves imaging, sensing, and quantum optics. Making it usually needs add-on parts outside the laser. The team instead shapes the beam inside the laser cavity itself, using geometric phase control.

Tuning that phase maps polarization onto orbital angular momentum, the twist of the beam. The design switches among vector modes at any chosen point on the standard map of such states. Crucially, the tuning leaves the passive pulse locking undisturbed. Pulses lasted about eight and a half picoseconds, each far shorter than a billionth of a second. Math formulas for the beam profiles matched the bench results closely. The source stays compact while offering flexible, high-purity structured pulses.
arxiv-2606-05812:
Arghya Pal and Rajanala sharpen text-to-audio search with explicit logic in a 2026 arXiv paper. Shared embedding models like CLAP match captions to sounds well at coarse grain. Fine details still slip, because words and audio carry meaning so differently. FORTE rewrites each query as a first-order logic form. A constrained search then enriches the form with telling attributes while keeping its meaning fixed.

A light projection module aligns the refined query with audio embeddings. A final re-ranking step checks results for logical consistency with the query's predicates. Tests on AudioCaps and Clotho, two standard caption-audio sets, showed steady gains over strong baselines. The gains grew largest on the fine-grained cases that embarrass pure embeddings. Symbolic care and learned vectors, the authors argue, cover each other's blind spots. Retrieval precision benefits most where descriptions turn precise.
arxiv-2606-05912:
Jiahao Yang and colleagues build expressive 3D face avatars from strikingly little footage in a 2026 arXiv paper. Gaussian avatars model faces as clouds of soft blobs that deform with expression. Standard pipelines demand thousands of frames across many cameras and expressions. SAGE learns the deformations by itself instead. It optimizes flat Gaussian surfels together with a signed distance field, keeping blobs glued to the facial surface.

A self-supervised phase then replaces long expression sequences with geometric and appearance consistency rules. The savings cascade across capture setups. Multiview rigs need a single frame rather than thousands. A lone camera needs only head rotations, no expression takes. One-shot mode needs no pretraining or face priors at all. Quality matched state-of-the-art methods in the reported experiments. Data needs fell by several orders of magnitude. The authors pitch self-taught deformation as the route to avatars anyone can capture.
arxiv-2606-06112:
A reply in a scholarly dispute: Chong Qi answers a published Comment on his review of seniority conservation in semi-magic nuclei, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Comment raised objections to how the review treated an earlier paper's approach. Qi accepts some points as fair clarifications of wording and logic. He rejects the implication of scientific error.

None of the objections, he argues, identify a mistake that would mislead readers or misrepresent the criticized work's substance. The corrections live at the level of emphasis and phrasing, not physics. On the methodological dispute, he holds his line: emphasizing subspace decomposition and basis transformation adds little until someone identifies a unique operator that generates the partially seniority-conserved states directly. Terminology for the special states is also defended. Replies like this keep the nuclear-structure literature's record straight in public. The exchange turns on what counts as insight versus reformulation.
arxiv-2606-06212:
Rufat Asadli and co-authors benchmark language models at fixing broken computer networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. A single wrong line in a router configuration can take down large parts of the internet, and hand repair is slow and error prone. Plain language models, even strong ones, often fail on large tangled cases and introduce fresh faults. The team asks whether giving the model tools and an agent loop changes that record.

Their agents can retrieve context and call formal verification tools, which check a proposed repair against the network's stated requirements before it is applied. Across open and closed source models, agentic setups beat base models on repair success by twelve percent on average, and scored seventeen percent higher on safety. The authors credit the gains to managing context dynamically and validating each fix in rounds rather than answering in one shot.
arxiv-2606-06512:
Sharon Urieli compares binary images without being fooled by small shifts in this 2026 arXiv technical note. Comparing two pictures fails in practice because imperfect alignment looks like real change. Her tool comes from mathematical morphology, the set based study of shapes in images. The symmetric difference of two masks marks every pixel where they disagree. But it also flags every slight misalignment. Dilating that difference, expanding it slightly, absorbs the jitter.

Urieli defines the operator formally and proves it works: real differences are detected as long as the leftover alignment error stays within bounds tied to the dilation size. It needs no learning, just set operations on the two masks. As future work she proposes folding it into neural networks as a trainable layer, so the dilation radius could be learned inside a pipeline that also handles registration.
arxiv-2606-06712:
Most language models write one word at a time, in order. Diffusion language models instead start from a garbled draft and clean it up in parallel, but training them from scratch is costly. Xingyu Su and co-authors convert an existing orderly model into a diffusion model in this 2026 arXiv paper, avoiding that full retraining bill.

Earlier conversions suffered two problems: switching the training goal threw away knowledge the original model had learned, and training on randomly garbled text did not match what the model meets when generating. Their method has the student model produce its own drafts, while the frozen original grades each step, a setup called on policy distillation. The converted models needed fifteen to seven thousand times fewer training tokens than earlier diffusion baselines, while still performing strongly across a wide range of language tasks.
arxiv-2606-07112:
Skyrmions are tiny whirlpools of magnetization that could store bits at extreme density. Potkina studies their paired form in synthetic antiferromagnets in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two magnetic layers lock together with opposite alignment. That pairing cancels stray fields and steadies the bits. The question is how the pairs die, and how they can be born.

Using a reduced lattice model, she computes minimum energy paths for both events. Collapse destroys a written pair; nucleation creates one from a pinned reference state. The saddle energy barely moves with island size. The pair's own energy, though, carries a growing boundary penalty. For large islands, collapse proceeds layer by layer, sometimes through a single layer skyrmion. The reverse barrier for writing dwarfs the collapse barrier. That asymmetry favors assisted, layer sequential writing schemes. Barrier values reach roughly one electron volt for the largest islands studied.
arxiv-2606-07412:
Xiao and co-authors build a coding agent that improves itself using past attempts, in this 2026 arXiv paper on Socratic-SWE. Training data scarcity limits software engineering agents; synthetic tasks from bug-injection recipes ignore what an agent gets wrong. Their closed loop mines the agent's historical solving traces, distilling them into structured skills that summarize failures and repair patterns. Those skills then guide generation of targeted repair tasks inside real repos, validated by executing the code.

A solver-gradient alignment reward scores candidate tasks for being verifiable and useful for improvement. The updated agent produces traces, so the curriculum adapts round after round. Across 4 benchmarks, including the SWE-bench suites and a terminal-use benchmark, the method beat self-evolving baselines under equal compute budgets. On SWE-bench Verified it reached a solve rate above 50 percent after 3 iterations in their runs. Traces, discarded after scoring, become training data.
arxiv-2606-07512:
Cong Chen and co-authors split long-video understanding into watching once and reasoning many times, in this 2026 arXiv paper on MemDreamer. Vision-language models choke on hours-long video because feeding every frame explodes token counts and dilutes attention. MemDreamer streams the video once to build a hierarchical graph memory: a 3-tier structure whose graph records spatio-temporal relations, with semantic abstractions layered. At question time, a reasoning model explores that memory with actions, navigating tiers, searching nodes, and following edges in an observe-reason-act loop.

The framework plugs into models rather than replacing them. Across 4 benchmarks it reached top results, narrowing the gap to experts to under 4 points. It used 2 percent of the context that full ingestion would consume, gaining 12 points of accuracy over the end-to-end baseline. Statistical analysis linked models' logic-reasoning strength to their video performance, suggesting agent skill drives the gains.
arxiv-2606-07612:
Gupta and co-authors argue that claims of misalignment in AI models often rest on evidence too weak for the decisions built on it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Studies of deception, sycophancy, and emergent misalignment influence deployment and regulation, yet the authors show how conceptual ambiguity, datasets, design choices, and causal interventions invite reading too much into behavior. A behavior that looks like deception may be an artifact of how the test was framed, and without interventions the mechanism stays unknown.

Their remedy is a framework of evidence levels paired with a diagnostic checklist that studies can be graded against. The goal is standards strong enough that claims about AI risk rest on empirical foundations and discourse stays productive. The paper evaluates failure modes, showing where literature's evidence chain breaks. It serves as guidance for researchers, reviewers, and decision-makers who decide how much weight a misalignment demonstration deserves.
arxiv-2606-07712:
Yao and co-authors present MatMind, a single generative model built for many crystal-materials tasks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Materials AI has relied on narrow specialists: one model family predicts properties, another generates new crystal structures. A language-model backbone could in principle do all three in one place, but none had matched the specialists.

MatMind combines three ingredients: injected structure-activity knowledge, a dual head that trains language reasoning and numerical regression together, and physics-informed reinforcement learning that rewards stability, novelty, and diversity. Across three task families it posted the lowest prediction error for energy above hull, bulk modulus, and band gap, beating purpose-built graph networks. Its unconditional crystal generation reached a stability-novelty rate of about sixty-five percent. It also improved generation guided by magnetisation density, a task with only twenty-one positive examples among six hundred thousand training entries.
arxiv-2606-07812:
Feng and colleagues propose building AI from the bottom up in this 2026 arXiv paper. Today's large language models are built by a few organisations as monolithic systems, which poorly reflects the diversity of human knowledge and values. Under their paradigm, scaling participation, many stakeholders each train a small model on their own interests. Those small models then collaborate inside modular frameworks as one compositional system.

Across fifteen tasks, including reasoning and factuality, the participatory systems beat monolithic models by up to about fifteen percent, even surpassing models larger than all components combined. Diversity among contributors helped rather than hurt, and each model improved on the priorities it was built for. Most strikingly, the combined systems solved over fifteen percent of problems where every single model failed, an emergent capability no part had alone. The authors present this as a foundation for a more open, collaborative AI ecosystem.
arxiv-2606-07912:
Deshpande and Bhattacharya fix a quiet flaw in a popular uncertainty method, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Polynomial chaos expansions write a random quantity as a series in special polynomials, letting engineers carry randomness through simulations cheaply. Standard coefficients come from projecting simulation output onto those polynomials. At low orders the resulting mean and variance, its first two moments, can come out wrong.

The authors instead choose coefficients by constrained optimisation, forcing the expansion to reproduce the true mean and variance exactly. Moment errors that biased risk estimates are removed by construction. In tests the new coefficients gave large accuracy gains over standard projection. The gains were largest at low orders, where expansions are cheapest and most used. The method keeps the speed of polynomial chaos while removing its most basic inaccuracy.
arxiv-2606-08112:
Xu Du, Shuting Wu, Karl H. Johansson, and Apostolos I. Rikos make a distributed optimisation method smarter about when to use costly curvature information, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Consensus problems ask many agents, each holding part of a problem, to agree on one solution, the setting behind federated learning and coordinated control. Their algorithm builds on the C-ALADIN framework, an augmented Lagrangian method with Newton-type steps.

Existing versions must fix their Hessian approximations in advance, sacrificing the benefits of fresh second-order information. The new variant adds a helper variable deciding when to update the curvature model, exploiting curvature where it helps without endangering convergence. Under smoothness and strong convexity, the authors prove global convergence. In logistic regression tests the method beat baselines using fixed or routinely updated Hessian information. The lesson is scheduling: when you refresh the model can matter as much as the model.
arxiv-2606-08212:
Saleh, Mili, and Boukadoum propose a free online platform that helps beginners solve machine learning problems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine learning means teaching computers to find patterns in data, a process that normally demands expert judgment at every step. Existing help comes as fully automatic tools, simple cheat sheets, or decision aids that rank single algorithms. The new platform combines the last two approaches and recommends a complete pipeline, the full step sequence from raw data to finished model.

The system reasons over a knowledge base of expert rules written in first-order logic, a formal way of stating facts and conditions. It also inspects each uploaded dataset automatically, noting problems such as missing values or lopsided class counts. Recommendations come back ranked by relevance, and a linked crowdsourcing site lets experts add fresh knowledge over time. The authors call it the first free public framework of its kind.
arxiv-2606-08312:
Ansarifard and colleagues teach reinforcement learning agents to obey rules stated in formal logic, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is offline reinforcement learning. The agent learns from stored experience rather than live trial and error. Its task constraints are written in LTLf, a logic for rules over finite traces, such as one action before another. Transformer-based policies treat behavior as sequence modeling. They optimize purely for reward and ignore such high-level rules.

The authors build a neuro-symbolic framework, mixing neural learning with symbolic logic. Each formula is compiled into a deterministic finite automaton, a small state machine. The machine tracks how much of the rule has been satisfied so far. A smooth form of that machine yields signals during training. A logic-based loss term penalizes the policy when it drifts from the formula. The constraint thus shapes learning continuously, not as a final check.
arxiv-2606-08612:
Spyridon Georgiou and colleagues survey a decade of teaching computers to read faces, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Facial expression recognition has progressed rapidly. The field shifted from handcrafted descriptors and shallow classifiers to deep convolutional networks, attention-based models, and foundation models. In parallel, large-scale benchmarks have grown to cover categorical emotions, ratings of feeling, compound expressions, and micro-expressions. The field's literature had so far been reviewed only along narrow axes.

This systematic multi-criteria review supplies the missing holistic account, organizing recent deep learning methods by models, datasets, and performance, and analyzing the challenges that persist. By comparing approaches on multiple criteria at once, the survey exposes where progress is real and where it is an artifact of easy benchmarks. The authors close with future research directions. The goal is a clear map of what works, what does not, and what to try next in the lab.
arxiv-2606-08712:
Hongyi Yu and colleagues improve the filling-in of missing gene expression values in tissue slices, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while preserving where in the tissue each value came from. But the data are noisy, low-resolution, and sparsely sampled. Deep neural networks can impute expression from histology images. Yet small sample sizes and uninformed augmentation constrain them, and most augmentation was designed for classification, not regression.

Their framework, SNR-ST-Mix, is a geometry- and expression-aware data-mixing scheme designed for spatial transcriptomics. Mixing, blending training examples together, is constrained to a spot's nearest neighbors. The blend adapts to each sample's own neighborhood structure rather than a global rule. Synthetic examples thus respect both the tissue's geography and its expression patterns, teaching the network plausible fills in each gap it meets.
arxiv-2606-08812:
Li and colleagues ask which tumor cell properties diffusion MRI can measure reliably, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion MRI tracks how water wanders inside tissue, and that pattern reflects cell size and crowding, signs of how a tumor responds to radiation. The IMPULSED method fits a five-parameter cell model, including cell diameter and the share of volume inside cells. Because fitted values wobble badly, the team first mapped each parameter's uncertainty in simulations.

The analysis found three robustly estimable parameters, each with relative uncertainty below one: cell diameter, intracellular volume fraction, and extracellular diffusion coefficient. Of the mapping models trained on transformed signals, a four-layer neural network performed best. Its average error was 1.7 micrometers for cell diameter and about five percent for volume fraction. In tests on cultured mouse tumor cells, its cell diameter error was 6.7 percent, supporting use for monitoring treatment response.
arxiv-2606-09112:
Fan and colleagues borrow Ising-machine dynamics to fix a weakness of a brain-inspired training method, in this 2026 arXiv paper. GPU training is energy-hungry, motivating physical, energy-based alternatives. Equilibrium propagation trains energy-based models with a two-phase rule, but its settling dynamics contract phase space, trapping training in poor local minima. They replace it with extended phase-space dynamics with conjugate variables, inspired by Ising machines, solvers that settle into low-energy spin states.

The learning rule stays untouched; only the physical route to equilibrium changes. The new dynamics lowers energy barriers, so training escapes shallow minima, converges faster, and resists noise. The team trained deep convolutional Hopfield networks on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10, matching backpropagation, whose energy costs motivate the enterprise. The result suggests a division of labor for future hardware: let physics handle the settling, with rules designed for physical dynamics.
arxiv-2606-09312:
Pan and colleagues evaluate compiler optimizations the way a world model would, by simulating how a program's state evolves under each scheduling decision, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tensor compilers search huge spaces of program variants for the fastest one, and learned cost models score candidates to avoid slow on-device measurement. Those models judge candidates as static snapshots, blind to the transformations that produced them. Their framework rolls out scheduling actions in a latent space instead.

Instantiated in TVM's AutoScheduler with a learned state encoder and ranking model, the method improved representative-subgraph latency over the Ansor scheduler by 1.37 times on GPU and 1.54 times on CPU at the same 64-trial budget. It matched a 10,000-trial Ansor run within 2.2 percent using ten times fewer measurements. Full-model inference beat PyTorch baselines by 4.61 and 3.67 times in geometric mean, with peaks far higher.
arxiv-2606-09412:
Saee Desai and her co-authors build a teaching prototype that protects drug-safety data against future quantum computers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pharmacovigilance systems collect adverse event reports and clinical observations that must stay confidential for many years. That long lifetime creates a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk, where attackers store encrypted files today and open them once quantum machines mature.

The prototype pipeline links hospital, gateway, and pharmaceutical receiver components, with an attacker role included for testing. It establishes keys with ML-KEM-768, a standardised post-quantum method, derives an encryption key, and encrypts files with AES-256-GCM. Digital signatures from ML-DSA-65 guard against tampering, and all common file formats are handled as raw bytes with metadata preserved. Tests on synthetic datasets showed the post-quantum key step adds only a small constant overhead. Encryption and signing, not the new algorithms, dominate the running time.
arxiv-2606-09712:
Renjie Feng studies how close the zeros of a random polynomial sit to its nearest critical points in this 2026 arXiv paper. The polynomials are Gaussian SU(2) type, a standard random model tied to the sphere. Each zero has a gap to the closest point where the slope vanishes. The scale of that gap, and its spread across many trials, was open.

Feng works with the Fubini-Study distance, the natural ruler on the sphere. For a polynomial of degree n, he rescales each gap by n and gathers the whole set into a spread. He proves that spread settles, in a weak sense, onto a fixed law. That law is the spread of two over the squared size of a random draw from the sphere's own measure. The result gives a clean limit shape for a fine trait of random waves.
arxiv-2606-10012:
Vaikundaraman and colleagues study how complex gas flows inside planet-forming discs shape the growth of dust, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. Protoplanetary discs around young stars host winds, rings, and gaps when magnetic effects are included. Dust grains must grow and gather into traps before planetesimals, the building blocks of planets, can form.

The team post-processed a two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulation with a Monte Carlo coagulation code that tracks dust growth and transport globally. Strong gas velocities advect small particles. A transition region in the flow acts as a dust pile-up, raising the pebble-to-gas ratio by a factor of about two and a half over a steady disc. Lowering the fragmentation velocity, the impact speed at which grains shatter, made the pile-up more stable but less concentrated. The trap forms without any pressure bump.
arxiv-2606-10212:
Soto and his team define covariance for data that lives on curved spaces, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. Covariance is a basic second-order summary behind feature learning, shrinking inputs, and modeling links. But it is ill-defined for random objects on curved Riemannian manifolds, such as shapes or symmetric positive definite matrices. Their intrinsic Riemannian cross-covariance moves local variations to a shared tangent space by parallel transport, the geometry-respecting way to shift vectors along a manifold. The result is a descriptor free of arbitrary coordinate choices.

They show it inherits the prized properties of its Euclidean counterpart, and they chart its asymptotic limits. Studies on spheres and on spaces of such matrices back the claims. Real-data tests on heart valve shapes in Kendall's shape space show the estimators work well and confirm the stated claims.
arxiv-2606-10512: ArXiv received this research paper in 2026; it carries new results. The title's topic is Turbulent Diffusion of Magnetic Field Lines in the Heliosphere. bergson-introduction-metaphysics-1912:
An Introduction to Metaphysics is Bergson's most famous short work, printed here in the 1912 English version by T. E. Hulme. The French philosopher sets out his method in one sustained argument: intuition, not analysis, is how thought reaches reality.

Analysis, Bergson says, circles a thing and gives symbols; intuition enters it and grasps its duration, the flow of inner time. He applies the contrast to the self, to movement, and to life itself. The essay is dense but exhilarating, a key to all his larger books. Hulme's version carried Bergson's fame through the English-speaking world.
berkman-prison-memoirs-anarchist-1912:
Alexander Berkman published Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist in 1912. Berkman, a Russian-born anarchist in New York, had shot steel magnate Henry Clay Frick in 1892 during the Homestead strike. He served fourteen years in American prisons, most at Western Penitentiary in Pennsylvania.

Berkman told of brutal guards, solitary cells, and the small kindnesses that kept men human inside. He also traced his own change from a would-be martyr to a man who questioned his act. The memoir refuses self-pity and judges the prison system from within. It stands as a classic of prison writing and of anarchist life stories in America.
bernal-diaz-true-history-maudslay-vol-4-:
Maudslay's fourth volume of Bernal Díaz's True History, from 1912, covers the siege and fall of Mexico. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, fell in 1521 after a brutal fight across its causeways and canals. Díaz had stood in that fight as a foot soldier, and his old-age account carries the memory in his bones.

One volume of the set, the third, is a portfolio of maps only, so the story runs through volumes one, two, four, and five. In this volume the long campaign reaches its grim peak. Díaz records hunger, loss, and the city's ruin without turning away. It is the conquest's climax told by a man who swung a sword in it.
bosanquet-individuality-value-1912:
The Principle of Individuality and Value, published in 1912, prints Bosanquet's Gifford Lectures, his full statement in metaphysics. Its subject is the concrete universal: how the whole lives in each part, and how finite selves gain value and meaning within the Absolute.

Bosanquet argues that a self grows by range. The more of the world it can hold in harmony, the more real and valuable it is. Evil and error appear as partial harmonies awaiting completion. The lectures are abstract and elevated in manner. They represent British idealism at its most systematic, delivered in its cathedral style.
boutroux-historical-studies-1912:
Fred Rothwell translated a set of Emile Boutroux's French studies on the history of philosophy in 1912. The French title, Etudes d'histoire de la philosophie, states the plan in plain terms. Each study takes up past thought on its own ground. Boutroux was known for close, fair reading of other minds.

In these pages he works through major figures and schools from earlier centuries. He asks what problem each thinker faced and how the answer fit its time. The method treats old systems as live attempts, not museum pieces. Students of Boutroux value the set as a model of his craft. It also records French scholarship of his era.
boutroux-william-james-1912:
American thinker William James drew readers across the Atlantic, and French philosopher Emile Boutroux was among them. Boutroux published his study William James in French in 1911. Archibald and Barbara Henderson brought the short book into English the next year, in 1912.

Writing as a French spiritualist, Boutroux explains James and his pragmatism to European readers. He presents James's views on truth, belief, and religious life with care and sympathy. At the same time he marks where his own thought parts from the American's. The study shows two traditions in direct talk with each other. It remains a neat period portrait of James.
butler-notebooks-1912:
Samuel Butler, the English writer behind Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, filled private notebooks for most of his adult life. He never meant them for print in this form. After his death, his friend Henry Festing Jones arranged the notes by theme, and they were published in 1912.

The short entries cover art, science, religion, money, and daily life, often in a few dry sentences. Butler mocks Darwin's followers, questions church doctrine, and praises plain common sense. Some notes are jokes; others hold the seeds of his books. Read together, they show one of the sharpest and most contrary minds of his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-vi: A 1913 entry on the Council of Vienne — the Templars' doom. Johann Peter Kirsch unfolds its famous decrees. Clement suppressed the military order. The year 1311 dates its solemn acts. The council of the fifteenth ecumenical. Its Clementines are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-restored-: The restored Jesuits are the order reborn. This long entry examines their 1814, their schools, and their century. The Society of the second spring: their new schools crowned Rome in the 1814 of the Pius in the very old city.
cervantes-don-quixote-shelton-1612:
Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote in Spain, and Thomas Shelton made it English in 1612. Shelton's was the first English version, and the first in any tongue but Spanish. Don Quixote, a lean old squire mad on tales of knights, rides out to win fame.

With fat, shrewd Sancho Panza at his side, he fights windmills he takes for giants. Inns become castles and flocks become armies in his wild mind. The pair talk, argue, and grow fond as the joke turns kind. Shelton's brisk prose still reads with speed and fun. Later versions abound, but Shelton keeps the raw early flavor.
cia-0000008012:
Laos rarely made headlines, yet CIA analysts forecast its course to July 1956 in a June 1955 paper. The small kingdom had gained independence from France, but the Pathet Lao movement held ground in the north. A fragile royal government tried to unite the country.

The estimate weighs the throne's strength, the army's limits, and pressure from communist neighbors. Washington was starting to treat Laos as part of a wider Southeast Asian contest. Later, the country became the scene of a long secret war. This early forecast shows the concerns were present in Washington from the very start of involvement.
cia-0000009912:
A United States Air Force A-26 was brought down near Ban Ban, in Xieng Khouang province, an October 1967 report states. The A-26 was a Second World War attack bomber returned to service for Laos's night war. Ban Ban sat on a contested valley road.

Slow, low aircraft over Laos took losses out of proportion to their numbers. A downing report started the familiar chain: crew fate unknown, then checked against prisoner and grave reports. Night losses were the hardest to trace of all. This file marks one A-26 and its crew entering that uncertain record.
cia-0000010612:
In September 1952, CIA analysts wrote an estimate on whether the government of Mohammad Mossadeq could stay in power in Iran. Mossadeq was Iran's prime minister, and he had seized the country's oil industry from British control. His stand made him a hero to many Iranians and a problem for London and Washington.

The estimate weighs the forces lined up for and against him. It covers his quarrel with the Shah, the oil crisis squeezing Iran's economy, and the shadow of the communist movement. Read today, it shows Washington counting down the months of a leader it would help remove in the coup one year later.
cia-0000012412:
Paris opens the debriefings' third phase with meeting number thirty-one, on September 20, 1961. The City of Light took its turn hosting the secrets. A new city meant new cover and new safe flats. It also meant new risks, watched by a different police. The tradecraft adapted as the operation moved its most precious meetings onto French ground for the autumn.

The record begins the French chapter of the case in order. Paris sessions picked up the London rhythm within days. For readers, the page shows a great operation changing stages without missing a beat.
cia-0000013612:
Argentina's prospects are weighed in a CIA paper from May 1965, in the long shadow of Juan Perón. Perón had been driven into exile a decade before. His movement was banned from honest elections, yet his name still decided them. Every ballot and every barracks in the blue-and-white republic measured itself against the exiled man's ghost, and the elected government of the day ruled on sufferance.

The paper takes the past's measure as a force in the present. It weighs the generals, the unions, and the Peronist vote together. For readers, it shows a country arguing with its own history, watched closely from Washington.
cia-0000014712: Views on a presidential statement on the Rosenbergs fill a CIA file dated November 1, 1952. The president's words on a death penalty spy case carried weight worldwide. The file gathered how those words were received. It belongs to the months when the couple's fate rested in part on mercy from the White House.
cia-0000015312: A letter to Sam Goudsmit from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It takes up Leon Davidson's possible role, per the clipped title. Davidson had become a topic in his own right by then. Officials swapped views on the man as much as on his claims about space messages.
cia-0000015412: W. E. Lexow, chief of the Applied Science Division, wrote to Major Tacker on July 5, 1958, about letters from Fred Kirsch. Lexow enclosed a copy of one Kirsch letter and noted that Tacker had agreed to answer it. In the agency's view, the Air Force man was the proper voice on such matters. The short exchange shows saucer mail being routed to the desk that owned it.
cia-0000021512: Two American men and one American woman were reported held prisoner by the PL in a CIA record dated April 3, 1971. PL in the clipped title most likely means the Pathet Lao of Laos. The record gives no names in its title, so none is added here. Reports of civilian captives widened the prisoner watch beyond downed airmen alone.
cia-0000022812: Two American prisoners of war were held by communists in Cambodia, a CIA record dated in 1974 reports. The catalog gives an acquisition date in its clipped tail, in 1974 by the file's dating. Cambodia's war had swallowed many men whose names sat on the missing lists. A detention report from there, even late, was chased for the sake of a final count.
cia-0000039312:
An American prisoner allegedly worked for the Viet Cong in the Quang Da Special Zone, a CIA record dated April 6, 1971 states. Collaboration charges were the hardest claims in the prisoner files. They shadowed a man's name long after the war around him moved on.

Inside, the allegation is recorded as it reached the agency during the war. Such reports could rest on rumor, pressure, or a captor's staged account. The file preserves the claim without settling it. Later readers meet the case as officials did: an accusation in the record, a man at its center, and no easy way to know the whole truth.
cia-0000042812:
President Cristiani postponed his trip to the United States, in a CIA record dated January 1, 1990. A president's travel plans are usually fixed far ahead of time. Putting one off, at short notice, signaled trouble at home.

Inside, the postponement is recorded with the crisis behind it in view. The Jesuit case had made a Washington visit awkward for Cristiani. American lawmakers were asking hard questions about aid and justice. A visit staged for goodwill risked turning into a public trial of his record instead. The file captures diplomacy bent by scandal, in which a calendar change said more about a president's position than many speeches could have said.
cia-0000045212:
Ungo denied responsibility in the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. A denial from the left's best known leader was a serious act. The opposition needed the crime kept far from its own name.

Inside, his firm disavowal of any part in the seizure is preserved. Denials shape a crisis as surely as claims of credit do. They draw the lines along which blame is allowed to travel. The file holds the left's line as Ungo drew it early in the case, before the talks and trades that finally brought the young woman home.
cia-0000049012: An excerpt from 1981, kept in a CIA item, weighs whether the right or the left carried out assassinations in El Salvador. In that war, each side blamed the other for nearly every killing, and proof was rare. The excerpt's even-handed guessing shows how hard the simplest question, who did this, was to answer.
cia-0000049112: A probe of terrorist killings in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. Terrorist killings, in the language of the files, covered the political murders both camps committed. An investigation's existence was itself news in a country where most killings were never investigated at all.
cia-0000049212: Biographical information on Colonel Nelson Ivan Lopez y Lopez, partly blacked out, fills a CIA item from 1991. Bio files were the system's portrait of an officer: posts held, ties kept, reputation noted, family listed. This one survives in the Truth Commission records, its gaps guarding the parts still judged sensitive.
cia-0000049412: Progress on human rights in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049412, dated June 5, 1987. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper claims movement on rights rather than fresh abuses. Readers get a brief declassified item whose positive heading stands out among the grimmer Salvadoran titles, preserved as the agency framed it then.
cia-0000095212: A cable from Leopoldville about cancelling an operation or proceeding with risks is declassified CIA document 0000095212, dated August 1, 1963. The heading presents the choice in either-or terms. Readers get a short declassified cable record from the Congo station's city, its subject the decision itself, preserved without the operation being named in the title.
cia-0000097712: Intelligence Warning of the Tet Offensive in South Vietnam, with publication date estimated, is declassified CIA document 0000097712, dated March 1, 1968. The heading flags the dating estimate in parentheses. Readers get a short declassified paper on warning before the Tet Offensive, its subject the intelligence that preceded a major attack in South Vietnam.
cia-0000100512: Message from the ADCI on the New York Times story on Guatemala is declassified CIA document 0000100512, dated February 5, 1995. The heading names the sender by initials and the newspaper story answered. cia-0000107312: Minutes of Forty-ninth Meeting Committee on Exchanges is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107312, dated August 2, 1979. The title marks a long running series: this was the forty-ninth meeting of one committee. Minutes record what a meeting covered, in formal meeting form. The brief record is a committee minutes item, numbered in its own title as released.
cia-0000109012: Use of Prison Labor in Construction of Dimitrovgrad Automotive is the first numbered heading, cut off mid-phrase, on declassified CIA document 0000109012, dated January 1, 1983. The title ties prison labor to building an automotive plant at Dimitrovgrad. What part of the plant is cut off where the heading ends. The brief record is a prison labor construction item from 1983.
cia-0000112812: Espionage - Herbert Moy is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112812, dated January 5, 1945. The title pairs a charge and a name: espionage, Herbert Moy. A companion file from October 1944 calls the same man an active collaborator. The brief record is a charge file, one of two Moy files in this wartime group of files there.
cia-0000117912: Guatemala: 1984-1995 is the whole heading on declassified CIA document 0000117912, dated August 5, 1995. The title is a country and a span: Guatemala, across eleven years, 1984 to 1995. The span ends in the same year the record is dated in the catalog. cia-0000119212:
An April 1984 CIA document lays out what the American intelligence community was doing about the prisoner and missing problem. By the mid-1980s the search for answers had become a standing mission with its own staff and routines. Several agencies shared the work, and this paper describes their actions.

Inside, the document divides duties and reports steps taken across the community. That kind of coordination paper shows how a wartime question became a long bureaucratic effort. It matters because it explains the machinery behind the searches, the briefings, and the reports to families that continued for years after the last troops came home.
cia-0000132412: Cuban developments are surveyed in a CIA document dated September 5, 1959. Eight months had passed since Castro's victory, and the revolution was still defining itself week by week. Washington watched every turn of the new regime with close attention. The short document gathers the latest changes as the agency saw them that autumn, while Cuba's final direction was still being argued over in Havana.
cia-0000132512:
Parochial schools being seized by the Castro regime fill a CIA item dated April 4, 1961. The headline also reports foreign priests being expelled, though the last word is cut short in the record. The revolution was moving directly against the Catholic Church that spring.

The item reports the seizures and expulsions as they were announced. Church schools had educated much of Cuba's middle class for generations. For readers, the entry marks a sharp break between the regime and one of the island's oldest bodies. It came days before the Bay of Pigs invasion hardened every line in Cuba.
cia-0000132612: A Lima meeting of left-of-center parties calling for unity fills item 12 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the word united, leaving the call unfinished. Peru's capital was hosting the region's moderate left that month. The short item reports the meeting and what the parties agreed to demand.
cia-0000135812: Weekly progress reports fill a CIA paper from 1954 on the Guatemala operation. Part of its headline subject was deleted before release. The reports cover the week of March 23 through 29, though the headline breaks off mid-word. A weekly rhythm ran through the whole covert campaign that year. The short paper keeps the reports for that week as filed.
cia-0000135912: Dated 5 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records a short summary of a meeting held on 17 June, cabled from Guatemala City under a May date. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. cia-0000136112: With a date of 3 April 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a visit by Salamander to Sherwood. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136312: Sent to SKILLET, ONTRICH, and SHERWOOD in June 1954, this LINCOLN cable passes on the latest reliable situation report from PBSUCCESS. Liberation forces had captured Chiquimula the day before, were joyfully received, and were advancing toward Zacapa, while aircraft damaged trains carrying troop reinforcements. Guatemala City's petroleum stocks were dwindling after bomb damage, with only days of supply left. The cable also flags talking points for each recipient's audience.
cia-0000136612: Dated 4 January 1961, a Spanish document from the declassified records of Brigade 2506. The first week of 1961 produced a thick run of these Spanish records, this one among them. cia-0000136712: The catalog gives this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document an estimated date of 5 January 1960, a full year before the brigade's known training peak and earlier than the unit's public history suggests. cia-0000136912: Learn all you can about an arms shipment, this April 1954 cable directs. A Swedish ship delivered the arms at Puerto Barrios, Guatemala. A contact in Stockholm is to be asked for aid. The catalog does not date the briefing more closely or name its topics, so this description does not place it before or after the landing. cia-06626812: WIESEL DOES NOT SEE TIMERMAN - 1979/09/05, a CIA document. The missed meeting. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.

cinquante-marveilleux-secrets-d-alchimie: Cinquante merveilleux secrets d'alchimie, 1912. The fifty secrets. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. coningsby-or-the-new-generation-pg7412: Disraeli's Coningsby — the new generation's political novel — follows young Coningsby through the making of modern Conservatism. The future prime minister wrote his own dazzling rise into brilliant fiction. The classic English political novel. Young England's hopes and follies parade through its brilliant pages.
conrad-twixt-land-sea-1912:
'Twixt Land and Sea, published in 1912, collects three long sea tales from Conrad's maturity. The title names his lifelong ground: the border where a sailor's ordered ship meets the disorder of shore life.

The most famous is 'The Secret Sharer', in which a young captain hides a fugitive officer in his cabin and finds a double of himself. 'Falk' tells of a captain with a terrible past fighting for love in Bangkok, and 'Because of the Dollars' turns on theft and loyalty in eastern ports. These tales show Conrad's sea world at its richest and most humane.
constitution-haiti-2012: Haiti's 1987 Constitution, amended 2012, frames its republic. It survived quakes. The Tower library holds the full text. It stood through ruin. Earth shook. Law trembled.
