Merging the hospital cancer registry with national claims data, the study covered adults newly diagnosed between 2013 and 2015 with colorectal, stomach, breast or lung cancer. Survival analysis began ninety days after surgery, counting chemotherapy started within that window, and statistical models separated the effects of dialysis status and treatment. The authors present the work as a basis for fairer, evidence-led drug decisions in this group.
pmc-13422812:
Bailly and colleagues set out a study protocol in 2026 for peer support for medical residents in Lyon, France. Residents often face anxiety, depression, burnout, and suicidal thoughts, and existing support has shown limited benefit. The PAESSM study will place Mental Health First Aid-trained peers inside a first-year resident cohort. About a tenth of first-years will train as certified supporters for their classmates.

The design follows two cohorts for twelve months: first-years with the peer network and second-years with usual support. Questionnaires every three months will track well-being on a standard scale, plus anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, job strain, and help-seeking. A qualitative part will explore supporters' own experiences and how the scheme runs in practice. Because groups are not randomised, the authors plan careful statistical adjustment and sensitivity checks.
pmc-13424012:
Scott M Friedman and eight colleagues present a plain-language summary of a statistical comparison between two eye injection drugs. The drugs are aflibercept 8 mg and faricimab. They treat diabetic macular edema and wet age-related macular degeneration. Both block vessel growth signals, and both promise longer gaps between injections, yet they have never met in a head-to-head trial.

The underlying study used a network meta-analysis, a method that chains trial results together to compare treatments indirectly. Outcomes were the number of injections needed, changes in vision, and changes in retinal thickness, which should fall when treatment works. The summary walks patients and clinicians through what the indirect evidence can and cannot say about the two regimens.
pmc-13424212:
Annica Heyne and three colleagues work out how self-driving laboratories, robot platforms that screen materials around the clock, can judge corrosion resistance quickly without losing predictive power. Full corrosion tests can take months, far too slow for early screening. The team therefore compared four alloys in salty water, including stainless steel and high-entropy mixes. Their aim was a short test sequence.

Their method starts by naming which long-term property a quick measurement must predict, then qualifies shortcut experiments against the slow gold standards. The result is a minimal electrochemical routine fit for automated platforms, aimed at corrosion protection and energy materials. The paper frames qualification, not just speed, as the missing discipline in materials acceleration.
pmc-13424312:
Li Yang and six colleagues uncover how the developing liver links cell division to the plumbing that drains bile. In mouse and human models, the tiny bile channels began forming exactly where liver precursor cells divided, and the channels lengthened in step with oriented divisions as the cells matured.

A polarity protein, PAR3, proved central: it gathers a partner protein at tight junctions and holds a growth signal, ERK/MAPK, in check along the cell's lower surface. With that restraint in place, channels elongate properly and hepatocytes mature. Without it, both falter. The authors present the pathway as a stage-by-stage mechanism tying liver architecture to function, with lessons for regeneration and metabolic liver disease.
pmc-13424512:
Larsdotter and colleagues surveyed in 2026 Swedish adults on palliative care, asking what people understand by it and where they would prefer to be cared for and die. A random sample of 3,750 people aged 16 to 90 years was drawn from the national register, and just under half replied. Grouping methods sorted respondents by their grasp of palliative care, care that eases suffering when cure is not possible.

Larsdotter found home was the top choice for both end-of-life care and death, picked by about six and five in ten respondents. Five understanding groups emerged, from full grasp to no opinion. People who understood that such care supports families leaned toward home or hospice. Those who wrongly believed it hastens death leaned toward hospital or nursing home. The full-grasp group held more women, older people, and university graduates. The authors link better public understanding to care that matches wishes.
pmc-13424612:
Aileen H. Hsi leads a ten-author study of whether social vulnerability, the neighbourhood-level burden of poverty, housing, and access problems, predicts survival in aggressive brain tumours treated at MD Anderson between 2020 and 2025. Cohorts held 398 patients with glioblastoma and 62 with a related grade 4 astrocytoma, with vulnerability scored at county and neighbourhood level from a national index.

In glioblastoma, vulnerability showed no association with survival at either geographic scale. The picture differed for treatment: patients from more vulnerable neighbourhoods had higher odds of missing complete tumour removal and lower odds of receiving treatment on a clinical trial. No survival link appeared in the smaller astrocytoma group. Reaching a top centre, the authors imply, does not erase access gaps.
pmc-13424712:
Lloyd and co-authors present a mathematical model in this 2026 engineering paper for a soft robotic catheter steered entirely by magnetism. Their design wraps soft magnetic rings around braided sleeves nested inside each other. A strong external field, such as the one inside an MRI scanner, then bends the device. No motors or cables are needed.

The team derived an energy-based model coupling magnetic torque to sleeve curvature. It captures awkward real behaviors like hysteresis, where the shape lags behind the command. It also captures bistability, where two shapes are stable at once. Testing inside a 7-tesla preclinical MRI scanner, predicted shapes matched measured deformation with a root-mean-square error of 4.4 degrees across the experiments reported. The authors position the framework as groundwork for closed-loop control and systematic design of magnetically steered medical robots.
pmc-13425712:
Jacquelina Achkar and coauthors tested a carbon monoxide breathalyzer for spotting smokers before joint replacement in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Smoking delays wound healing and raises prosthetic joint infection risk, yet patients often underreport use and clinics lack objective screening. Patients with end-stage arthritis listed for surgery at one academic center completed a smoking questionnaire and then blew into a validated handheld device.

Breath carbon monoxide was classed as low at 0 to 6 parts per million, borderline at 7 to 9, and high at 10 or above. Comparing answers with breath values shows how often self-report misses recent smoking before arthroplasty.
pmc-13426012:
Foster and colleagues tested in 2026 whether crossing two separated populations of a biocontrol moth could restore its vigor. The moth, Hypena opulenta, is released against invasive swallow-wort vines in North America, but control agents often lose genetic diversity through small founding groups and long lab rearing. One population had spent twenty-eight generations in the lab, another fourteen in Canadian fields.

Whole genome sequencing showed the two groups had already diverged genetically, and both carried low diversity. Their hybrid offspring carried significantly more diversity. Hybrid females also produced more pupae in the lab and stripped more leaves from host plants. In the field they produced the largest second generation of the three groups. The authors propose deliberate outcrossing before release as a practical way to strengthen control agents.
pmc-13427312:
da Cruz and colleagues used Brazil's 2023 national oral health survey in 2026 to study who has dental implants. The survey covered adults aged 35 to 44 and older adults aged 65 to 74. They compared two measures: what people reported themselves and what examiners actually saw during clinical checks.

Implant prevalence ranged from about one tenth to one fifth of the sample, depending on the measure used. For self-reported use, older age, higher income, private dental care, and seeking treatment or rehabilitation all raised the odds of reporting implants. For clinically observed implants, only the number of missing teeth showed a significant link. The authors say implant use reflects both access to services and real clinical need, and they urge fairer provision through the public system.
pmc-13427712:
Su and colleagues built in 2026 a neural network that finds and grades tertiary lymphoid structures, immune cell clusters that form inside tumors, on whole-slide microscope images. Grading these clusters matters because their maturity can forecast how a patient answers immune therapy. Slides are enormous, so models usually read small patches and miss the context around each patch.

Their network, GCUNet, uses a graph structure to pull in long-range and fine detail from beyond the target patch, then fuses that context with local detail. The team built four datasets across four cancers, covering hundreds of slides and more than fifteen thousand structures. On all four, GCUNet beat the best rival methods by a clear margin.
pmc-13427912:
Knut Asbjørn Solhaug and co-authors ask whether far-red light, wavelengths just beyond visible red, powers photosynthesis in the shade-dwelling lichen Lobaria pulmonaria. This old-forest lichen lives under dense canopies where far-red light is enriched. Their 2026 study combines light measurements under the canopy with gas exchange experiments.

Far-red photons made up as much as 32 percent of the usable light under the canopy, against 11 percent in open areas. Far-red light alone supported moderate carbon dioxide uptake, and rates rose sharply when it was combined with background red light, a synergy known as the Emerson enhancement effect. Per absorbed photon, far-red light was even more efficient than red light. The authors recommend sensors covering the extended range for ecological studies, and warn that standard electron transport calculations overestimate activity under strong far-red light.
pmc-13429112:
Yumeng Zhang and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, screening models that flag depression risk in older people on long-term dialysis. Depressive symptoms affect over half of this group in many surveys, and early warning could speed support. The team recruited 226 older maintenance hemodialysis patients at a Chinese university hospital and its branches. Questionnaires covered mood, symptoms, nutrition, physical performance, self-management, and self-reported sight and hearing.

Just over 54 percent screened positive for depressive symptoms. Five learning models all separated high- and low-risk patients about equally well. A simple Naive Bayes model calibrated best overall. Its top predictors were vision problems, hearing loss, symptom burden, nutrition score, and self-management. The models were checked only inside the same hospital system, so outside testing must come before clinic use.
pmc-13432812:
Pan Lu and co-authors mined a United States vaccine harm report bank in 2026 for links between shots and a joint disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own joints. Reports spanned 1990 to 2026 and topped eleven million. Joint-linked reports formed a tiny slice, near five thousand people in all.

Women filed most reports, and adults in the broad mid-age band led the counts. Most harms touched muscle and joint themes, and near half struck within a week of the shot. The COVID shot drew the most reports yet only a weak math flag. Three older shots drew far stronger flags: one for a tick-borne disease, one for German measles, and one against anthrax. The authors stress that the bank is passive: it can flag leads, never prove cause.
pmc-13433212:
Shuai He and co-authors told a 2026 case of a 33-year-old woman. She slid toward an adrenal crisis picture two days after surgery. The surgery cut out an adrenal tumor that tests had called non-working. One small dose of a steroid drug, given in surgery to block sickness, sits at the center of the time line. Her stress hormone and its driver both read crushed low as she worsened.

Her signs fit many post-surgery faults, from infection to clots to fuel swings, so no single cause could be locked. She rose on broad support care plus stress-dose hormone cover. Workup before surgery had skipped a key overnight test, so a quiet hormone leak from the tumor could not be ruled out. The authors urge full gland checks before such cuts.
pmc-13433612:
Antonella Muscella opened a 2026 collection on motor skill care for kids with growth disorders of the brain and body, framing clumsiness as a whole-web trait rather than a side fault. Skill grows from brain webs, sense loops, body states, and world offers in live trade. In autism, focus faults, and palsy alike, weak motor skill marks the core build.

Pieces in the set share a turn: motor acts voice deep webs that weigh forecasts, pick acts, and gauge body state. Brain scans in autism show wide web breaks, not lone path faults, behind the motor gaps. One thread runs through fitness, since motor skill may reach social life by way of body health rather than head on. The editor calls for care that treats the full web.
pmc-13434012:
Jianhua Cai and co-authors split a two-job catalyst in 2026 into two stages in space to turn light gases into ring stocks that anchor the chemical trade. Two-job builds rule plant work, yet steps tangle when sites sit cheek by jowl, a flaw the old closeness rule missed. The test road runs propane to the ring trio of benzene and kin.

Stage one strips gas to light links, while stage two stacks and rings those links in step with the feed. The split hit near-full gas burn and high ring share at strong heat, with the prized trio near the whole take. Live light reads and rate math back the match. Ring by-products from cracks shrank to a whisper, and cost reads held firm.
pmc-13434412:
Miao Li and a large team lift the power yield of organic solar cells in 2026 with a new electron taking molecule. Ring free designs are cheap to make but move charge poorly, which caps their yield. Side arms with phenyl rings were added to guide how the molecules stack.

The arms form extra weak bonds with the ends of nearby molecules. Fluorine on the arms adds still more contact points. Tight, neat stacks open charge paths in many directions at once. The best cell reached a yield of 19.12 percent. That mark sets a record for this low cost class.
pmc-13434712:
Houyu Wu and Eng Hoe Wee survey 350 university teachers in China in 2026 about trust and worry over artificial intelligence tools. Both scores sat well above the middle of the scale. Teachers felt able to use the tools yet uneasy about what they mean for the job.

Trust and worry moved in opposite ways with a strong link. Women reported more worry and less trust than men. Computing teachers felt most trust and least worry of any field. The mix suggests training should build skill and answer job fears at once. One size support will miss half the picture.
pmc-13434812:
Wentao Xu and coauthors add hydrogen to carbon double bonds with electric drive and shape control in 2026. Nickel, a cheap and common metal, carries the reaction with a tight fitting coat. Protons plus electrons supply hydrogen, so no high pressure gas is needed.

Shape purity runs high across conjugated esters and allylic alcohols. The coat must hold a nickel hydrogen unit firm, else hydrogen gas wins or nickel plates out. Computer work points to a nickel one hydrogen as the active form. Weak sticky contacts with the coat set which shape wins. Green synthesis gains a safe route to chiral stock.
pmc-13437712:
Yang Sheng, Yao Yao, and Hengcang Wang argue heart and vessel disease should be read as an immune and metabolic disorder steered partly by non-coding RNA. These RNA strands never build proteins, yet they tune gene activity across many cell types. Their 2026 review sorts patients by dominant mechanism rather than by disease label alone, sketching types such as artery inflammation, sterile injury, and fibro-inflammatory remodeling.

Short and long RNA species, plus ring-shaped ones, govern cholesterol handling in macrophages, inflammation alarms, vessel lining activation, and heart muscle scarring. The same molecule can protect in one cell and harm in another, which defeats simple good-versus-bad labels. Spilled RNA in blood could serve as a liquid biopsy, and RNA-based drugs are in reach. They frame the endotypes as research tools, not clinic tests, until trials sort patients by them and prove the sorting helps.
pmc-13439612:
Hua Tian surveys how everyday online life shapes Chinese netizens' sense of their festivals' world reach, reporting in 2026. Cultural soft power is often told as state messaging, yet ordinary users form their own judgements while scrolling and sharing. A survey of 1,540 domestic netizens measured online engagement habits, media format leanings, and feelings about traditional festivals abroad. Statistical modelling then traced links among engagement, perceived influence, group pride, and a sense of cultural empowerment.

More frequent online engagement tracked with stronger belief that the festivals carry weight worldwide. That belief in turn carried part of the link between engagement and collective self-esteem. A chain ran onward from esteem to feeling culturally empowered. Neither a taste for video over text nor time spent overseas changed the core pattern. Tian argues that daily interaction frequency, not media format, drives the effect.
pmc-13440012:
Jiaming Ye and colleagues count genital mycoplasma carriage and drug resistance among women in Hangzhou, China, reporting a 2026 review of laboratory records. These small bacteria can colonise the cervix without symptoms, and carriage in pregnancy raises clinical questions. The team analysed 1,177 cervical samples collected between 2017 and 2023, spanning pregnant women, new mothers, and women at routine checks.

Just over half of all samples carried mycoplasmas, with pregnant women highest at well over half. Ureaplasma species dominated by far, while Mycoplasma hominis stayed rare in every group. Carriage peaked among pregnant teenagers in the data. Resistance testing worried the authors: most isolates resisted gatifloxacin, with large shares also beating ciprofloxacin and roxithromycin. The findings give local clinicians current carriage and susceptibility figures for guiding treatment in pregnancy.
pmc-13440312:
Kanai and Ichihashi grow self-copying RNA strands in the lab to test how parasites shape change. Parasite strands copy fast but make no useful product. Host strands do the work that keeps both alive. The team grew six groups of strands. Some groups held many parasites. Others held few. Groups with many parasites changed fast between groups. Yet hosts inside each group stayed much alike.

Groups with few parasites split, for a short time, into up to three host lines. The team reads this as loose pressure when hosts copy about as well as each other. Parasites kept hosts sharp but held back new forms inside a group.
pmc-13441512:
Nobutaka Doba and colleagues stop stubborn puncture bleeding after variceal injection therapy by pressing with an extra-long scope cap, reporting a 2026 case. Injection sclerotherapy seals bleeding veins in the food pipe, yet the needle holes themselves often bleed, sometimes hard. Balloon pressure is the usual first rescue. Their patient, a 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and returning varices, bled from the first puncture site during treatment with ethanolamine oleate.

Balloon compression failed to settle the bleeding. Direct pressure with a long transparent cap, protruding twelve millimetres against the standard four, achieved prompt control. At the second puncture in the same session, the team applied the long cap immediately after needle withdrawal as a planned step, and bleeding stopped again. The authors argue that the rescue deserves routine status, and they note that compression timing for this method is barely documented.
pmc-13441812:
Tong Xin and colleagues build a prediction model for brain dysfunction during sepsis in arthritis patients, centred on a blood ratio. Rheumatoid arthritis patients face raised sepsis risk, and sepsis-associated encephalopathy is hard to spot early. The neutrophil-to-albumin ratio bundles inflammation and nutrition into one number. Records from eighty-nine patients at two centres built it, with thirty-seven more at a third centre held back for outside testing.

Brain dysfunction struck about a quarter of the building group and carried far higher twenty-eight-day mortality. Three machine learning methods agreed on six predictors: organ failure score, infection markers, stay length, age, and the ratio itself. The chosen model discriminated strongly in both the building data and the outside cohort. A web tool packages the calculator for bedside use. The authors present the ratio as a worthy addition to early warning in this group.
pmc-13443312:
Yudai Takarada builds a layered model of how effort feels during exercise in a 2026 review. Blood flow restriction cuffs, which squeeze limbs during light work, make effort soar out of step with load. That odd gap lets each layer of effort sense show its hand.

Low layers read body state through nerve fibers and vessel stretch sensors. Mid layers run through the motor cortex, whose ease drops while helper zones step up. Top layers weigh fatigue, hidden goals, and arousal, and they retune how raw signals count. Cuff work swells each layer's voice in turn. Repeat rounds may reset effort marks for good. The model casts felt effort as a rebuilt verdict, never a raw body read.
pmc-13443512:
Rubtsova reviews a distinctive immune cell population that grows with age and autoimmunity in this 2026 article. Age-associated B cells carry two markers, T-bet and CD11c, and were first described in old female mice. They are now linked to human diseases including lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis. Their numbers track disease activity there. Their formation depends on several signals, plus a master regulator called ZEB2.

The review stresses that these cells leave the blood and settle in tissues. There they do damage locally. In kidneys, inflamed joints, salivary glands, and fat, they produce autoantibodies. They also present antigens and release inflammatory signals. They also appear in spinal fluid in multiple sclerosis and in Alzheimer's disease inflammation. A link with Epstein-Barr virus is discussed as one route connecting infection to autoimmunity.
pmc-13444312:
Rushikesh Dave and colleagues report a ureter trapped at the sacroiliac joint in a 77-year-old woman in a 2026 case paper. The ureter, the tube that drains the kidney, sat pinched where pelvis bones meet, a spot with just six past reports in print. Her visit was for chronic low back pain, not urinary trouble.

Dye CT scans showed the right ureter caught at the joint, worn by advanced joint decay. Dye exit lagged by 10 to 12 hours on the scans, yet her kidney work held stable and she felt no urinary signs. Past no-trauma cases needed surgery or drain tubes. Her team chose watchful care alone, a first for this rare trap. The authors urge scan readers to keep the trap in mind for odd back pain.
pmc-13447112:
Nicola Calonaci and colleagues studied how many copies of a mutated gene a tumour carries, a measure they call gene mutant dosage. Standard tests usually note only whether a mutation is present, ignoring how strongly it is dosed.

The team built a computer method that infers mutation copies from standard tumour sequencing, without needing a healthy tissue sample. Across 60,000 cancer samples they measured dosage for over half a million mutations. Dosage patterns in over 20,000 patients yielded 46 tumour-specific markers tied to survival, 13 of them invisible to simpler yes-or-no tests. Dosage also linked to whether cancer spread, and to which organs it spread to, sharpening prognosis.
pmc-13447212:
Kentaro Ito, Kae Yamazaki and Anna Natori test a milk protein over three menstrual cycles in a 2026 trial with healthy Japanese women. Period-related symptoms can lower quality of life at work and socially. Short-term use of the protein, called alpha-lactalbumin, had earlier eased physical symptoms, prompting a longer and stricter test.

One hundred forty women aged twenty to thirty-nine received the protein or a placebo, with neither side knowing which. The main symptom questionnaire showed no clear overall gain, before periods or during them. Smaller exploratory checks hinted at less weight gain and clumsiness before periods, plus better role and social scores. Urine measures and most other items did not differ, so the authors call for further studies before drawing firm conclusions.
pmc-13447312:
Yuhuan Song and colleagues track lupus-related deaths in the United States from 1999 to 2023 in a 2026 nationwide analysis. Lupus, where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, still causes early death despite better care. Long-term national data split by sex, race, age and place were thin, especially across the pandemic years.

Death certificate data listing lupus anywhere among causes were drawn from a national database. The age-adjusted rate fell over the full period, from just above one per hundred thousand to well below that level. Annual deaths still rose slightly, and the trend dipped, rose again, then fell sharply in recent years. Women, older adults and Black patients carried the highest rates throughout, while southern states and non-city areas improved least.
pmc-13447712:
Vasanthan, Suko, and Visaria wrote this 2026 letter to the editor about a study of blood pressure variability monitoring by Lykka and colleagues. That study measured how reproducibly 24-hour monitors capture swings in blood pressure in untreated hypertensive patients, finding nighttime measures less reproducible than daytime ones. These correspondents raise methodological points they say matter for interpreting such results in practice.

The cuff inflating every 15 minutes may itself disturb sleep, they note. That can distort nighttime readings. Self-reported sleep times add further variability. They suggest sleep trackers as a check. They also question the statistics: kappa agreement scores looked poor despite moderate correlation measures, partly because a 75th-percentile cut-off creates threshold effects. Finally, they ask how blood pressure medicines, excluded from the original study, would change variability.
pmc-13448112:
Yoon commented in 2026 on a Swedish registry study asking whether worn spinal levels next to a past fusion need decompression alone, or a longer fusion. Surgeons face this choice often, and Yoon notes the clinic saying that no spine operation should be promised as the last. The study drew on Swespine, which captures most Swedish spine surgery.

Among 2,521 patients, repeat surgery was more common after extended fusion at every check. At ten years it reached about a third of that group, against about a quarter after decompression alone. Yoon praises the finding but urges caution: the groups differed from the start, since fusion was chosen for patients with slippage, deformity, or segment pain. Adjustment cannot erase that tilt. For a well-chosen patient, Yoon backs decompression alone as the smaller, safer operation.
pmc-13448212:
Pu and colleagues review stress fractures, the overuse bone injuries of active people, in this 2026 article. These fractures arise when repeated loading outpaces the bone's repair capacity, so microdamage accumulates in otherwise healthy bone until resorption and formation fall out of balance. The authors trace the cellular and molecular steps of both the injury and its healing.

Healing begins with woven bone laid down on the surface to stabilize the crack, a process called intramembranous ossification, followed by remodeling that replaces it with mature bone. Reported treatments range from anti-osteoporosis drugs and anti-inflammatory medicines to low-intensity pulsed ultrasound. The authors argue future work needs larger animal models that mimic the human condition, and deeper study of physical therapies and their mechanisms.
pmc-13448412:
Amelia Munson and colleagues test how heat, low oxygen and predator threat combine to shape fish behaviour in a 2026 experiment. Warming and oxygen loss often arrive together in fresh waters, yet studies usually vary one stressor at a time. Two common species, common minnows and three-spined sticklebacks, may balance those demands differently depending on their needs.

Minnows and sticklebacks were exposed to warm or cool water at full or low oxygen, before and after a model predator appeared. In minnows, each stressor's effect depended on the other, with sociability rising in warm water only when oxygen was low. Sticklebacks simply grew busier in warm water at both oxygen levels. After the predator, group differences vanished as activity dropped overall. Stressor combinations, not single factors, govern outcomes here.
pmc-13449412:
Changyu Chen and colleagues uncover in 2026 a gene-regulation trick that liver cancer uses to grow more aggressive, centered on the RNA-binding protein ZCRB1. Tumors often shorten the tail region of a gene's message, the 3 prime untranslated region, and that trimming can free the message from normal brakes. ZCRB1 was abundant in both first-time and recurrent liver tumors, and patients with high levels fared worse.

In these cancers, a growing share of ZCRB1 messages carried the short tail, which raised the protein's output and pushed malignant behavior. The team traced part of that effect to a second protein, GOLM1, whose message ZCRB1 binds and controls after transcription. Blocking or restoring pieces of this chain changed how strongly the cancer traits appeared, showing GOLM1 partly carries ZCRB1's tumor-promoting role. The authors frame the shortened tail as both a warning sign and a possible drug target.
pmc-13449812:
Sumanjali Reddy Kanmantha Reddy and colleagues present in 2026 a case where the true source of a patient's weakness sat in the neck, far from the spine surgery he had just undergone. Degenerative cervical myelopathy, the commonest cause of non-traumatic spinal cord dysfunction in adults, usually announces itself with neck pain, clumsy hands, and reflex changes. Their patient, a 67-year-old man with severe lumbar stenosis, received decompression surgery from L1 to L4 for back and thigh pain.

Afterward he developed new weakness confined to his legs, with no neck pain and no arm symptoms at all. That pattern, a false localizing sign, sent the team imaging the whole spine, where cervical cord compression from degenerative changes explained the deficit. The authors draw the lesson plainly: unexplained weakness after lumbar surgery demands a high suspicion for cervical myelopathy and complete spine imaging before the real lesion is missed.
pmc-13450012:
Abrahams Ocanto and a very large team report in 2026 early results from a prospective study of online adaptive, MR-guided stereotactic radiation for localized prostate cancer. The prostate shifts daily and sits against rectum and bladder, so the team replanned each session on fresh magnetic resonance images, allowing margins as tight as two millimeters without gel spacers. Acute toxicity stayed low: side effects of grade two or worse touched three percent of patients for urinary symptoms and none for bowel symptoms. Patients themselves reported minimal impact on urinary, bowel, and overall quality of life. No biochemical failures, the blood-marker signal of returning cancer, appeared during the first year. The authors suggest the adaptive workflow itself, not margin shrinkage alone, deserves credit for the gentle safety profile, while longer follow-up tests durability.
pmc-13450612:
Shihao Cui and co-authors show in 2026 that burnt peat soils give off far less methane when they are flooded again than unburnt soils do. Drained peatlands leak large amounts of climate gases, yet reflooding them often sparks a surge of methane. Fire is growing more common on these drained fields and ruins farm yields.

Soil from badly burnt sites cut methane output by more than nine tenths once reflooded, when set against unburnt soil. Fire left the soil carbon more stable, raised its acidity score in the mild direction, and shrank the genes that make methane. The team urges planners to target recent burn scars first, with most of the world gain lying in Asia.
pmc-13451812:
Mehdi Boostani and a large team show in 2026 that a skin scope can spot sun damage in mouse skin weeks before any tumor shows. Sun rays drive quiet harm across wide skin fields, yet early checks rest on judgment calls. The team used hairless mice and a laser scope that images skin layers without cutting.

Five skin features split sun-exposed skin from shielded skin, with a broken honeycomb pattern and mixed cell shapes the strongest marks. Trained readers sorted exposed from clean skin with high hits and few false alarms, both early and late after the sun course. The authors back the scope as a painless way to catch hidden sun harm in skin clinics.
pmc-13451912:
Beatriz Thomasi and Brian Gulbransen frame in 2026 the gut's microbes as a tuner of gut-brain talk. That talk runs both ways through nerves and chemical paths, and faults in it feed a set of gut ills, from irritable bowel to lasting constipation. Microbes sit inside that talk as active players, not bystanders.

The gut's trillions of microbes shape nerve growth, immune tone, and body fuel use, which in turn steer brain and gut health. The piece sorts what is known about the paths and signals in play and where hands-on use still lags. The authors argue that learning what to tune, and how, is the field's next hard step toward new care.
pmc-13453612:
Rebecca Newell and four co-authors evaluate a peer mentoring pilot that supports racially minoritised applicants aiming for UK public health specialty training. Such applicants win places at lower rates than peers, a gap not explained by ability or effort. Their 2026 study matches Black and South Asian applicants with current trainees as buddies across two recruitment rounds in South East England.

In the first round, 13 percent of mentored applicants reached interview and 4.3 percent won offers, below the national offer rate of about 9.8 percent. The second round flipped the picture: 17.2 percent reached interview and 10.3 percent won offers, against a national rate near 5.7 percent. Applicants said the scheme raised their confidence and cleared up the process. The authors call the pilot workable and valued, while warning that small numbers limit firm claims.
pmc-13453712:
Ethan M Larson, Brian D Dalm, and Kristy L Townsend review electrical stimulation therapies for diabetic nerve damage, a common cause of burning foot pain. Drugs for this pain mostly dull it and can carry heavy side effects, while the nerve loss marches on. Their 2026 review covers spinal cord, nerve root cluster, and peripheral nerve stimulation, drawing on trials and lab studies through June 2026.

The implanted options cut pain by more than half in hard to treat patients and lowered opioid use. Beyond pain relief, the signals seem to help nerves heal: swelling eased, tiny blood flow improved, and nerve fiber counts in skin rose. Each site works its own way, from widening small vessels to waking the cells that wrap nerve fibers. The authors call for trials that track hard signs of regrowth, such as eye surface nerve imaging.
pmc-13454812:
Noelle Curtis-Joseph, Audra Laubi, Melanie Ortiz-Alvarez de la Campa, and Peter Belenky show, in a 2026 mouse study, that early gut microbes decide whether a strong obesity gene fully takes effect. The mice lack the leptin receptor, a classic genetic route to weight gain and high blood sugar. Antibiotics given from birth to eight weeks reshaped the gut community.

Treated mice gained far less weight and had much lower blood sugar, without eating less or absorbing food differently. Sequencing showed one bacterial family nearly wiped out, while two others bloomed. Feeding back a single cultured species from the lost family restored the high blood sugar, though not the weight. The authors conclude that this microbe is a direct driver of the sugar problem, proof that even hard genetic obesity leans on the microbiome.
pmc-13455112:
Zhen Yi and five colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a prediction chart for patients whose slipped lumbar disc returns after a modern two-portal endoscopic operation. The team reviewed 257 patients treated for single-level disc herniation, of whom 24, about nine percent, suffered a recurrence. Thirty clinical and scan measures were collected for each patient.

Statistical screening distilled twelve independent risk factors for recurrence. The chart built from them separated future recurrences sharply, scoring near 0.98 in the training group and 0.95 in the check group on a standard accuracy curve. Fit checks looked clean, and decision analysis showed useful benefit across a wide risk range. The authors offer the nomogram for counseling patients before surgery and for flagging who needs closer follow-up after it.
pmc-13455412:
Oh and a Korean team studied 517 patients who had surgery after endoscopic removal of early colorectal cancer failed to be curative. They asked how often cancer was left and what signaled it. Rules push extra surgery on high-risk pathology features, yet many find nothing, so true residual rates were worth pinning down across four hospitals.

Independent predictors of leftover cancer included the dissection technique, piecemeal removal, and positive side or deep margins, with odds ratios from 5.51 up to 10.30 in the multivariable model. Node spread was signaled by invasion depth of at least 1,000 micrometers, poor differentiation, vessel invasion, and positive deep margin. Patients with zero or one risk factor had residual rates under 1 percent, supporting personal decisions.
pmc-13457212:
Rui Li, An Huang, Xue Ding, Shuangyun Peng, Yanjv Yu and Yezhou Xiang published this 2026 remote sensing study on mapping celery fields from drone images. Celery looks similar across growth stages, and shadows, bare soil and mixed planting blur field boundaries. Standard neural models tend to miss edges and textures. The authors propose WaveletUMamba, a network that boosts detail using wavelet transforms while keeping a wide view of the scene.

Three additions do the work: a module that masks low-frequency content to sharpen edges, a dual-gated module fusing detail with global context, and a supervision module that keeps growth stages distinct. On their test imagery the method reached a mean intersection-over-union score of 88.70 percent and a mean F1 score of 93.90 percent for the mapped areas. That beat the second-best model, UNetMamba, while staying efficient. Removing each module in turn confirmed each one contributed.
pmc-13457812:
Songmei Zhai and co-authors mapped how fibroblasts, the cells that build scar-like tissue, switch on inside injured kidneys. Their 2026 study combined single-nucleus gene sequencing with spatial mapping, which records where genes are active inside tissue. They integrated 619,137 cell nuclei from 80 samples and sorted the fibroblasts in the injury environment into ten subtypes, looking for which subtype drives the scarring process that pushes kidneys toward failure.

One subtype stood out, named FIBEMT because its cells carry a strong epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition program, a state change that makes cells more mobile and fibrous. These cells scored high on scarring pathways and were linked with poorer kidney function in the data. A regulator gene called SOX4 appeared to promote their activation, and the subtype clustered mainly in the renal papilla, the innermost part of the kidney, alongside a partner cell type there.
pmc-13459212:
Helen Morley and co-authors interviewed the staff tasked with raising breast cancer screening rates among ethnic minority women in Britain. Most research asks minority women themselves about barriers. This 2026 study turned to the implementers: seventeen staff who run screening equity work took part in semi structured online interviews. Their accounts were analyzed for themes to find why uptake gaps persist despite decades of effort and a national average uptake near the 70 percent target.

Three themes emerged. First, screening systems are designed around the service rather than communities, creating mismatches that translation and cultural training alone cannot fix. Second, wider societal racism and hostile immigration policies erode trust and deter attendance. Third, staff described inventive grassroots workarounds, but these depended on individual initiative rather than system support. The title quotes a participant: they know the barriers, yet nothing changes.
pmc-13460212:
Thitapa Luepiyapanich, Nitipatana Chierakul, Wanchai Dejsomritrutai, and Sutat Pipopsuthipaiboon studied in 2026 a breathing pattern called PRISm in Thai hospital patients, filling a Southeast Asian evidence gap. In PRISm, one breathing measure falls while the ratio between measures stays normal. Their cohort drew 1,300 adults tested at Siriraj Hospital in 2017 and 2018, followed through March 2024, with prevalence calculated under two competing definitions.

Depending on definition, prevalence ranged from a few percent up to about eight percent overall. People with PRISm were older and more often had heart failure, and their death risk ran more than double that of normal testers, staying significant after adjustment. Repeat testing showed the pattern is unstable: many people shifted to normal, obstructive, or restrictive patterns over time.
pmc-13461312:
Wang, Peng, and Patterson studied in 2026 what builds resilience in United States adolescents, using data from the international PISA 2018 school survey. Resilience was split into three parts: self-efficacy, perseverance, and a sense of meaning in life. The team weighed school factors, such as teacher support and the felt climate of cooperation or competition, against one personal factor, mindset.

Wang found every factor positively predicted resilience overall. Teacher support and a competitive climate also predicted a stronger growth mindset, the belief that ability can grow. A cooperative climate, by contrast, linked to a weaker mindset score. Mindset carried an indirect effect only for teachers' academic support, not for the other routes. The authors argue schools need a comprehensive push: academic backing, emotional understanding, a balance of cooperation and competition, and mindset support together.
pmc-13461512:
Emrullah Sonuç and colleagues built an AI system that classifies skin lesions by fusing magnified skin photos with patient details. Seven lesion classes look deceptively alike, and rare classes are scarce, so image-only systems often stumble.

The pipeline balances the data by synthesising rare cases, aligns photos with records, then fuses features from a vision transformer network. A stacked pair of classifiers, SVM plus KNN, tuned by automated search, made the final calls on each lesion. On the HAM10000 dataset the stack reached 98.55 percent accuracy and a ROC-AUC of 99.88 percent across the seven classes. Heat maps showed the model looking at the lesion areas doctors would check, Sonuç reports, though outside validation is still needed.
pmc-13461712:
Ronald Irwanto Natadidjaja and colleagues study, in a 2026 report, a digital guide helping Indonesian hospitals choose first antibiotics wisely. The tool, called e-RASPRO, sorts patients by risk and ties choices to the World Health Organization's Access, Watch, and Reserve grouping of antibiotics. Access drugs are preferred first choices, while Watch drugs need more care because resistance is a bigger worry. Ten hospitals took part.

The team gathered monthly prescribing data for 2024 and compared how fitting the first vein-given choices were against amounts of each drug class used. More fitting choices in lower-risk patients went with more penicillin, an Access drug, and less use of a Watch group of strong cephalosporins. The links held after time trends were removed. The authors are clear the study shows correlation, not proof the tool caused the shift. Still, the pattern fits the goal of steering care toward safer first choices.
pmc-13462012:
Rachele Simeon and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, questionnaires capturing quality of life reported by patients with rare genetic diseases. Such diseases bring burdens that clinic measures alone miss. The team hunted for questionnaires built or checked for rare genetic conditions. They mapped what each questionnaire covers using a world framework of functioning, disability, and health, and judged quality with a checklist.

Fifty-nine studies covered 45 questionnaires across 29 rare diseases. Most questionnaires were built for one disease, though general and adapted ones appeared. Content centered on body functions and daily activities, while surroundings, social life, stigma, and access to care were thinly covered. Studies most often checked consistency and whether the tool measures what it claims. Qualities such as picking up change were rarely tested. Only three earned the top recommendation grade. The authors urge better coverage of social and care-access topics in future tools.
pmc-13462112:
Shen-Bo Fu and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, the protein HMGB3 in esophageal carcinoma, cancer of the food pipe. The cancer is often lethal and lacks markers for detection and risk sorting. HMGB3 had been flagged as a cancer-promoting gene in other tumors, yet its role here was undefined. The team combined cancer databases with lab tests on tissue and cells.

HMGB3 ran high across cancer types and was overactive in food pipe tumors, where high levels went with advanced stage and poor outlook. Genes linked to HMGB3 clustered around immune control, cell sticking, and DNA handling. Immune cell patterns inside tumors shifted with HMGB3 level, and drug sensitivity was checked against it. Staining and cell tests confirmed the high levels. Lowering HMGB3 in cells slowed growth and invasion. The authors present HMGB3 as a candidate marker and target for this cancer.
pmc-13462212:
Tuulia Enbom leads a 2026 farm study in Finland on management factors raising the risk of a diarrheal disease in dairy calves caused by Cryptosporidium parvum. The parasite spreads between animals and can infect people. Disease depends on many care practices, not the germ alone. The team compared farms with confirmed disease against farms with no outbreaks in herd health records.

Seventy-seven case farms and 152 control farms supplied data on herd health, management, surroundings, and calf care. Five factors stood out with higher risk: larger herd size, moving cattle between farms, and weak separation of sick calves from healthy ones. Too little time for calf care and teams of five or more people sharing daily cattle work also raised risk. Control farms were not tested for the parasite, a limit the authors note. They advise tighter farm biosecurity, and say the findings can target prevention where it counts.
pmc-13462812:
Yu Na Kim and colleagues dissect, in a 2026 study, how cinnamon essential oil kills a crop bacterium, Xanthomonas euvesicatoria, which causes bacterial leaf spot on pepper and tomato. The oil is a known antimicrobial, yet its exact attack routes were unclear. Electron microscopy, viability checks, and gene-activity reading charted the bacterium's response. The oil killed in a dose-dependent way, with a minimum level that stopped growth.

Treated cells leaked through damaged membranes and became far more sensitive to salt stress, while their slime layers thinned. At a sub-lethal dose the bacteria entered an energy crisis: the membrane enzyme making their fuel fell sharply, and cells stretched, a sign division had stalled. Gene data backed the picture, with energy, division, and movement genes switched off and stress defense genes switched on. The authors call the oil a multi-target biopesticide candidate that could break resistance.
pmc-13463112:
Romano‐Gude and a large team map nitrogen processing by microbes in a subterranean estuary in this 2026 study. In these underground mixing zones, groundwater meets seawater beneath the shore, and microbes there decide how much nitrogen reaches the sea. The team sampled a Mediterranean site with naturally high nitrogen. They took samples at several depths and at varying distances from shore, in both winter and summer. They measured microbes and their nitrogen-related genes.

Microbe numbers, activity, and diversity shifted strongly with water chemistry and aquifer depth, but changed little between seasons. Different zones hosted different nitrogen pathways: ammonia-oxidizing archaea dominated fresher groundwater, while bacteria that remove nitrogen as gas were enriched in deep salty layers. Models using microbial properties predicted nitrite and ammonium levels better than models using environmental variables alone, showing the microbes' central role.
pmc-13463512:
Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 study of resveratrol, a grape compound with antioxidant fame that the body barely absorbs. The team packed it into tiny lipid particles designed to enter intestinal lymph, the drainage route that bypasses the liver's first-pass breakdown. Rats with a new conscious lymph-collection system, and mice on a twenty-eight-day safety course, tested the idea.

Blood levels of resveratrol rose about sevenfold with the particles. Lymph collection proved the route: particles traveled through gut lymph vessels straight into the blood, skipping the liver pass that destroys most of the dose. Daily dosing in mice for twenty-eight days produced no safety signal in the reported checks. The conscious animal model is itself an advance, since anesthesia and restraint in older models distort absorption. Lymph routing could rescue many poorly absorbed natural compounds.
pmc-13463612:
Adam and colleagues used single-nucleus RNA sequencing in 2026 to map cell types inside Wilms tumor. Wilms tumor is the most common kidney cancer of childhood, and these cases had favorable histology. The method reads gene activity one nucleus at a time. Untreated tumors were compared with atlases from fetal kidney and healthy neighboring tissue. The cancer's blastemal, stromal, and epithelial parts were sorted by gene patterns.

The blastema is the tumor's least mature part. It closely resembled early fetal kidney progenitor cells. Those cells sit midway toward forming a nephron, the kidney's filtering unit. Lineage boundaries proved leaky in the tumors. Genes normally limited to the nephron line, PAX2 and PAX8, also appeared in tumor stroma. A stromal marker called POSTN turned up inside the blastema. Some fetal pathways stayed switched on across tumors. Others lit up only in single samples, revealing drug targets unique to individual children.
pmc-13463812:
Suwen Li and four co-authors review bedside tests that spot food or fluid leaking into the airway of ICU patients on breathing tubes. Such leaks can seed ventilator-linked pneumonia, a grave lung infection. Tracers and chemical markers promise early warning, yet studies use mixed methods and cutoffs.

From six databases the team kept sixteen studies that fit their two-part frame of leak spotting and pneumonia forecasting. Blue-dye sight checks worked unevenly and could not be pooled with confidence. Airway alpha-amylase, a saliva enzyme, forecast pneumonia with middling accuracy across studies. The authors judge the proof base too thin and too varied for firm bedside rules today.
pmc-13464112:
Georgopoulos and colleagues reviewed in 2026 metastases to the male breast, cancers that spread to the breast from elsewhere in the body. Such cases are exceptionally rare in men and barely described, and no review had focused on them alone. The team gathered 98 studies covering 192 reported cases and charted their clinical, imaging, tissue, and treatment features.

Georgopoulos found patients averaged 58 years at diagnosis. Breast spread appeared on average about 32 months after the first cancer, usually amid widespread disease. Prostate cancer, lung cancer, and melanoma were the commonest sources. Tissue testing with marker stains was key to telling spread apart from a new breast cancer. Treatment aimed at the underlying cancer, while surgery served mainly to confirm the diagnosis and control the local lump. The authors offer the synthesis as a reference for clinicians facing this rare picture.
pmc-13465112:
Yi Xiao and seven co-authors review how omics tools, genome-to-metabolite readouts, are reshaping food flavor science. Taste panels judge flavor by feel, while machines list flavor chemicals without saying how they arose. The review sweeps genomics, gene activity, proteins, metabolites, and fats, then asks what the stack still misses.

Most studies stop at listing features that differ between foods, the authors find. Single readouts each catch one layer of a web that spans genes to scent. The team proposes a causal frame: join the layers, then test claims with hands-on interventions. Artificial intelligence earns a role for chewing through the joined data. Cheap real-time readouts remain a stated goal for the field.
pmc-13465712:
Dolkar, Hexiang Bai, Ziyu Wang, and Jihong Yang fermented Marselan grapes together with Fu brick tea to see how the mix changes red wine, reporting in 2026. Fu tea is a post-fermented tea that carries a helpful fungus, and the team tried four tea levels from none up to a gram and a half per liter. The goal was a drink with richer flavor and color.

More tea steadily lowered alcohol while leaving fermentation otherwise healthy. Tea-linked phenolic compounds rose sharply, with chlorogenic acid nearly doubling to become the leading one. Color readings shifted toward a steadier brick-red tone, and the total phenolic load tracked that shift better than any single compound did. Aroma analysis added further detail on the changed profile.
pmc-13466312:
Vasiliki Androutsopoulou and colleagues survey the writings on amyloid disease reaching the chest aorta, in a 2026 review. The disease leaves clumps of misshapen protein in tissues all through the body. Its effects on the heart are well known. Bulges and tears of the thoracic aorta, by contrast, are rare and seldom reported.

They gathered what is known about causes, testing, symptoms, care, and outlook when amyloid reaches this large vessel. Most clumps come from one of two proteins, a light chain or transthyretin. The survey maps a scattered field so doctors can spot a rare but dangerous overlap.
pmc-13466412:
Paulina Turko, Bogusław Antoszewski, and Marta Fijałkowska examine how a body scanner's belly fat rating relates to age, sex, and the familiar body mass index, in a 2026 study. The clinic cohort held 326 adults admitted over three months to one plastic surgery practice. Waist and hip measures joined the electrical impedance scan, which estimates fat, muscle, and bone from a weak current.

Men averaged a slightly higher body mass index than women in the group. The authors cross-checked weight categories against the device's visceral fat classes and modeled the rating against age, index, and gender together. Their aim is practical: showing where a quick scan adds information that a height-weight ratio cannot give.
pmc-13466712:
Rong Wei, a hematologist, reflects on a transplant patient whose test results spelled success while the overall outcome turned catastrophic, in a 2026 essay. The patient, a middle-aged mother with stubborn acute myeloid leukemia, received a half-matched stem cell transplant. Her marrow report showed complete remission with full donor cells, the outcome the team had hoped for after months of risk and expense.

Wei describes sitting with the family before the procedure, when the patient chose to proceed for the sake of her young children, fully aware the treatment might fail. The family's savings were already largely spent. The essay presses a hard distinction: clearing leukemia is not the same as restoring a life.
pmc-13467112:

Scratch testing is a rising way to judge how cement materials crack, yet standard formulas assume an idealized groove shape. A probe instrument and three-dimensional scans captured the true profile in white cement paste.

Load rose steadily to a set maximum while groove depth grew with it, and sideways force followed a curved relation to depth. The grooves sprang back by about a quarter after the scratch passed, and real widths ran noticeably wider than formulas predict because edges chip away. Corrected geometry feeds a fracture model for fairer toughness numbers.
pmc-13467912:
Ping-Chia Cheng and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of how well ultrasound features, stiffness imaging and needle aspirates separate benign from malignant salivary gland tumours before surgery. They reviewed 271 patients whose tumours were removed between 2015 and 2025, all with ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration plus a pathology diagnosis, and tested which imaging traits predicted cancer.

pmc-13468612:
Sierra and colleagues studied in 2026 chitosan-coated nanoliposomes, tiny fat bubbles used to carry drugs, and how the coating polymer's chain length affects them. Chitosan, a shell-derived polymer, came in low, medium, and high molecular weights. The team first charted the coating solutions, then made the bubbles by ethanol injection with ultra-high-pressure mixing, coated them, and tracked size and charge at once and after four weeks of storage.

Sierra found a clear turning point in solution behaviour that set the coating strength to use. Bare bubbles measured about 150 to 200 nanometres wide, with even sizes and a strong negative charge. Coating made them bigger and less even, and softened the charge while staying negative, a sign of a light surface layer rather than full wrapping. Bubbles mixed under high pressure and coated with medium or high weight chitosan held up best under heat stress storage.
pmc-13468912:
Lai and Jin introduce a research collection on AI-driven plant intelligence. Their 2026 editorial frames a problem. Protecting crops is squeezed by food insecurity, climate change, and biodiversity loss. The ecological costs of chemical inputs add pressure. Conventional protection, meanwhile, stays experience-driven and input-heavy. Precision plant protection promises productivity with fewer chemicals but must adapt to fields that vary in space and time.

The editors read them as one transition: agricultural AI moving from isolated recognition tasks toward integrated systems that perceive, learn, and respond within real agroecosystems. Multimodal sensing and ecological sustainability are the twin themes they emphasise for the field's next stage.
pmc-13469012:
Jia Ren and six colleagues published this 2026 study identifying fibronectin 1, a matrix protein known for scarring roles, as a master switch for lactylation after heart attack. When heart muscle is starved of blood, lactate piles up, and lactate-derived tags, called lactylation, remodel protein behaviour, yet what drives the process was unclear. pmc-13469312:
Shuoxuan Zhao and co-authors describe in 2026 how the influenza A virus disarms a human protein that normally helps cells fight infection. The protein, called ACSL3, strengthens a cell stress system known as the unfolded protein response, which can slow the virus down. Blood data from mildly ill flu patients showed higher ACSL3 levels, hinting at a protective role.

Gene screening and follow-up experiments in cells and animals confirmed that ACSL3 limits several flu strains. The protein works through two stress sensors in the cell, boosting helpful inflammation while holding back a form of cell death. The virus answers by sending ACSL3 to the cell waste system for destruction. That shift lets infected cells die quietly, which helps new virus particles escape and spread.
pmc-13470012:
Bonte and colleagues reported a surprise in 2026: briefly blocking a lysosomal enzyme protected dopamine neurons against one form of cell death, ferroptosis. They then challenged the cells with several death triggers, tracking lipid chemistry and a protective enzyme called GPX4.

Only one death route was blunted: cells resisted ferroptosis triggered by RSL3, while other killers worked as usual. The blocker reshaped membrane fats, cutting the ether-linked lipids ferroptosis feeds on, and raised GPX4, the enzyme defusing those fats. Both changes were temporary, gone by twenty days. pmc-13470112:
Xueqian Jiang, Jialun Wu, and Jiabei Liu lay out in 2026 a tiered workflow for honestly testing geographic prediction models. Nearby places resemble each other, so random test splits flatter models that will face new regions. Their workflow separates three questions: filling gaps inside a known area, separating clusters within it, and transferring to a distinct region altogether.

Checks stack coordinate clusters, random folds, a size matched random control, network communities, administrative holdouts, and one outside region stress test. A demonstration used 211 Baltimore house sales predicted from building traits. Random scores beat clustered scores, and holdouts of whole districts or regions cut performance further. pmc-13470712:
Teshome and colleagues use computer modeling in this 2026 study of magnesium sulfate hydrates, compounds whose formula counts attached water molecules from zero to seven per salt unit. Their calculations show each drying step costs more energy than the last, because direct attraction between magnesium and sulfate ions grows stronger than the hydrogen bonds among water molecules as hydration falls. pmc-13471212:

Textbooks blame rupture of the central slip, the tendon band over the middle joint. A patient arrived with a deformity that appeared instantly and could not be straightened by hand. Yet the central slip was largely intact, prompting the team to test alternative injury patterns on cadaver fingers.

The anatomical study used 16 cadaveric fingers and created isolated tendon injuries in controlled combinations. Cutting the central slip alone, or one lateral band alone, never produced the stuck deformity. Combining a longitudinal tear of one lateral band with rupture of the neighboring collateral ligament did so consistently, dropping the band below the joint axis. Ferrazzini argues this overlooked pattern explains immediate, irreducible cases and should guide early diagnosis and surgery.
pmc-13471512:
Zarinfar and co-authors linked frailty to quality of life in older adults in southern Iran, using data from the Bushehr Elderly Health Program. Their 2026 cross-sectional study covered 2,367 people aged 60 and older with a mean age of 69.3 years, classifying frailty by the Fried phenotype and scoring well-being with the SF-12 survey.

Frailty affected 8.0% of participants, 191 people, while many more sat in the pre-frail middle group. Frail elders scored far lower on physical quality of life, with an adjusted difference of −9.51 points against the non-frail, and had 13.77 times the adjusted odds of landing in the lowest physical score quarter. Mental quality of life dipped mainly for the pre-frail, a smaller and less certain effect.
pmc-13471612:

Their 2026 multi-centre design uses a stepped-wedge rollout across paramedic services, with time to return of spontaneous circulation as the main outcome.

In the team's local data, 84% of children got their first dose more than five minutes after paramedics arrived, and 29% waited over ten minutes. Only 2 to 10% of these children survive to hospital discharge nationally, and local survival was 6% in their sample.
pmc-13472912:
Li and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the roles of extracellular vesicles in heart failure. Vesicles are tiny membrane parcels cells release, carrying proteins, fats, and RNA messages between cells. The review covers how vesicles shape inflammation, energy failure in heart cells, muscle thickening, scarring, cell death, and blood vessel growth in the failing heart. Stem cell-derived vesicles show protective effects in early studies, and engineered vesicles can ferry drugs or RNA to target tissue. The authors also discuss how current heart failure drugs interact with vesicle pathways. They argue vesicles connect mechanism to clinic: one entity serving as messenger, marker, and medicine.
pmc-13473112:
Hao Qin and co-authors model green choices by high-tech factories in 2026 under a green credit system run by banks. Green microgrids, which supply clean power on site, sit at the heart of the study. Gains from selling green tech and from cleaner operations pulled firms toward low-carbon choices on their own. State research aid helped spark new microgrid tech, while very large rewards bred reliance on aid. Fair fines tied to green credit pushed firms to comply. The model helps leaders tune support so clean shifts last.
pmc-13474512:
Ruoxi Hong and co-authors map tumor diversity in triple-negative breast cancer in 2026 with a place-aware method. This cancer type lacks the usual drug targets and spreads early. The team cut tiny zones from primary tumors and matched spread sites under a microscope. Each zone gave DNA and RNA for deep reading.

Zones differed in gene faults and activity, with some areas alike throughout and others fading with distance. One cell state tied to energy-burning pathways marked poorer outlook and weaker response to immune drugs. Spread sites kept traits from their source clones, hinting that cell character partly survives travel. Place-aware maps could guide biopsy and drug choice.
pmc-13474612:
Phillips and co-authors interviewed the frontline staff who receive people returning to HIV care after treatment breaks at two Cape Town public clinics. Their 2026 qualitative study spoke with five nurses, three counsellors, and three administrative clerks, analyzing the clinics' inner workings through an implementation-science framework.

A booked day can reach 110 patients before walk-ins arrive, and poor communication curdles the welcome returnees get. The two clinics together carry nearly 9,000 people on antiretroviral therapy by 2023 program data, so friction at re-entry is a volume problem as much as an attitude problem. pmc-13474712:

Their 2026 cross-sectional study paired body mass index with questionnaires on perceived discrimination and modeled the pathways between them.

pmc-13474812:
Tse and colleagues followed 10 Chinese women recovering from bipolar disorder through nine months of creative practice in a 2026 study built around their own photographs and words. Participants painted or wrote, then used a method called photovoice, where people document their lives with pictures and discuss them with researchers. The project ended with a public art exhibition and a human library event, where visitors could hear the artists' stories in person.

Some women also described sharper perception during depressive phases, and their drive to finish pieces depended on how meaningful the goal felt to them personally. Sharing work on social media built community, motivation, and confidence, supporting the authors' call for care that builds on patient strengths.
pmc-13475012:
Smith and colleagues in Australia worked in 2026 with Aboriginal Elders to fix a weak link in health research. The link is how finds get told back to the people who took part. Rules for such telling exist, but teams rarely use them well. Their case grew from a 2024 workshop where 29 advisors shaped a local healthy lifestyle plan. The work ran as action research, with Elders as co makers, not guests. Talk from the day was taped and read for themes. Two stood out: work in true partnership, and leave a legacy. The book, with art and forms for all ages, now serves as that record. Print copies went to all who took part at first, and a free copy sits online.
pmc-13475612:
Bai examines in 2026 how AI-driven smart libraries shape student choices. Bai introduces algorithmic academic framing, meaning the way recommendation systems steer what students notice and pick. Survey data were gathered at time-lagged points from 328 students at three universities in China.

That indirect path grew stronger when students felt confident using AI tools. It weakened when students felt cognitively overloaded, meaning their mental resources were stretched thin. Bai argues these systems act as cognitive infrastructure, and that library platforms should be designed to support confidence while limiting overload.
pmc-13476212:
Xuwen Wang and co-authors hunt breast cancer risk genes tied to exosomes in 2026 using public data and machine learning. Exosomes are tiny parcels cells use to trade messages. Drug, protein, and regulator maps were drawn around the five genes. Docking tests checked how well candidate drugs fit the gene products.
pmc-13477012:
Qi Wang and co-authors argue in 2026 that internal cell stores shape the calcium signals that drive plant immunity. Calcium spikes are among the earliest signs a plant has sensed attack. Known defense switches at the cell surface let calcium flood in from outside. Yet attack-linked signals are longer and more patterned than surface influx alone explains.

The piece gathers that scattered proof into an organelle-centered view. Breeding or editing store channels could tune crop immunity.
pmc-13478612:
Wang and co-authors studied a flexible thin-spray coating for coal mine roadways in 2026, a layer meant to seal and support the rock surface around tunnels. Standard sprayed concrete cracks and peels, while the new ductile material bends without breaking. The team modeled both materials with two simulation packages and then trialed the coating underground in the bottom extraction roadway of Changping Coal Mine.

Simulations showed the ductile coating improved the stress state in the shallow rock around the tunnel and helped the rock carry more of its own load. It also suppressed sliding of loose blocks between anchor rods, the steel bolts that pin the rock, better than rigid concrete did in the models. Field measurements matched, with overall tunnel deformation kept under control, and the authors mark two rock combinations, poor rock with medium-hard beds and general rock with soft beds, as best suited.
pmc-13478812:
Georgie Berry wrote a 2026 Viewpoint pushing back on the snowflake label attached to Generation Z and its rising mental distress. Berry writes both as a youth mental health researcher and as a member of the Matilda Centre Youth Advisory Board. The piece accompanies national survey work showing Australian youth disorder rates climbing from about 23 percent in 2007 to about 36 percent in 2022.

They pointed instead to economic insecurity, precarious work and housing, lingering COVID-19 disruption to schooling and productivity, and the mixed effects of digital media. Berry frames rising distress as a rational response to unstable conditions rather than personal failure. The piece closes on a governance demand: young people must sit inside research and policy rooms as leaders, not subjects.
pmc-13478912:
Wang and a team in China probed in 2026 a chicken or egg riddle in hard to treat epilepsy: does brain swelling cause drug failure, or trail it? Near a third of epilepsy patients keep seizing on drugs. The team gave rats a burst of bacterial toxin, by belly shot or brain shot, then sparked a long seizure bout. Rats were then classed by whether two drugs in turn could stop later fits.

The early burst made the long bout easier to spark, so swelling can light the fuse of the disease. But burst rats did not end up drug proof more often than plain rats. Rats that did turn drug proof told a split tale: their brain cores held high levels of two heat signals, with nerve loss. The authors frame swelling as a phase based player, a spark at the start and a mark of the stuck state.
pmc-13479212:
Molly Fitzgerald, Mathew Kelley, and Reginald Williams published a 2025 centennial reflection on the Harkness Fellowship. The program was founded in 1925 to bring health professionals to the United States for a year of immersion. Styled as a reverse Rhodes Scholarship, it now draws mid-career fellows from nine countries and many professions. The authors draw on archives, program records, alumni interviews, and case studies.

Three leadership lessons stand out across the century. Fellows innovated most when they challenged assumptions carried from home systems. Learning traveled in both directions, since hosts changed practice too. Careers bent toward system-level leadership after the fellowship year. The reflection uses one program's history to argue that crossing geographic and disciplinary borders remains a powerful way to grow health system leaders.
pmc-13479412:
Elise C. Tarbi and coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study of video visits for serious illness conversations with rural cancer patients. Remote visits remove travel burdens, yet they change the sensory and relational space where hard news and goals-of-care talks happen. The team interviewed rural adults who were receiving cancer care or had finished recently.

Interviews probed which clinician behaviors made patients feel genuinely connected through a screen. The analysis sits inside a basic science framework for serious illness communication research. Patients described concrete practices, such as pacing, eye contact with the camera, and involving family members, that preserved trust at a distance. The authors translate these accounts into guidance for clinicians whose most sensitive conversations now happen by video.
pmc-13479612:
Krishnan and co-workers in Norway and the United States found in 2026 a way to read laser hit molecules in plain chemical words. Their math frame, time based coupled cluster theory, tracks how a molecule's electrons dance under light with high truth. Its snag was sense: the raw sums did not say which electron jumps made which flash of the spectrum. The team recast the sums as weights on set electron layouts, which can be watched as the dance runs.

With the recast, each light peak could be named by the jump that made it. They proved the way on four small molecules with ten electrons each, from water to methane, and matched a trusted older method line by line. Deep core jumps were named too. Twin demos, on a neon atom and on a pumped gas, showed the weights can track fast light tricks as they run.
pmc-13479712:
Xinyue Chen and coauthors present a 2026 randomized trial of individualized breathing support for small children during heart surgery through the right side of the chest. Collapsed lung areas after surgery are common in this setting, driven by the heart-lung machine, side positioning, and ventilation. A fixed air pressure setting may not fit every child's lungs.

Children aged six months to five years were randomized to standard protective ventilation at a fixed pressure or to pressure titrated by driving pressure measurements, repeated after positioning and after bypass. Both groups received lung recruitment maneuvers. Outcomes were collapsed lung on imaging and blood oxygenation after surgery. The trial tests whether personalizing one ventilator dial improves recovery in a fragile population.
pmc-13479812:
Minghao Ji and coauthors published a 2026 prediction study of abnormal heart rhythm after esophagus cancer surgery. Postoperative atrial fibrillation or flutter lengthens hospital stays and adds complications, so prevention should target the patients most likely to benefit. The dataset covered 623 patients who had radical esophagus removal for cancer.

Candidate risk factors were screened one by one, then combined in models built by backward selection. Model quality was judged by discrimination scores, calibration checks, and formal fit tests. A nomogram, a paper scoring chart, and a random forest algorithm were all developed from the same data. The authors aim to give surgical teams a validated bedside estimate of rhythm risk before the operation, so monitoring and preventive drugs can be concentrated wisely.
pmc-13479912:
Jiajun Lan, Zhikai Qin, and Yuming Zhang published a 2026 systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of whole-body vibration training for balance in older stroke patients. Standing vibration platforms are marketed as passive exercise, and dynamic balance is a decisive factor in falls after stroke. Five databases were searched through late December 2025 for randomized trials with mean participant age of at least sixty.

Twelve trials qualified for pooling. Effects were computed from change scores between groups, using a three-level statistical model that respects multiple outcomes per study. Subgroup analyses, dose-response modeling, and robustness checks explored what drives benefit: vibration settings, session dose, and patient characteristics. The authors aim to tell rehabilitation teams whether the platforms earn their clinic space, and at what settings.
pmc-13480112:
Frazer A Tessema and co-authors report a 2026 case where two rare conditions combined to strain care. A woman with Eisenmenger syndrome, a late stage of an unrepaired heart defect that reverses blood flow, also carried a gene-confirmed vessel condition that forms fragile tangles in organs. She arrived with acute bleeding in the gut, low blood pressure, and worsening blue tint to the skin.

Teams from several specialties weighed clashing risks: bleeding from fragile vessels, clots from sluggish reversed flow, and low oxygen throughout. Scans mapped the vessel tangles, and a heart catheter study gauged pressures. Care mixed a vessel growth blocker, two lung pressure drugs, an acid blocker, iron, and a drug to lift blood pressure. The case shows why such patients need joint planning, since steps that help one condition can worsen the other.
pmc-13480512:
Kexin Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 study of single sugar chains threading through tiny solid pores, aimed at better drug purity checks. Heparin, a blood thinner built from sugar units, can hide a toxic look-alike that standard tests catch slowly. The team fed heparin through silicon nitride pores and timed each passage with fast electronics, varying acidity to change chain shape.

Even with top-grade kit, chains shot through bare pores too fast to tell heparin from its contaminant with trust. Simulations of the signals helped map how chains get caught and slide, and how charge and flow tug them along. The authors sketch fixes such as pore coatings or slower transit fluids for later work. For now the study marks the speed limit that any pore-based heparin checker must beat.
pmc-13482012:
Wu and three colleagues in China weighed in 2026 the pooled proof for magnetic brain stimulation as a help for weak thinking across brain and mind diseases. The method, short named HF-rTMS, pulses a magnetic coil on the scalp to stir brain cells. The team gathered twenty nine prior meta-analyses, each itself a pool of trials, that covered six diseases. They re-pooled the lot and graded how firm the proof was.
