Schizophrenia and attention deficit cases gained a small to fair amount. Parkinson's disease and deep depression showed no clear gain at all. The catch was quality: near half of all outcomes sat in the weakest proof grade. The authors urge big, shared trials before wide clinical use.
pmc-13482212:
Nina Randolph-Koranteng and co-authors present a 2026 policy comparison on support for teen girls and young women in small-scale mining areas of Ghana and Uganda. These young workers face poor sexual health outcomes tied to poverty and thin clinic access. The team read fourteen global and twenty-seven national policy papers from 2010 to 2023 across mining, health, gender, and youth themes.

Global and national papers aligned on teen health, universal care, youth jobs, and child labour bans. National papers stressed services, schooling, and trade skills yet never named mining-community teens as a distinct group with stacked risks. Without that naming, their mix of money and health needs stays off budget lines. The authors urge policy writers to flag these young women as a priority group in plain terms.
pmc-13483612:
Zhuoya Zhang and co-workers sort blood pressure patients on a high plateau in China into self-care types. Their 2026 study took place at a hospital in Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture. Care was checked from late 2024 to mid 2025. The team used a grouping method that finds hidden types, then asked what traits place a patient in each type.

Trust in one's own skill played a part in all three types. Help, health knowledge, and faith in self also played roles. Care that fits the weak spot of each type should beat one-size advice.
pmc-13485612:
Carlos Cifuentes-González benchmarks a specialty-tuned language model against general models and medical students at screening papers for a systematic review. Published in 2026, the comparison sits inside a registered review of retinal vasculitis, using 1,030 randomly drawn records from an initial haul of 5,533. Two eye experts supply the gold standard, with disagreements settled by adjudication.

The tuned model, named UveAItis, reached 93.3 percent accuracy with strong agreement scores, clearly beating the base general model, a rival general model, and final-year students. It recovered 65.4 percent of expert-included papers after consensus, while students recovered only 22.3 percent. Fine-tuning on a narrow specialty task, rather than raw model size, drove the gap. Review teams facing thousands of abstracts gain a validated shortcut that still needs expert oversight.
pmc-13487212:
Rony and co-authors built a lightweight network that outlines organs and lesions in medical scans without needing a data-center computer. Outlining, called segmentation, demands both crisp boundaries and whole-image context, which small models usually trade against each other. Their 2026 framework, SwiftMSeg, mixes a convolutional encoder with a transformer module that shuttles between local detail and global context, then decodes at several scales.

Tested on colonoscopy, pathology, ultrasound, and MRI datasets, the model scored overlap values between about 0.85 and 0.90 across the four scan types. Its boundary error on MRI was the lowest figure highlighted, at about sixteen units on the distance measure used. Performance held up on an external dataset the model had never trained on. pmc-13487912:
Melinda Cservenak and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on learning after birth, carried out with an automated home cage system called IntelliCage. Female mice were compared across pregnancy, the period after giving birth, and a nonpregnant state. Tasks measured place learning, reversal learning, where a learned rule changes, and drinking on a fixed schedule over a long observation period.

Mothers after birth learned places faster, adapted better when rules changed, and kept learned information more reliably than the other groups. The authors link this gain to the demands of caring for pups, such as finding food and responding to changing needs. Results may inform wider research on how reproduction shapes brain function.
pmc-13488212:
Yu Nosaka and colleagues report a 2026 case pairing two rare infected aneurysms in a 58-year-old woman in Japan. Infection of a heart valve had sent infected clots to the lungs and blocked the heart's outflow path. Scans during antibiotic treatment found a small infected bulge in a lung artery branch, at high risk of bursting. Doctors first sealed the lung artery bulge with coils through a catheter, lowering the risk of catastrophic bleeding on the heart-lung machine. pmc-13490412:
Lukomska and colleagues hunted a rare cell population in the mouse retina marked by the protein nectin-3, hoping it might hold regenerative potential. Such marker cells maintain reserve populations in other tissues, but the retina's version was unmapped. Their 2026 study sorted the cells from embryonic stages through adulthood, counted them, read their gene activity, and located them under the microscope at each age.

Their share peaked near four percent shortly after birth, settling near one and a half percent in adults. Microscopy placed them with the ganglion cell layer, distinct from the retina's support scaffolding. Lukomska reads them as a specialized neuronal lineage with basal identity.
pmc-13490512:
Ghosh and team studied a vivid atomic partnership in solution between the blue donor, an charge-rich blue hydrocarbon, and p-chloranil, an charge-hungry partner. When donor meets acceptor, a charge-transfer complex forms and drinks in near-deep-red light. The complex announced itself with a distinct uptake band centered near 808 nm, in the near deep-red. Two reading approaches returned strong binding constants, both in the tens of thousands on the reported scale, confirming tight bonding. Math showed the partners align so their charge clouds overlap efficiently, explaining the strong coupling. pmc-13490612:
Kathryn La Capria and colleagues run an attention experiment on cannabis vape advertising among young adults in a 2026 United States study. Noticing social effect claims showed a similar pattern, with the largest intention link of the pitches tested. Creativity claims linked only with intentions. The authors warn that benefit framing may pull new users in.
pmc-13491812:
Dingkang Wang leads a ten-author team profiling in 2026 how a salt-loving yeast used in fermented foods rewires its chemistry under salt stress, and whether added functional protein helps. The team used high-resolution mass spectrometry to compare yeast chemistry with and without protein supplementation at high salt.

Amino acid handling, antioxidant defenses, and nutrient transport all strengthened, while membrane fat pathways were tuned toward more flexible membranes. pmc-13491912:
Edith K Wakida and six colleagues explore in 2026 whether district health management teams could champion suicide prevention in rural Uganda under the World Health Organization's LIVE LIFE framework. Success, they warned, needs training, practical tools, mentorship, transport money, and room in district budgets. pmc-13493712:
Laura Mateu-Arrom, Alejandro Molina-Leyva, and Eva Vilarrasa systematically review in 2026 whether pairing biologic drugs with surgery beats either alone in hidradenitis suppurativa, the painful recurring abscess disease of skin folds. Only eight studies with 508 patients qualified, sorted by timing into surgery before biologics, surgery after drug induction, and truly simultaneous care. Most evidence was retrospective and weak.

Complications and serious side effects did not rise consistently with the added surgery. Wound healing time, a crucial outcome for patients, was reported so poorly that the reviewers could not judge it. Heterogeneity blocked any pooled analysis, and the authors label their support preliminary pending prospective trials.
pmc-13493912:
Priyadharshini G and Vetriselvi T build in 2026 a featherweight vision model that spots weeds among young crops for farm robots. Their architecture braids a compact convolutional network with attention blocks that reweight important features, then a transformer stage that reads the scene as a sequence. The Adam training optimizer delivered the best test accuracy at ninety-seven percent, slightly ahead of its label-smoothed variant and clearly ahead of RMSProp. pmc-13494112:

Retrieval practice means pulling facts from memory rather than rereading them, and it aids learning in many groups, most strongly when feedback follows. Participants memorized unrelated word pairs, then practiced by recall, by recall with feedback, or by restudy.

In the first experiment, 40 autistic and 40 non-autistic adults heard the pairs aloud. The second used written pairs, added restudy trials, and enrolled larger groups. Feedback after an early recall attempt helped both groups in both experiments. The second experiment also showed recall practice beating restudy even without feedback. The authors conclude that these well-known learning gains extend to autistic learners, which matters for teaching and therapy design.
pmc-13494212:
Marjolein T Bulbaai leads a 2026 cohort study of fish eating and bowel growths in people with Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition that sharply raises bowel cancer risk. They followed 1,816 carriers who reported their fish intake on food questionnaires at entry. Over a median of seven years, about four in ten developed a bowel growth, classed as an adenoma, a serrated lesion, or cancer. Total fish intake showed no link with risk, either at the highest intakes or per small daily rise, and no subgroup stood apart. Canned fish alone hinted at slightly higher risk per small daily rise, a signal the authors say needs more study before anyone acts on it.
pmc-13494312:

The authors call the saving modest and note the design cannot split local action at the block site from drug action through the whole body.
pmc-13495312:
Mingshen Lin and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether lifelong social isolation pulls body makeup in two directions at once among older Chinese adults. The pattern paints a quiet risk: shrinking strength without the weight signal that usually alerts doctors. Subgroup and extra checks supported the split. The authors urge early action on isolation to head off hidden functional decline before disability sets in.
pmc-13495512:

For the other they engineered a guide RNA that props up the weakened true site, lifting correct splicing from about a tenth to near three fifths. The authors offer the pair as a flexible template for treating splicing diseases, while stressing the work is still in dishes, not patients.
pmc-13498412:
Ananya Murali and colleagues present in 2026 a single case that revisits infusions of white blood cells for a patient with dangerously low infection-fighting cells. Their patient was a 39-year-old man whose leukaemia followed earlier cancer treatment and resisted standard chemotherapy. His neutrophil count rose briefly and modestly, and the fungal infection cleared during that window. He later died from the underlying leukaemia, which had never responded to treatment. The authors use the case to weigh the short-lived benefit against the practical difficulty of arranging such infusions.
pmc-13499112:
Gordon and colleagues pooled study data in 2026 on how blood-based residual disease testing compares with PET imaging for predicting survival in large B-cell lymphoma after first treatment. Scans judge response by tracer uptake, but a fifth to a third of patients who look clear later relapse. Patients with a positive blood signal fared poorly even when scans looked clear, with only about 40 percent free of progression at two years. The blood result split outcomes inside both scan groups. The authors call the test a robust predictor and urge trials of care guided by it.
pmc-13500112:
Marcia L Stefanick and colleagues report nine years of activity results from the Women's Health Initiative Strong and Healthy trial, known as WHISH. Their 2026 paper tests a light-touch, remotely delivered programme meant to raise physical activity and cut sitting time in older women.

A total of 49,331 women aged 66 to 99 were randomised to the programme or to usual activity, using a consent design in which most intervention participants passively agreed to receive materials. Over a median 8.7 years, the intervention group reported modestly more walking, aerobic exercise, total exercise, and strength sessions, and slightly less sitting, than the comparison group. Benefits were largest in the youngest group, aged 66 to 76, for aerobic exercise and sitting time. The authors conclude the programme modestly slowed age-related declines in activity.
pmc-13501612:
Jennifer E Miller leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 study of cancer trials that succeeded at enrolling Black and LatinX patients in line with disease burden. Successful strategies clustered at five levels, from patients and communities up to policy. Teams budgeted in advance for patient expenses, co-created education with communities, and used patient navigators. They engaged clinicians early, simplified protocols, widened eligibility, and ran the trials through community and satellite hospitals. Sponsors backed it with leadership commitment, enrollment dashboards, performance incentives, and staff training. The authors offer this playbook as a route to cancer evidence that travels.
pmc-13501712:
Zilin Chen leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 cohort study that links higher HDL cholesterol, the so-called good cholesterol, with greater glaucoma risk in older Chinese adults. Data came from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. The analysis followed 7,510 people over 45 who had no glaucoma at the 2011 baseline, recording new self-reported cases through 2018. Over seven years, 224 participants, 2.98 percent, developed glaucoma. Each extra millimole per litre of HDL carried a hazard ratio of 1.57 for new disease after adjustment. People with low HDL, below 1.0 in the same units, had a lower risk than those with normal levels, with a hazard ratio of 0.63 on that comparison. pmc-13501812:

Pecans pack monounsaturated fats, plant sterols, fibre, and polyphenols, yet trial results had never been pooled comprehensively. The pair searched five databases through November 2025 and found ten eligible trials in adults. Random-effects models combined the changes in blood lipids, glucose measures, body size, and blood pressure.

Pecans lowered three lipid measures significantly: total cholesterol by a weighted mean of 8.49 milligrams per decilitre, LDL cholesterol by 7.42 in the same units, and triglycerides by 14.06 on that scale. The lipid trials agreed with each other closely, showing zero measured heterogeneity. Nothing convincing emerged for HDL cholesterol, glucose, insulin, weight, waist size, or blood pressure. Triglyceride benefits appeared only in trials lasting over four weeks. The authors back pecans as a lipid-friendly food.
pmc-13503112:
Ridderbos and colleagues issued consensus recommendations in 2026 on how urine samples should be collected and handled before albumin and protein testing, the markers used to find and stage chronic kidney disease. The report stresses that 24-hour and single samples answer different questions, that timing and repeat measures matter because levels swing naturally, and that heat, cold, and delay can distort results. It gathers the evidence into practical procedures meant to cut biological and lab variation between clinics and studies. The authors present the shared standard as a base for more trustworthy kidney monitoring and fairer comparison of trial results across sites.
pmc-13504212:
Emel Özcan-Gökçek leads a team linking variants in the growth hormone gene to body traits in European sea bass, in a 2026 study. The hormone steers growth, appetite, and breeding in fish, so its gene is a natural place to look for breeding markers. Farm output depends heavily on growth rate.

Reading a stretch of the gene, the team found five haplotypes and ten new single-letter variants. Two changes swap amino acids in a key helix of the hormone. Fish type at three spots in the gene tracked weight and body lengths in clear ways. One haplotype outgrew all others on weight and length traits. The authors propose it as a marker for selective breeding under Mediterranean farm conditions.
pmc-13504812:
Bingjun Yu leads a team asking how age shapes outcomes in sudden pancreas inflammation, in a 2026 study of more than a thousand patients. The illness varies a great deal by cause and course. Older patients arrive frailer, yet it was unclear whether age itself drives bad outcomes.

pmc-13505012:
Xuhan Zhu leads a team reviewing transformer models in dentistry, in a 2026 systematic review. Transformers are AI networks that weigh context across a whole image, a strength over older local methods. Dental uses have spread fast, but no full synthesis of their worth existed.

The search gathered 112 studies from 2020 to 2025. Most used hybrids that pair classic image networks with transformer parts; a smaller set used pure transformers. Hybrids beat pure models across tooth mapping, decay spotting, implant placement, and jaw assessment tasks. Scores dropped five to eight points when models faced outside data, a warning about real-world fit. The authors cite small labeled data sets and uneven test methods as the main brakes on clinic use.
pmc-13507012:
Sergio Cornelio-Martínez and colleagues compare, in 2026 work, gut microbes in the land slug Deroceras laeve under two diets. One group ate a rodent feed, while the other ate fresh vegetables for three months. The team sampled stomach and intestine contents and read bacterial DNA to name groups and predict what they do.

One broad bacterial group dominated both gut parts, yet its share fell on the vegetable diet while variety rose. A single genus, Rahnella, led in both diets. Predicted work shifted with diet in the stomach, with fat building favored on rodent feed. Core tasks in the intestine stayed stable. Diet clearly reshapes the slug gut community.
pmc-13508212:
Saleh Alsarhan and Jagan Kumar Baskaradoss study sick leave tied to muscle and joint disorders among dentists in Kuwait, in 2026 work. Dentistry strains the neck, back, and hands, yet national figures for Kuwait were missing. The team mined health ministry records from January 2022 to October 2023, covering 2,735 dentists. A keyword search of leave records, refined in both English and Arabic terms, flagged episodes linked to these disorders. Statistical models then weighed which traits tracked with taking such leave.

Over two fifths of the dentists had at least one such sick leave episode in that window. Dentists in their thirties faced higher odds than those under thirty, while dentists over fifty faced lower odds. Women had higher odds than men, and rates varied by region. The authors argue for ergonomic support aimed at early and mid-career dentists, where the burden falls hardest.
pmc-13508312:
Courtney Davis and Kumudhini Rajasegaran test a workshop where trained teen actors play patients to build medical students' confidence in sensitive talks, in 2026 work. Teen care often requires broaching substance use, sexuality, mood, and safety, and trainees report shaky confidence there. Students on a children's hospital rotation in Singapore joined a three-hour workshop of coached role-plays with structured feedback. Confidence was surveyed just before the workshop and again four weeks later. A total of 147 students took part.

Overall confidence rose sharply and held at the four-week check. Gains covered every measured area, including interviewing teens and explaining confidentiality. Some of the biggest jumps came in taking a sexual history and asking about sexual orientation, areas students had rated lowest at the start. Students rated the actors' feedback and the role-play practice as the most useful parts. The authors recommend this format for teaching psychosocial risk assessment.
pmc-13508412:
Mohammad Aleinati, Jennifer Spiegel, Trung Le, and Justin Lui set out the protocol for a sham-controlled trial of balloon widening for ear pressure problems, in 2026 work. The condition, baro-challenge Eustachian tube dysfunction, causes ear pain and pressure trouble when altitude or depth changes, as in flying or diving. The balloon procedure is done in the office under local numbing, yet strong proof is missing because symptoms are largely self-reported. Adults who failed standard care at Canadian tertiary centers will be assigned to the real procedure or a sham one.

Neither patients nor outcome checks will know which procedure each person had. The main measure is symptom change on a tailored seven-item questionnaire at six weeks. As the first blinded sham test in this group, the trial aims to separate true benefit from placebo effect before the procedure spreads further.
pmc-13509012:
Adillon and colleagues varied the bridge inside a family of molecules that deliver a proton and an electron. That combined move, called proton-coupled electron transfer, underpins fuel-forming and fertilizer chemistry. Their 2026 study uses cobaltocene-based mediators carrying an acid group, in four versions differing only in the covalent link between the electron donor and the proton donor. One version was made through a late-stage palladium-catalyzed coupling.

Adillon measured transfer equilibria and reaction speeds against a series of aryl ketones. The driving force barely changed across the family, and every mediator reacted through a single concerted step rather than separate proton and electron hops. The version with a bent phenylene bridge reacted fastest despite having the weakest driving force. The authors attribute this to favorable orbital contact between the ketone and the mediator's ring system. The work shows bridges tune speed by preorganizing partners, not by thermodynamics.
pmc-13510012:
Elena Tanase and eight co-authors compare substance use and service outcomes across psychiatric care settings in Romania, in 2026 work. The group studied 128 adults with severe mental illness who had spent at least a year in one of three settings: hospital care, long-term residential care, or protected community housing. A standard screening tool scored substance involvement, with tobacco left out of the severity score.

Substance use outside tobacco peaked in hospital care, sat in the middle for residential care, and ran lowest in community housing. Mental quality of life ran lowest among hospital patients who used substances and highest among community residents who did not. Greater severity went with poorer mental quality of life and higher yearly care cost, even after other factors were counted. Feeling more in control of daily life went with better outcomes.
pmc-13510112:
Ozan Kılıçkaya and Serap Şahin study how a targeted DNA strand changes fat chemistry inside glioblastoma cells, in 2026 work. The strand, called AS1411, binds a protein that sits in excess on the surface of these brain tumor cells. The pair treated a standard glioblastoma cell line and mapped its full fat profile with high-resolution chemical analysis after treatment.

The strand killed cells within a day, and fat profiles shifted widely. Several long and highly unsaturated fat types rose or appeared only after treatment, while saturated fats in two other classes also climbed. Those shifts stiffen cell membranes and lower their fluidity. At the same time, fats that feed a specific form of cell death called ferroptosis grew more common, leaving cells more open to that death route. The authors say the fat map points to paired treatment ideas worth testing.
pmc-13510412:
Qingqing Ma and colleagues report a newborn screening study, published in 2026. It covers citrin deficiency in Hefei, China. This inherited disorder causes liver bile build-up in babies. Nearly 925,000 newborns were screened. Tandem mass spectrometry was the method. Screening ran between 2016 and 2025. Positive cases were confirmed by gene sequencing.

Seventeen cases were found. This is about one in fifty-four thousand births. Two further cases were missed by the screen. The commonest mutation was a small deletion in the SLC25A13 gene. Most children did well with diet guidance and treatment. One had lasting growth problems. Missed cases led the authors to recommend retesting. Any baby with prolonged jaundice should be retested despite a negative screen.
pmc-13510812:
Miroslav Pohanka develops a crystal-based biosensor for measuring melatonin, the hormone that sets the body's daily rhythm, in 2026 work. Melatonin levels in saliva and blood sit very low, which makes them hard to measure with simple tools. The sensor uses a quartz crystal coated with a melatonin-linked protein, plus stacked antibody layers that amplify the signal when melatonin in a sample competes for binding.

The assay was tuned to the tiny range found in the body and could detect melatonin in a drop-sized sample at levels matching natural amounts. It stayed selective against likely interfering substances and matched a standard lab test almost exactly on shared samples. Real human saliva tests confirmed it works in practice, and prepared sensors kept working for at least 140 days. The author offers the method as a simple, sensitive option for noninvasive hormone checks.
pmc-13511312:
Abena Adaboh and six colleagues published this 2026 report on newborn pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart disease at two hospitals in Accra, Ghana. The oxygen test catches heart defects before symptoms, but adoption in low- and middle-income countries lags. The team built the programme on a modified American Academy of Pediatrics protocol, trained staff to run it, and then surveyed staff about what worked and what broke down.

Staff felt instructed but asked for simulation practice in handling failed screens. Obstacles piled up: newborns were hard to locate across wards with paper records, equipment wore out, and arranging ultrasounds after failed screens was hard to coordinate. Early discharges and intensive care admissions cut coverage among the highest-risk babies. Still, the pilot raised staff awareness, sharpened diagnoses and proved feasible. The authors say lasting expansion needs stronger referral networks plus investment in children's cardiology and heart surgery.
pmc-13511712:
Eugen Kvašňák offers a comparative narrative review, published in 2026. It covers brain stimulation delivered at 40 hertz. This rhythm is tied to communication between brain areas. It is disrupted in several brain disorders. The review compares five delivery routes. They include sound and light flicker. Weak electric current through the scalp is another. Magnetic pulses and combined multisensory stimulation complete the five.

The review draws on animal work and early human studies. Single sessions rarely improve thinking. Multi-week programmes show more promise. Some groups show brain rhythm and biomarker changes. Combined multisensory stimulation shows the strongest early signal in Alzheimer's disease. The author stresses that evidence is preliminary. Large controlled trials are still required.
pmc-13512212:
Alina Cernasev and colleagues report a public health study, published in 2026. It compares HPV vaccination barriers and supports among women in Tennessee. Women with and without HIV were compared. Women living with HIV face much higher cervical cancer risk. The team explored perceptions in both groups. They sought what blocks or encourages vaccination.

Both groups were largely unaware of the HPV vaccine. Understanding of the virus itself was limited. This held despite the far greater risk for women with HIV. Their cervical cancer rate is about six times higher. Doctors, nurses, and pharmacists are pivotal advocates, the authors argue. Targeted education is needed, especially for women living with HIV.
pmc-13512412:
Francesco Sessa and eight co-authors review DNA methods for naming burned, broken, or mixed human remains, in a 2026 systematic review. Fire and decay shred the usual identification routes, and disaster teams must work with what survives. Two databases were searched through June 2026 under standard review rules, and 37 studies passed screening. Findings were sorted into core DNA practice, newer genomic tools, and disaster case use.

Heat exposure, tissue choice, and sampling strategy governed how much DNA could be recovered. Teeth and dense outer bone gave the best yields again and again. Standard marker panels still anchor most identifications, while newer sequencing approaches widen what damaged samples can reveal. The authors blend lab evidence with field practice into one frame, aiming to help disaster victim identification teams pick sampling and testing routes that fit the condition of the remains.
pmc-13514112:
Ilker Çermikli, Tufan Alatli, and Salih Kocaoglu test a bedside ultrasound method for guiding fluid resuscitation in emergency patients bleeding from the upper gut, in 2026 work. Giving too little or too much fluid both harm such patients, and static measures predict response poorly. A mini fluid challenge gives a small test dose and watches the change in a heart outflow measure. Eighty-five patients joined the single-center study between February 2024 and February 2025, split by treatment period into guided and standard care groups.

The ultrasound measure was captured inside the target window for every enrolled patient, proving bedside feasibility in undifferentiated bleeding cases. The measure was shared with treating teams only in the guided group and kept offline in the standard group. Its link to in-hospital death was explored as a secondary question. The authors present feasibility as the firm result and outcome links as early signals.
pmc-13515612:
Feng Zhao and five colleagues design a micromanipulator that stretches tiny movements into larger ones, in a 2026 engineering study. Such tools grip and place objects in jobs like fibre alignment and micro-surgery, where the drive motor moves only a whisker. Their three-stage design stacks a stiff rhombus unit, a bridge unit, and two parallelogram units, all flexing as one piece of material. A piezoelectric actuator, which moves when voltage is applied, drives the stack.

The team built a maths model of the stretch ratio, then tuned hinge thickness, hinge length, and rod sizes to push that ratio up while keeping strength and stiffness within limits. Computer simulation and bench tests confirmed the optimised design. The final device magnified movement far better than the starting version without going floppy. Zhao's team offers the method as a guide for building stronger high-magnification manipulators.
pmc-13516012:
Li and Luo investigated a 2026 biomarker study on a tiny RNA molecule in tuberculosis, the lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The molecule, miR-151a-3p, helps control gene activity, and its levels might separate healthy people from patients. It might also reveal who will fare worse during treatment.

The study enrolled 101 people with latent infection, 102 with active disease, and 63 healthy volunteers for blood testing. Levels of the molecule fell stepwise from healthy to latent to active disease, and the drop marked higher risk. In infected immune cells grown in the lab, restoring the molecule partly reversed cell death and inflammation. Li shows it acts by targeting TP53, a gene that drives cell stress responses.
pmc-13516212:
Mya Murray and six colleagues run a three-arm hunt for eye problems linked to gabapentin and pregabalin in a 2026 study. These drugs treat seizures and nerve pain, and reports of side effects keep rising. One arm listened on Reddit for user-described eye troubles. A second mined the United States adverse-event database from 2015 to 2025 for serious reports. A third reviewed the published literature from 2014 onward.

Reddit users described blurred vision, double vision, and light sensitivity for both drugs. The safety database showed positive signals for eye disorders against three comparison drugs. Pregabalin out-reported gabapentin for cataract and blindness by wide margins. The literature backed retinal concerns but offered little high-quality proof, though animal work suggests a plausible route through a retinal calcium-channel protein. Murray's team calls the signals worth validating in proper clinical studies.
pmc-13516912:
Wang and colleagues build a machine learning force field, a computer model that predicts the forces between atoms so simulations of molecules can run fast. Their 2026 system, called GeoNet, aims to capture both short range forces, such as bonds between near atoms, and long range forces that act across a molecule. Past models often missed the direction and distance of long range pulls and wobbled when a molecule changed shape.

GeoNet uses a form of attention, a method that weighs which parts matter most, over a graph linking atoms to larger molecular fragments. Extra training steps keep its answers steady across shape changes, and a fusion module shifts the balance between short and long range forces to suit each atom's local setting. Across the test sets, GeoNet beat ten leading rival models while also being the smallest model and the fastest to train.
pmc-13517212:
Shen and colleagues assessed in 2026 whether micro- and nanoplastics, tiny plastic particles in the environment, can injure the womb lining and harm pregnancy. They used a structured framework that scores evidence on reliability, dose, risk strength, and consistency, and they added their own lab test on human endometrial cells.

The evidence pool covered 21 published studies plus the team's cell experiment. In the lab, polystyrene nanoparticles raised reactive oxygen species inside womb lining cells, weakened their energy-producing parts, and increased cell death. Levels of three proteins needed for embryo implantation also fell. Combining all evidence gave a score in the framework's moderate-risk range. The authors present this as a structured first estimate, given how few direct studies exist so far.
pmc-13517712:
Ayla Sandıkcıoğlu Gümüş spends a year measuring radon in drinking wells along an active Turkish fault in a 2026 monitoring study. Radon gas seeps from rock into groundwater and adds a quiet radiation dose, yet fault zones lack long records. Fifteen wells near the Sultandağı Fault were sampled every two weeks from June 2021 to June 2022, and doses were computed separately for infants, children, and adults.

Levels averaged about six becquerels per litre and stayed under the world health guideline everywhere. One well passed the stricter American guideline. Seasons nudged the values without dramatic swings. Infants drew the highest estimated doses and lifetime cancer risk, though all groups stayed in low territory. Gümüş offers the year-long series as baseline evidence for regional risk work, with a watch note on the few hotter wells and on protecting the youngest drinkers first.
pmc-13518812:
Wenzeng Xu and colleagues identify in 2026 a bacterial weapon that helps Acinetobacter baumannii, a hard-to-treat hospital pathogen, dodge the immune system. The protein, VgrG2, is delivered by the bacterium's type VI secretion system, a molecular syringe. How such effectors attack human cells, beyond fighting rival bacteria, was poorly known.

VgrG2 works two ways at once. It switches off production of the Csu pilus, a surface hair that immune cells use to spot and grab the bacterium. It also overactivates Rac1 inside phagocytes, wrecking their internal skeleton and driving a vacuole-filled cell death called methuosis. Killing these sentinel cells lets the bacterium persist and spread, making the VgrG2-Rac1 link a drug target.
pmc-13518912:
Tirumalasetti Supraja and Kankanala Srinivas present a 2026 hybrid algorithm for splitting color images into levels using multiple thresholds. Good segmentation underpins object recognition, medical imaging, and satellite analysis, yet classic methods converge slowly and ignore how neighboring pixels relate.

Their method starts from the Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm, which mimics hummingbird foraging, and seeds its population with four low-discrepancy patterns for wider coverage. Spatial context from nearby pixels sharpens the segmentation goal, measured by minimum cross entropy. A Great Deluge acceptance rule, which lets slightly worse solutions pass early on, guards against local traps during refinement. Benchmarks against rival metaheuristics favored the hybrid, and the code is public.
pmc-13519612:
Enju Liu and Edie Weller published this 2026 simulation study on how adherence distorts trials of prenatal multiple micronutrient supplements in low- and middle-income countries. The supplements raise gestational weight gain and improve outcomes, yet pregnant women often take only part of the course. Building a simulation on a published meta-analysis, the authors generated trial datasets of 250 to 4,000 women, with adherence ranging from 50 to 100 percent. They measured how far the estimated benefit drifted.

As adherence fell, the estimated weight-gain benefit shrank and the error grew. With 2,000 participants, bias ran from 0.66 at half adherence down to 0.14 at 90 percent adherence on the adequacy scale used. Enlarging the sample did not reduce the bias at all: a 4,000-woman trial with low adherence was just as misleading as a small one. The authors stress that raising adherence, not recruitment, is what protects both trial conclusions and actual benefit for mothers and babies.
pmc-13520312:
Xia Zhao, Li Zhang and Nan Jin compare in 2026 two treatments for phimosis in boys, where the foreskin cannot retract normally. One option gently stretches the opening with a balloon device, while the other is standard circumcision surgery.

Records covered 200 boys aged 2 to 12 years treated during 2024, split evenly between the two methods. Cure rates at six months were near equal, at 98 percent for balloon treatment and 100 percent for surgery. Balloon care took far less time, healed faster and caused less pain. Parents also reported satisfaction and home-care details, which helps families weigh a foreskin-preserving choice.
pmc-13521212:
Larissa Wenren and colleagues interview in 2026 caregivers whose children live with complex heart disease and missed clinic visits. Missed visits can worsen health. Missed visits can also push care into emergency rooms. The team asked what blocks visits and what helps families return.

Talks covered 19 caregivers at one children's hospital. Black and Hispanic families were sought on purpose. Spanish speakers were included as well. Blocks spanned booking access and telehealth limits. Missed physical exams on video visits worried parents. Housing, transport and job strain added weight. Trusted doctor ties helped families stay in care. Parent ideas for fixes close the study.
pmc-13521912:
Gil Marcio Avelino Silva leads a 2026 project that reads drilling mud gas with machine learning in Brazil oil search. Mud traits and drill heat can warp the gas signal from deep fluids. Clean reads guide costly drill choices in real time.

Data came from 104 search wells. Lab fluid data and expert geology calls served as truth checks. Two depth curves came out of the work. One scores likeness to known fluids along the well. One grades heat damage from drilling itself. A ridge model won the field slot for smooth, clear curves. Boosted tree models scored best on raw numbers alone.
pmc-13522312:
Aoyun Yan and colleagues build in 2026 a gadolinium agent aimed at osteosarcoma for neutron capture therapy. Osteosarcoma is the top primary bone cancer in children and teens. The therapy kills tumour cells with tight aim. Survival gains stalled since standard surgery and drug care settled decades ago.

A short peptide homes to a surface marker on these cancer cells. The peptide links to a ring that holds gadolinium tight. Lab and animal checks showed sharp targeting. Safety signs looked good as well. Neutron shots then curbed tumours far better with the agent in place. Healthy tissue near the tumour should gain from the tight aim.
pmc-13522512:
Ahamed and co-authors introduced a 2026 artificial intelligence model that designs molecules from written descriptions. Drug and materials researchers want molecules with stated properties, but older generators follow text prompts poorly. Their model, Mol-CADiff, builds molecules step by step with a diffusion process guided by causal attention to the prompt.

Causal attention means each building step can only use information that came before it, mirroring how molecules assemble. Ahamed strengthened links within the text, within the molecule, and between the two so the output tracks the request closely. The model beat rival methods on making varied, chemically valid molecules that matched specified properties. It can also sample freely without any prompt, which widens its use in early drug discovery.
pmc-13522612:
Rushdy M Ahmed and co-authors characterize purslane seed oil and test its biological activity in a 2026 laboratory study. Purslane is a widespread edible weed valued for healthy fats. The oil was analyzed for phenolic and flavonoid content, meaning plant compounds linked to protective effects, and was tested for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cancer cell effects.

The oil held notable levels of both compound classes, and its antioxidant activity rose steeply with dose, reaching near-complete activity at the highest concentration. Effects against three cancer cell lines were weak to moderate, and lower concentrations showed anti-inflammatory activity compared with a standard drug. Chemical analysis found the oil rich in two main constituents. The authors call for animal studies and safety testing before any application is proposed.
pmc-13523312:
Ruirui Ji and colleagues propose a causal reinforcement learning method for inferring gene regulatory networks in a 2026 study. Knowing which genes switch others on or off is central to understanding cell function and disease, yet correlation methods cannot show direction and deep learning models are hard to interpret. Their framework searches network structures directly, guided by causal principles.

Tests on a standard benchmark dataset and on single-cell data from six cell types showed better inference accuracy, sparser structures, and stronger biological plausibility than mainstream baselines. Interpretability analysis and pathway checks showed the inferred networks matched known biology in both shape and function. The authors present the approach as a scalable way to model causal structure in large gene expression datasets.
pmc-13524812:
Zhang, Zhang, and a large team tackle a materials nuisance: graphene nanoribbons, atom-precise strips of carbon with tunable electronic gaps, clump together so strongly that single-ribbon devices stay out of reach. Their 2026 shielding strategy wraps each ribbon in a cyclophane, a ring-shaped molecular cage that holds neighbours at bay and, by squeezing, strains the ribbon itself. They synthesised three shielded ribbons with different cage chain lengths, plus model compounds, and probed them with terahertz spectroscopy.

Shorter chains made charge carriers move faster, with short-range mobility climbing from under two hundred to well over three hundred in the reported units as the cage tightened. The gain came thanks to lighter effective carriers and longer times between collisions. Computer estimates confirmed the shorter cages carried higher strain and weaker ribbon-to-ribbon attraction, explaining the clean dispersion.
pmc-13525712:
Shuqi Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 materials study building a four-boron molecular framework for yellow light-emitting diodes with unusually pure color. Multiple resonance emitters are prized for narrow emission bands in displays. A pattern placing boron atoms in the ortho arrangement promised redder emission than the usual pattern but was rarely achieved because synthesis is hard.

Using an indolocarbazole core, the team installed four boron atoms in a single borylation step at well-defined sites. The molecule emits bright yellow light with a spectral width of only 24 nanometers and shows an improved rate for converting triplet states back to light-producing singlets. A non-sensitized device reached 36.5 percent external quantum efficiency, among the best results at long wavelengths. The route offers guidance for complex emitter synthesis.
pmc-13526712:
Emmanuele Schorn and colleagues report a 2026 ten-year cohort study on immune abnormalities in young children with transient neutropenia, a temporary drop in a key white blood cell type. The condition often involves antibodies against neutrophils, yet links with wider antibody-system problems were poorly mapped. The setting was a Swiss pediatric tertiary center.

The cohort held 92 children aged up to six years seen between January 2014 and December 2023. Among 68 children with detailed immune testing, about seventy-seven percent showed humoral abnormalities, split between mild and moderate grades. Those children had neutrophil antibodies less often, higher minimum neutrophil counts, and shorter neutropenia, yet over a third lacked adequate vaccine antibodies. The authors recommend routine immune assessment for counseling and timely boosters.
pmc-13527912:
Brandon M. Roberts and eight colleagues report a 2026 study of DNA methylation in service members hospitalized after exertional heat illness. Methylation is a chemical tagging system that helps control gene activity. Blood samples came from 36 people with heat exhaustion, 18 with heat injury, and 50 with heat stroke. Samples were collected over time and read on a genome-wide array.

At diagnosis, heat injury and heat stroke shared reduced methylation in key pathways. Those pathways govern heat sensing, defense against oxidative damage, and blood vessel tone. Later patterns split apart. The heat injury group shifted toward repair of nerves and stress-hormone control. The heat stroke group kept suppressing metabolic regulators and showed ongoing inflammasome activity, a driver of inflammation. The signatures may point to treatments that aid recovery.
pmc-13528012:
Jiyang Tang and six colleagues describe a 2026 two-step technique for placing a steroid implant behind the eye's choroid layer. The route, called suprachoroidal delivery, targets the back of the eye while sparing the front. The team built an injector from a fine needle and a catheter. First they injected a gel to open the space. Then the implant was placed through that same opening.

The method was used in a 37-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks. She had bleeding and swelling in her left eye from advanced diabetic disease, right after vitrectomy surgery. Scans confirmed the implant sat in the opened space. Vision improved from 4/20 to 20/50 by twelve weeks. Eye pressure stayed stable and the retinal cysts cleared. The authors call the approach feasible, pending larger studies.
pmc-13528112:
Aurèle Nicolet, Laurent Suppan, and Loric Stuby test whether ambulance crews can gather a new heart signal before hospital in a 2026 pilot study. The signal, called a cardiac electrical biomarker, is read from a standard twelve-lead ECG. It aims to flag heart muscle starved of blood. Data came from an ambulance service near Biel, Switzerland, in 2023. The service covers about 120,000 people.

Seventy candidate patients were found, and sixty qualified. Enrollment averaged about 7.7 patients a month. That pace could feed a bigger study. Practical snags included patchy telemetry links, workflow pressure, and thin documentation. Success rates for capturing the signal could not be pinned down, since failed tries were not always logged. The authors say the next study must record every attempt, success or not.
pmc-13532612:
Daisy Maharjan and colleagues study in 2026 anal cancer screening with a test that names high-risk HPV types in detail. Anal cancer is rising in women, people with weak immune systems, and men who have sex with men. The single-centre study enrolled 117 high-risk people from May 2024 to May 2025.

Cell tests were abnormal in 41 percent of cases, and valid HPV results came from 104 people. Most positive results were types other than 16 and 18, while type 16 linked more with abnormal cells. Twelve people had biopsies, so the authors treat the links as early clues, not proof.
pmc-13536612:
Leeza Mujahid and colleagues test in 2026 whether leaf sprays of salicylic acid and GABA protect barley from chromium poisoning. Chromium in soil cuts growth and yield, and spray aids are cheap to apply. Pots compared two barley types with and without chromium stress and spray mixes.

Chromium raised harmful peroxide and cut leaf water, green pigment, and nutrient uptake in both types. Spraying both aids together cut chromium build-up, restored water and pigment, and lifted growth and yield the most. One barley type coped better overall, suggesting spray plus variety choice as a paired defence.
pmc-13536812:
Qingqi Zhang and colleagues review contact zones between two cell structures and their role in innate immunity in a 2026 synthesis. The zones link the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, acting as hubs for calcium balance, fat handling, energy control, and cleanup of damaged parts. The review gathers evidence on how those jobs steer first-line immune defenses and what happens when the zones break down.

Healthy zones help tune inflammation alarms and antiviral signaling, while faulty zones leak mitochondrial material that keeps alarms switched on. Immune activation can in turn damage the zones, creating a self-feeding cycle tied to autoimmune disease. The authors highlight control points within the zones as possible drug targets for calming overactive innate immunity without shutting defense down entirely.
pmc-13539712:
Murat Polat and colleagues compare body shape indices against menopausal symptom burden in a 2026 clinic study. Body mass index misses central fat placement, so a roundness index and a shape index built to reflect belly fat were tested alongside it. Among 638 women aged 44 to 56 years, half transitioning and half postmenopausal, symptom burden was scored with a menopause quality of life scale and activity was surveyed.

All three indices rose with symptom burden, with the shape index correlating most strongly, then roundness, then body mass. Links survived adjustment for age, smoking, chronic disease, and activity. Women with obesity scored worst on every subscale, while overweight women oddly scored below normal-weight peers. The authors say central fat indices add clinical information beyond body mass.
pmc-13539912:
Huang and co-authors remove a metabolic gene to see whether its absence worsens diabetic kidney damage. Their 2026 paper uses CRISPR editing to knock out Fndc5, a gene tied to glucose control and mitochondrial health, in mice, then induces diabetes with a high-fat diet plus streptozotocin. Kidneys and metabolic tissues were examined at fifteen weeks alongside weekly blood and urine checks.

Surprisingly, knockout mice carried a slightly milder sugar burden than normal diabetic mice, yet their urine protein, a damage marker, matched. Their kidney filters fared worse: more expansion of the filtering tuft's core, thicker basement membranes, and more flattened podocyte feet. Their mitochondria were more swollen with more disrupted internal folds, alongside more oxidative damage and fragmented DNA. Genes driving mitochondrial splitting rose while a fusion gene and energy-production components fell. The authors conclude FNDC5 loss accelerates mitochondrial breakdown in diabetic kidneys.
pmc-13540012:
Zhichun Liu and six colleagues follow, in a 2026 cohort study, whether childhood trauma predicts how well teenagers with major depression respond to treatment over half a year. Trauma is already known to raise the risk of developing depression in adolescence.

One hundred fifty young patients completed questionnaires on early abuse and neglect plus scales for depression, sleep, and suicidal thinking. Emotional neglect and physical neglect each affected roughly six in ten participants, and emotional abuse about half. Young people with trauma histories, above all emotional abuse or neglect, had lower odds of a good response at twenty-six weeks. The authors press for routine screening and support for exposed teenagers.
pmc-13540812:
Holy Brown and seven colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, psychoactive drug use among students at colleges and universities in Rivers State, Nigeria, with attention to study habits and grades. Recruitment through multistage sampling reached 1,707 students between August 2024 and February 2025.

About eight percent reported drug use, led by alcohol and marijuana, most often for stress relief or recreation. Men, undergraduates, and students with more money in hand had higher odds of use. Users reported more trouble concentrating, sleeping in lectures, missing classes and assessments, and failing courses. Average grade scores, surprisingly, did not differ significantly between users and non-users.
pmc-13540912:
Yufang Sun and colleagues track root bacteria in a 2026 field study. The plant is a desert grass, Leymus racemosus. It grows in the Kalamaili Nature Reserve in Xinjiang, China. The team asked how its root-zone bacteria change across its life. They also asked how the shifts line up with nutrient flows.

Soil came from thirty plots at three growth stages. The stages were seedling, flowering, and maturity. One genus, Arthrobacter, stayed central at every stage. It tracked stable nitrogen in the soil. Bacillus surged at flowering, when demand peaks. At maturity, the microbe network grew more cooperative. Plant demand fell then, and nutrients built up in the soil.
pmc-13542112:
Yasaman Jamshidi-Naeini leads a 2026 audit of whether nutrition research on potatoes and colorectal cancer can be reproduced and verified by outsiders. Trust in nutrition science runs low, and this literature serves as a test case for a new appraisal process.

Eighteen studies were gathered and graded with four quality tools. None shared data publicly, and the team obtained data for only two studies after asking authors directly. Results could be fully reproduced and verified for just one study. Most studies carried a high risk of bias with weak reporting and shaky methods. The authors call for routine data sharing and stronger rigour across nutrition research.
pmc-13542212:
P Layton and colleagues develop a dating tool in 2026. The tool dates leather book bindings without harming them. It reads chemical decay with reflected infrared light. Medieval manuscripts stay intact under this method. Expert dating by handwriting is slow and scarce. A fast scientific complement would help libraries.

The team worked with codicologists and conservators. They linked age-related chemical changes to a decay clock. External reflectance spectroscopy reads that clock. The method is non-invasive and quick to interpret. Its estimated uncertainty is about sixty-six years. Such a tool could date large collections at scale. It could also reveal the skills of historical binders.
pmc-13543612:
Yanhong Shen and colleagues published a 2026 survey study of what protects Chinese college students against suicide risk, centred on social-emotional competence, the skill set for handling feelings and relationships. More than twenty-four thousand students at one university completed scales for competence, depression, self-esteem, and suicidal behaviour. The analysis tested whether competence lowers risk through depression, and whether self-esteem changes any of those links.

Competence was tied to lower suicide risk both directly and indirectly, because more competent students were less depressed, and depression raised risk. Self-esteem moderated every path in the model. Curiously, the competence-to-depression and depression-to-risk links looked weaker at high self-esteem in the detailed slope checks, even as self-esteem strengthened competence's direct benefit. Building emotional skills and self-worth together, the authors argue, is the safer prevention strategy.
pmc-13545612:
Tian and colleagues built in 2026 a machine learning model that tells lung adenocarcinoma subtypes apart before surgery using CT scans. Subtype guides personal treatment, but standard imaging reads it poorly. The team gathered 3,038 patients from four hospitals, split into training, test, and checking sets. Radiologists outlined tumors, and the model blended clinical details, image texture measures from the tumor and its rim, and deep learning features.

Tian's fused model beat every single-source model, with discrimination scores that held up from the training set to the separate checking set. It separated the lepidic subtype, the slowest-growing pattern, most reliably, while middle and fast patterns were harder. Explanation tools showed which features drove each call, and checks of calibration and clinical benefit supported real-world use. The authors present the model as an aid for planning care before an operation.
pmc-13546712:
Oscar David Aguilar-Vega and co-authors examined in 2026 how a pre-calving diet designed to prevent metabolic disease changes the chemistry of colostrum and milk in first-time Holstein mothers. Eight cows were split between a plain diet and the same diet plus anionic salts for the three weeks before calving. Their first milk and later milk were profiled with a chemical separation technique.

Thirty-four compounds were found in colostrum and 31 in milk. Treated cows tended to show less of some fatty compounds and more of a few others, yet no single compound differed with statistical confidence, and the predictive models were weak. With only four cows per group, the authors frame the shifts as exploratory and call for larger studies.
pmc-13547412:
Shiqi Sun and colleagues tested in 2026 an extract of kudzu root, Pueraria lobata, against diabetic kidney disease in rats, focusing on an inflammatory alarm complex called the NLRP3 inflammasome. Sixty rats were divided among healthy controls, untreated diabetic animals, extract-treated animals, and groups where the alarm was deliberately switched on, with or without the extract. Kidney function, oxidative stress, and tissue damage were measured after chemically induced diabetes.

The extract restored much of the lost body weight, roughly halved two waste markers in blood, and cut oxidative damage while boosting antioxidant defenses. It also lowered the alarm complex's components sharply at gene and protein level. Forcing the alarm on blunted these gains, supporting the proposed mechanism. The authors offer the work as validation for a traditional remedy.
pmc-13548612:
Steffimol Rose Chacko Kaitholil and colleagues read blood gene activity in twenty lambs fed rising amounts of microalgae oil, in a 2026 study linking diet to methane output. Livestock methane is a climate target, and algae supplements had earlier promised cuts. The team sequenced RNA from blood to find host responses tied to the oil dose and to each animal's own emission level, which varied widely between individuals.

Measured methane output did not fall significantly as oil intake rose. Blood signals still shifted: sixty-four genes changed with oil dose, clustering in fat metabolism and steroid building pathways that may benefit the animals' metabolism. Seven other genes tracked with higher methane production and pointed to nucleotide metabolism and immune activity. The two gene sets never overlapped, suggesting diet responses and emission differences run on separate host tracks.
pmc-13548712:
Ziyan Zhang and colleagues run a small double-blind trial of cord blood cell infusions for young children with autism and immune irregularities, in a 2026 single-center study. Immune inflammation is increasingly suspected in some autism cases, and cord blood mononuclear cells can calm immune activity. Thirty-four children aged three to eight were randomly assigned to four weekly infusions of donor cord blood cells or placebo, on top of their usual rehabilitation, and followed for thirteen weeks.

Children receiving cells improved more on a standard social responsiveness scale, with the clearest gain in social cognition, one of the scale's domains. Other rating scales were also tracked for behavior and daily living skills. No major treatment-related adverse events occurred. The authors describe the results as preliminary evidence of safety and possible benefit, in a carefully selected subgroup of children with autism.
pmc-13550412:
Shiho Murakami and colleagues test a blood protein as the second step in sorting fatty liver patients whose first screening score lands in the gray zone, in a 2026 study. Care pathways for metabolic liver disease start with a cheap index, yet many patients fall in its indeterminate band and need another test before scanning. The candidate, a collagen fragment measured by automated immunoassay, was compared against two rival blood tests using MRI stiffness scans as the referee.

In the building group of 347 patients, the collagen marker sorted about two thirds of gray-zone patients correctly for significant scarring, matching one rival and beating the other. A separate validation group of 126 patients gave similar figures. The authors say performance is numerically on par with the established test, and they call for prospective work on workflow and cost before adoption.
pmc-13550912:
Miguel Alberto Rincón Pinzón, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 map of research on games in teacher training. The field grew as schools took up game-like learning. Yet its path in the age of smart AI tools was unclear. The team merged two large databases for the years 2016 to 2025. They kept 1,223 papers after screening.

Output rose fast from 2020 on. Citation links showed three roots: drive theory, tech uptake models, and game-based learning work. Word clusters centered on games, AI, and digital learning. By 2025 the field had shifted toward smart, adaptive tools. The team turns that shift into plans for schools and future work.
pmc-13551712:
Chengzhi Wang, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study asking whether draining the abdomen helps after surgery for a perforated appendix. Routine drainage is discouraged, yet need may vary with contamination severity. The single-center study covered 278 patients operated between 2021 and 2025, graded by a trauma association scale and compared with statistical weighting to balance groups.

In the most severe grade, drainage did not significantly reduce abscess risk in the reported analysis and was linked to more overall complications in regression modeling. Drained patients also stayed longer in hospital and cost more in the figures given. In milder grades no significant differences appeared, so the authors question routine drainage across severity levels.
pmc-13551812:
Shuo Cao and Tao Zhang published a 2026 case report of endometriosis growing on the omentum, the fatty apron inside the abdomen, in a 45-year-old woman. Such extra-pelvic disease is extremely rare, and her presentation was unusual: heavier, longer periods without the classic pelvic pain, and no prior surgery or pelvic infection. Scans showed bloody fluid in the abdomen, an encapsulated pelvic collection, and multiple omental nodules.

A tumor marker was mildly raised while another stayed normal, and fluid cytology found no cancer cells, leaving the cause unclear before surgery. Pathology after surgery confirmed omental endometriosis. The authors urge considering the diagnosis in premenopausal women with unexplained bloody ascites, and they discuss fertility-sparing surgical management.
pmc-13554112:
Olívia Dózsa-Juhász leads a five-author team studying what shapes how women feel about their bodies in a 2026 survey. Two hundred ninety-one women aged eighteen to forty-five answered online questions. The team measured body appreciation alongside activity, sitting time, sleep quality, body mass, and monthly premenstrual symptoms. Standard questionnaires supplied each score, and the data were weighed together in one model.

Heavier body mass, stronger monthly symptoms, poorer sleep, and longer sitting time each tied to lower body appreciation. Monthly symptoms also tied to worse sleep and to more moderate activity at work. Sleep quality showed a similar link with work activity. Fun-time activity showed no clear links at all. The authors urge joined-up support covering rest, sitting habits, and menstrual health.
pmc-13554212:
Su Xian leads an eleven-author team sorting more than one hundred thousand patients into groups by their disease patterns in a 2026 study. Health records hold rich but messy data on diagnoses, drugs, and tests. Without any labels, the team clustered 100,272 patients from a large research network. Seventy groups emerged, each with its own mix of conditions, shaped strongly by age and sex.

When diseases first appeared predicted a person's age with surprising accuracy, and tied to death risk too. Gene effects showed early, then faded as aging took over. Several groups carried heavy disease loads and signs of aging before their time. A second group of patients confirmed those high-risk clusters, giving doctors leads for targeted care.
pmc-13558512:
Bernadett B Huszti and thirteen colleagues published this 2026 study proposing a cardiovascular risk tool for dermatologists. The tool is the cumulative duration of severe psoriasis, the total months a patient has spent with severe skin symptoms. Severe psoriasis is tied to heart disease, but linking its duration to coronary damage was unproven. Ninety-eight symptom-free patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis underwent heart CT calcium scoring and vessel ultrasound, and were compared with 248 controls.

Psoriasis patients carried more coronary calcium than controls. A severe duration of 60.5 months emerged as the threshold: patients above it had higher calcium scores, about 215 against 58, plus more severe coronary disease on CT grading than those below it. Peripheral artery measures trended the same way without reaching significance. Because the duration can be captured with a questionnaire in a skin clinic, the authors offer it as an early warning that flags patients for cardiovascular workup.
pmc-13559112:
Ying Meng and three colleagues surveyed parents whose children underwent emergency gastric lavage, a stomach washout used after poisoning, and measured how much conflict parents felt while deciding. The 2026 cross-sectional study drew 266 parents from one tertiary children's hospital between January 2025 and February 2026. A purpose-built 20-item scale captured their uncertainty and pressure.

Conflict ran high: over nine in ten parents passed the threshold for significant decisional conflict. Regression pointed to five factors tied to worse scores, among them being unmarried, divorced, or widowed, and having less schooling. Parents without a medical background, with younger children, or with lower family income also struggled more. The uncertainty and pressure subscale scored highest of all dimensions. The authors recommend tiered support, such as plain-language illustrated aids and dedicated companions for parents facing the decision alone.
pmc-13559412:
Xuefen Chen and Chen Gong review thirteen patients who carried two lung diseases at once: lung cancer and nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease. Their 2026 retrospective case series spans January 2020 to January 2025 at a single institution. Sequencing of samples identified which mycobacterial species each patient harbored.

Adenocarcinoma was the commonest cancer type, found in seven of the thirteen patients. Mycobacterium avium complex and Mycobacterium abscessus led the infections. Eleven patients received anti-mycobacterial therapy, while two were watched after their symptoms eased under cancer treatment alone. Tailored ordering of the two treatments let most patients finish their cancer therapy. Two early-stage patients had surgery delayed until after a short course of infection treatment. Three patients had died by last follow-up, at a mean of about nineteen months. The authors note that infection control did not visibly worsen during combined care.
pmc-13559812:
Shizhen Qing and three colleagues describe a 33-year-old man with aneurysms-osteoarthritis syndrome, a hereditary connective tissue disorder now classed as Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 3. Their 2026 case report centers on a newly identified SMAD3 mutation behind his disease. He arrived with abdominal pain, a severely sunken chest, and aneurysms scattered through several arteries.

Genetic testing and vascular imaging together confirmed the diagnosis. Rather than tackling every lesion at once, the surgeons staged the work. Stage one embolized and ligated a pseudoaneurysm on the superior mesenteric artery. Stage two placed an endovascular stent graft across a dissecting aneurysm of the celiac artery. The authors use the case to argue for staged intervention when aneurysms crowd multiple territories. They also stress early detection in this syndrome, where the aneurysm burden tends to run higher than in related disorders.
pmc-13560112:
Fangfang Tian and three colleagues build prognostic models for natural killer/T-cell lymphoma from clinical data and PET/CT imaging. Their 2026 retrospective study analyzed 114 patients scanned before treatment. Variables ranged from age and albumin to Epstein-Barr virus status and a radiomics score distilled from scan texture. Three selection methods competed to choose the predictors.

Best subset regression beat the other two approaches. Its survival model combined albumin, viral status, the scan's maximum uptake value, a lumbar-to-liver uptake ratio, and the radiomics score, reaching a three-year area under the curve of 0.883 in the reported results. A separate progression model used age, viral status, and the Ki67 growth marker. Bootstrap checks supported the models internally. The authors offer the combined clinical-radiomic tool for sorting patients by risk and tailoring treatment plans.
pmc-13562212:
Hoang-Thi Buis and colleagues test whether a pain-signal monitor guiding opioid dosing beats standard bedside judgment during keyhole endometriosis surgery. Their 2026 randomized, single-blinded trial assigns 111 women not yet in menopause to monitor-guided dosing or usual care checks, both inside the same layered pain plan. Women with endometriosis face stronger after-surgery pain from sensitized pain pathways.

Total opioid use did not differ clearly between the groups for either fentanyl or remifentanil in the adjusted comparison. Pain scores matched at every postoperative checkpoint, and recovery room stays matched too. Surgery length, not group, tracked both opioid use and recovery time. Monitor readings themselves showed no association with drug use or pain. Higher pre-surgery pain ratings on a set scale did predict worse late recovery pain. The authors conclude the device added nothing over good standard care here.
pmc-13562512:
Merlijn van Breugel and six colleagues teach a deep learning model to read the fine pixel patterns of the material between cells in tissue slides. Most image tools target cells or whole structures, leaving the extracellular matrix, the woven scaffold of connective tissue, largely ignored. Human eyes can barely tell two airway wall layers apart in standard pink-and-purple stained slides. The 2026 method steers the model toward those cell-free zones and blanks out cells at random so they cannot mislead it.

Trained this way, the model separated the two airway layers with a test score of 0.84 on the standard curve measure. The team then applied the approach to lung tissue from people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease as a proof of principle. Differences across patients became measurable quantities. The authors offer the pipeline as a reusable way to study tissue scaffolds that routine microscopy overlooks.
pmc-13563812:
Ge Sun and six colleagues infuse a low dose of esketamine during gynaecological surgery and measure whether patients wake up less exhausted. Postoperative fatigue delays recovery and no proven counter exists. Their 2026 trial was single-centre, double-blind, and placebo-controlled: women having elective laparoscopic surgery were randomised to an esketamine drip during the operation or to saline. Fatigue on the first day after surgery, scored on the Chalder scale, was the main outcome, with recovery quality, pain, drug use, and safety events tracked.

Fatigue struck 23.3 percent of the esketamine group against 40.0 percent of controls, a difference on the edge of significance at P = 0.050, firmer in the follow-up sensitivity analysis. Fatigue scores, recovery quality, and pain ran better on the first and third days, and the group needed less opioid and less blood-pressure support. Harm events matched. The authors call the drug promising for smoother recoveries.
pmc-13563912:
Manar M. Alshammari and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis asking whether metformin, added to standard rheumatoid arthritis drugs, improves disease control. Four randomized trials with 350 participants were found through searches of four databases up to the end of 2025, and trial quality was checked with a standard risk-of-bias tool.

After three months, patients receiving metformin showed lower inflammation scores, lower disease activity scores, and less disability than comparison groups in the pooled results. Because only four small trials were available, the findings read as promising rather than settled. Clinicians get a compact summary of what the limited trial evidence can and cannot support.
pmc-13569512:
Hehe Bai, Miao Guo, Nanbo Zheng, and Xiaojing Nie build, in a 2026 study, a prediction chart for low blood potassium caused by a widely used hospital antibiotic combination, piperacillin with tazobactam. Records of 643 treated adults from 2021 to 2025 were used to find risk factors, and the chart was checked in separate patient groups.

About nineteen percent developed low potassium, usually mild, typically around day five. Older age, lower body mass, intensive care admission, higher daily dose, and lower starting potassium each raised risk. The five-item chart separated high- and low-risk patients well in every test group. Ward teams could use it to order earlier potassium checks for patients most likely to dip.
pmc-13572412:
Wan Lin, with seven colleagues, ran a 2026 study of why lung adenocarcinoma stops responding to the drug cisplatin. This lung cancer type kills more people than any other cancer. The work centres on a gene switch called KLF15 and on the cell powerhouses, the mitochondria, that it helps build.

Resistant cancer cells held low KLF15, fewer powerhouses, and lower levels of harmful oxygen byproducts. Restoring KLF15 made cells in dishes and tumours in mice respond to the drug again. KLF15 switched on a partner gene, PGC1α, which drives powerhouse growth. Removing that partner undid the gain and brought resistance back. Cell groups with few powerhouses or low KLF15 were resistant from the start. The pair marks a fresh target for beating drug failure.
pmc-13575212:
Jian Huang and three colleagues present a method for finding impact forces on composite panels using a single sensor, in a 2026 paper. Impacts can damage aircraft-style structures invisibly, yet real working conditions bury the impact signal in noise and other loads. Their sensor is a fibre Bragg grating, a fibre-optic strain gauge.

The method first splits the noisy strain signal into clean vibration modes. A fingerprint drawn from those modes is matched against a precomputed map to locate the impact on a grid. A sparse calculation then rebuilds the force history over time. Tests on a composite plate shaped like a simplified airfoil located impacts at over 90 percent success, even with added harmonic and white noise. Force rebuilds were also accurate.
pmc-13576212:
Anqi Liu leads a 2026 study presenting ResSAT, a model that predicts gene activity maps of tissue from ordinary stained microscope images. Spatial transcriptomics measures which genes are active at each spot in a tissue slice, yet the process is slow and costly. Standard H&E stained images are cheap and routine, and tissue structure in them tracks gene patterns.

Benchmark tests on ten public Visium datasets put it ahead of rival methods. The predicted maps kept the spatial patterns that matter for biology, according to the authors. They present the model as a cheaper, faster route to many gene activity profiles.
pmc-13576412:
Terrell and colleagues ran a community-engaged trial in 2026 testing whether a weight-loss drug can lower body stores of persistent organic pollutants. The community studied was heavily exposed to a flame retardant called PBB. One hundred participants were randomised, blinded, to the fat-blocking drug orlistat or placebo for six months, with blood tests at set points.

Eighty-nine participants finished the study, a high retention the authors credit to community dedication. The orlistat group lost about two kilograms more than the placebo group on average. Despite that extra weight loss, blood levels of PBB and other pollutants did not differ between groups or fall over the six months. The authors conclude that mobilising fat with orlistat did not translate into lower pollutant burden in this timeframe.
pmc-13578312:
Nasir Assad and colleagues grow tiny manganese oxide particles with help from a plant extract, in a 2026 clean water study. Factory dyes stain waste water and resist normal treatment. Juice from a horsetail plant both formed the particles and kept them stable, replacing harsher chemicals. Tests confirmed round particles a few dozen nanometers wide with a steady surface charge.

Under sunlight the particles broke down two dyes and one toxic compound at close to nine tenths removal within about one hundred minutes. The same batch kept working through five reuse rounds with little loss of power. Dose and acidity both shaped the results, with plain neutral water working best. The authors pitch the plant made particles as a cheap, green option for dye laden water.
pmc-13581612:
Lee and colleagues report a 2026 study of how bacteria sense the proteins of phages, the viruses that infect them. The team mapped the family across bacteria and archaea and tested what each branch senses.

The survey found at least 90 distinct STAND families tied to antiviral defense. One unstudied family, Avs7, detects the main shell protein of tailed phages. Three structure images show it forming a butterfly-shaped four-part unit around its target, with a host protein built in as support. Bacterial immunity watches the whole phage toolkit, not just one part.
pmc-13584112:
Pasold and colleagues release in 2026 a satellite image dataset for spotting energy, transport, and storage infrastructure across Germany. Existing remote sensing benchmarks rarely capture how these structures appear together in real scenes.

The collection holds 10,000 true-color image chips from the Sentinel-2 satellite, each showing a square of land just over five hundred meters across. Every chip is labeled independently for substations, power plants, storage tanks, railway lines, and major roads. Several labels can therefore apply at once.
